title: Exploring Various Datasets of Bay Area and Finding Useful Insights for Policymakers
text:
2 Introduction

2.1 Rationale for CRS
According to USGS Website, all maps in USA uses some projection in the State Plane Coordinate System (United States Geological Survey, 2023). It is plane coordinate system in which each state is divided up to six zones, depending on geometry of the state (United States Geological Survey, 2023). These zones use a Mercator or Lambert conic projection which preserves the shape and scale over smaller areas like zcta’s or tracts. 
By looking into Map of USA State Plane Zones NAD83 in ArcGIS website (ArcGIS Hub, 2020), we can identify that Bay Area is in California Zone 3. Therefore, we are going to use EPSG: 2227 – NAD 83 California zone 3 (ftUS).  


2.2 Description of Data
Airbnb Listings Data of San Francisco, Oakland and San Mateo are extracted from Inside Airbnb Website. Chosen Variables from the list of socio-economic metrics of the ACS are Median Household Income (B19013_001E) and No. Of People aged 18-64 who has computer and Broadband Internet Subscription (B28005_011E). We also use Bay Area Zip Code Areas.
For additional Datasets, we are going to use No. of Vehicles (light-duty) 2020 per zip code and Average Electricity Utility Rate 2020 (Commerical Rate) per zip code, both investors owned and non-investor owned utilities. 
Note: API Key can be obtained by signing up at http://api.census.gov/data/key_signup.html for Census Data. We, then use tidycensus package to get ACS data from US Census Bureau.


Code for setting up API Key
census_api_key(J_API_KEY , install = TRUE, overwrite = TRUE) # Please replace 'J_API_KEY' with API Key obtained from census bureau
# Below message is differently coded output for checking system environment variable(CENSUS_API_KEY), not the output of above line


[1] “API key to get Census data is successfully set up.”


2.3 Data Extraction and Pre-Processing
We are making two API calls to retrieve Median Household Income (B19013_001E) and the No. of people aged 18-64 who have a computer and Broadband Internet Subscription (B28005_011E) from ACS 2016-2020 separately. This approach is more efficient and straight-forward than making a single API call with two variables. The latter can results in a spatial or non-spatial file with a long-format attribute table, which, in turn, needs to be converted into a wide-format table for analysis.
We are extracting values of two variables for entire US. Then Later, we filter out zip codes specific to Bay Area. This is because, some califorina zcta’s extends into other states, Which results in error while extracting zcta’s related data for specific states (‘zip-Determining which US zipcodes map to more than one state or more than one city?-Geographic Information Systems’, 2021). According to US Census Bureau, All ZCTA’s codes are valid US Zip Codes(United States Census Bureau, 2023).

Spatial Resolution: zcta’s level
Time: 2020



Cleaning and pre-processing Data
median_hh_income <- get_acs(  # get_acs is a function, we are using to get ACS Suvrey data from US Census Bureau
  geography = "zcta",         # we are specifying geography unit for variable we getting, like, ZCTA, Tract, County, State etc.
  variables = "B19013_001E",  # we are geeting MEDIAN HOUSEHOLD INCOME, "B19013_001E" is variable name in ACS
  year = 2020,      # we are getting census data collected from 2016-2020
  geometry = FALSE  # we use geometry of bay area zipcode shapefile from berkeley library, not ACS Data
) %>%
  rename(estimate_MedianHhI = estimate) %>%   # we are renaming retrieved variable(estimate to appropriate name ( estimate_Median_HhI)
  select(GEOID, estimate_MedianHhI)           # we are selecting only GEOID(ZCTA's CODE, also ZIP CODE), estimate Value (ignoring MOE)

# Retrieving Internet Use Variable
internet_use <- get_acs(      # get_acs is a function, we are using to get ACS Suvrey data from US Census Bureau 
  geography = "zcta",         # we are specifying geography unit for variable we getting, like, ZCTA, Tract, County, State etc.
  variables = "B28005_011E",  # we are geeting No.of People aged 18-64, who has computer and Broadband Internet Subscription, "B28005_011E" is variable name in ACS
  year = 2020,                # we are getting census data collected from 2016-2020
  geometry = FALSE            #  we use geometry of bay area zipcode shapefile from berkeley library, not ACS Data
) %>%
  rename(estimate_InternetUse = estimate) %>%  # we are renaming retrieved variable(estimate to appropriate name ( estimate_Internet_Use)
  select(GEOID, estimate_InternetUse)          # we are selecting only GEOID(ZCTA's CODE, also ZIP CODE), estimate Value (ignoring MOE)

us_zip <- left_join(median_hh_income, internet_use, by = "GEOID") # simply join two datasets by GEOID to get Dataset in req format

Two Additional Datasets:
We will be using Commerical Electricity Rates Dataset for Both investor-owned and non-investor owned utilities per ZIP Code.


Code for Data cleaning and Pre-processing of Electricity rates data
non_iou_data_c <- non_iou_data %>%  # Data cleaning process for additional datasets, 
  select(zip, comm_rate) %>%       # we select only zip, commerical rate from non-investor based utilities
  group_by(zip) %>%                # we group them by ZIP
  summarise(
    Avg_Non_IOU_Comm_Rate = mean(comm_rate, na.rm = TRUE)  # Mean of different Non-Investor Based utilities per ZIP
  )
  

iou_data_c <- iou_data %>%
  select(zip, comm_rate) %>%      # we select only zip, commerical rate from Investor based utilities
  group_by(zip) %>%               # we group them by ZIP
  summarise(
    Avg_IOU_Comm_Rate = mean(comm_rate, na.rm = TRUE)  # Mean of different Investor Based utilities per ZIP
  )

electric_u <- non_iou_data_c %>%
  full_join(iou_data_c, by = "zip")%>%   # Join both Investor-owned and Non-Investor utility datasets by zipcode
  mutate(
    Avg_IOU_Comm_Rate = replace_na(Avg_IOU_Comm_Rate, 0),    # replacing any NA values with 0
    Avg_Non_IOU_Comm_Rate = replace_na(Avg_Non_IOU_Comm_Rate, 0 ),  # replacing any NA values with 0
    Combined_Avg_Comm_Rate = (Avg_Non_IOU_Comm_Rate + Avg_IOU_Comm_Rate ) / 2  # using average as statistic for combined Commerical electricity Rate
  )%>%
  select(zip, Combined_Avg_Comm_Rate) %>% rename(ZIP = zip) %>% mutate(ZIP = as.character(ZIP)) # selecting only ZIP and New Statistic, ignoring rest

  select(-Date, -Model.Year, -Fuel, -Make) %>%     # we are only selecting Zip.code, Vehicles and Duty cols, and ignoring rest

title: Exploring Various Datasets of Bay Area and Finding Useful Insights for Policymakers
text:
3 Methodology

3.1 No. of AIRBNB Listings with Mean Price per ZIP Code Areas
Bay Area Airbnb’s Listings, We downloaded have Longitude and Longitude coordinates, So initially, We set CRS of Listings to EPSG: 4326 - WGS84. Then, We perform CRS re-projection into EPSG: 2227 – NAD 83 California zone 3 (ft-US).
We then, perform spatial join for Bay Area ZIP Code Areas and AIRBNB Listings, which results in Overlay Shape-file. This will enable us to understand geographical distribution of AIRBNB Listings and their charactertics over Bay Area ZIP Code Areas.

Code for pre-processing of Shapefiles
listings_bayarea_sf <- listings_bayarea %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude")) %>% # creating point shapefile from coordinates
  st_set_crs(4326)                                  # setting CRS to geodetic system of earth (4326, WGS84) as they are long, lat coords

listings_bayarea_sf_transform <- st_transform(listings_bayarea_sf, crs = 2227)   # Now, Changing CRS to mentioned Project CRS
overlay_listings <- st_join(bayarea_zipcodes, listings_bayarea_sf_transform)     # Performing Spatial Join to create overlay Shapefile of Airbnb Listings and Bay area ZIP shapefile

st_crs(overlay_listings) == st_crs(listings_bayarea_sf_transform)                # Verifying CRS of New shapefile

[1] TRUE
We need to plot No. of Airbnb’s and their mean price per zipcode in Bay Area. To find out necessary variables, we group by Zip Code and count no. of non-NA price rows of listings in each zip code and use function(mean) to find mean price of those listings.

listings_bayarea_zip <- overlay_listings  %>%  # creating new dataframe with no.of Airbnb's per ZIP and Mean Price per ZIP
  group_by(ZIP) %>%                     # group by ZIP
  summarise(
    count_airbnb = sum(!is.na(price)),      # counting non-NA price rows for listings
    mean_price = mean(price, na.rm = TRUE)  # calculate mean, ignoring NAs
  )%>%
  filter(count_airbnb != 0) 


listings_bayarea_zip1 <- listings_bayarea_zip %>%
  select(count_airbnb, everything())  # Changing the order of attributes for interactive map

listings_bayarea_zip2 <- listings_bayarea_zip %>%
  select(mean_price, everything())%>% # Changing the order of attributes for interactive map
  mutate(mean_price = round(mean_price, 1))  # rounding mean price to one decimal place.

Based on standard statistics for both Count and Mean Price variables of AIRBNB’s per zip code, Minimum value of count variable is 1 and first quartile is 71, so first class is divided accordingly. Median of count variable is 172 and standard deviation is 162.5, so, second and third class is divided as defined. Finally to identify outliers, As Third quartile is 257, standard deviation is 162.5 and Maximum Value is 794, last class has 500 as its lower boundary.
Minimum value of Mean Price variable is 71 and first quartile is 154, so first class is divided accordingly. Median of Mean Price is 204 and standard deviation is 297.9, so, second and third class is divided as defined. Finally to identify outliers, As Third quartile is 282.6, standard deviation is 297.9 and Maximum Value is 1818, last two classes have been divided 1000 and 1800 as their lower boundaries respectively.
New forms of spatial data like Airbnb data can offer latest snaphots of how people are are using spaces and leads to real-time insights. There will generally have high Heteroskedasticity and also provide detailed data at granular level such as individual Airbnbs. On other hand, New form of spatial data like Airbnb data never represent all segments of markets. Collection of Data can introduce measurement errors due to less standard methodologies.
Airbnb data is dynamic and reflects real-time changes in market, like social media or GPS data. Like social Media or GPS data, Airbnb data is user-generated. This is quite different from census-type of data.

Code for Maps of Count and Price of AIRBNBs per ZIP
tmap_mode("plot")   # Interactive mode
map1.11 <- tm_shape(listings_bayarea_zip1) +  # listings_bayarea_zip1 is just re-arrangement of listings_bayareaa_zip with first column as count_airbnb
  tm_fill( "count_airbnb",style="fixed", title = "No. of Airbnb's per ZIP", alpha = 1, breaks=c( 1, 72, 172, 359, 500, Inf), palette = "-viridis")+ 
  tm_borders()+
  tm_text("ZIP", size = 0.3)+
  tm_view(set.view = c(center_lon, center_lat, zoom_level))

map1.12 <- tm_shape(listings_bayarea_zip2) +  # listings_bayarea_zip2 is just re-arrangement of listings_bayareaa_zip with first column as Mean Price
  tm_fill( "mean_price",style="fixed", title = "Mean Price of Airbnb per ZIP", alpha = 1, breaks=c( 74, 155, 287, 501,1000, 1800, Inf), palette = "-viridis")+
  tm_borders()+
  tm_text("ZIP", size = 0.3)+
  tm_view(set.view = c(center_lon, center_lat, zoom_level))















3.2 Median Household Income and No.of People aged 18-64 who has Computer and Internet Subscription per ZIP Code Areas
We filter Median Household Income and Internet Use Variable for Bay Area Zip Codes. Then we join ACS Dataset to Bay Area ZIP Code Areas shapefile. As an additional step, we remove all ZIP codes where Internet Use variable is missing.


Code for Cleaning Attribute information in Shapefile
bay_area_zipcodes <- bayarea_zipcodes$ZIP   # Creating new var with Bayarea ZIP codes

bayarea_zip_vars_data <- us_zip %>%        # Filtering ACS Data with Two variables, by Bay Area ZIP codes
  filter(GEOID %in% bay_area_zipcodes)%>%  # Using Bay Area ZIP codes variable, created above
  rename(ZIP = GEOID)                     # renaming GEOID with ZIP

bayarea_zip_vars <- bayarea_zipcodes %>% left_join(bayarea_zip_vars_data, by = "ZIP") %>% filter(!(is.na(estimate_InternetUse))) # Joining two vars from ACS with bayarea_zipcodes shapefile which is downloaded from berkeley library and also removing NA values of Internet Use variable.

Based on standard statistics for both variables of ACS per zip code, Range and Standard Deviation for both variables are large, We use Fisher-Jenks Data Classification method, because of highly-skewed data.
Bay Area ZIP Code Areas is Mixed-Use Type of Neighborhood. Most of neighborhoods have medium Household Incomes and High Internet Subscriptions. Socio-Economic Indicators like Median Household Income and Internet Use helps in delineating this typology of Neighborhood. San Francisco and Oakland have more-affulent neighborhoods due to High Internet Usage and medium Household Income, whereas San Mateo have High Household Income Neighborhoods and Medium Internet Usage.
Based on the given Classification, Reasonable Hypothesis will be that AIRBNB would cluster in San Francisco and Oakland, due to High Internet Usage and Medium Household Income (Middle to High-Class Residential Areas). AIRBNB listings would also cluster in Areas with low commercial electricity rate and High No.of Vehicles.

3.3 MAP 3: Average AIRBNB Price and Internet Use Variable per ZIP Code
We compare the Average Price of Airbnb Listings per ZIP code with the estimated Internet Usage to observe any spatial relationships.
Based on standard statistics for Internet Usage (People) per zip code, we use Fisher-Jenks Data Classification method because of highly-skewed data.
Apparently in San Francisco, ZIP Code areas with High Internet Usage have High AIRBNB Listings. ZIP Code Areas with 5,500 people or more using internet, have high price for AIRBNB Listings.


Code for Maps of Avg Price and Internet Use per ZIP
tmap_mode("plot")

# Find the intersection of ZIP codes present in both datasets
common_zips <- intersect(listings_bayarea_zip2$ZIP, bayarea_zip_vars$ZIP)

# Filter both datasets to only include the common ZIP codes
map3.1_data <- listings_bayarea_zip2 %>% filter(ZIP %in% common_zips)
map3.2_data <- bayarea_zip_vars %>% filter(ZIP %in% common_zips)

map3.1 <- tm_shape(map3.1_data) +
  tm_fill("mean_price", style="fixed", title = "Mean Price of Airbnb per ZIP", alpha = 1, breaks=c(74, 155, 287, 501, 1000, 1800, Inf), palette = "-viridis") +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_layout(legend.outside = TRUE, legend.outside.position = "bottom")

map3.2 <- tm_shape(map3.2_data) +
  tm_fill(col = "estimate_InternetUse", alpha = 1, palette = "YlGn", n = 5, style = "fisher", title = "Broadband Internet Connection (People)") +
  tm_borders(lwd = 0.3) +
  tm_layout(legend.outside = TRUE, legend.outside.position = "bottom")

tmap_arrange(map3.1, map3.2, ncol = 2)











3.4 MAP 4: Spatial Auto-Correlation
Calculating list of neighbors(Neighborhoods) and Queen-based Spatial Weights Matrix for Bay Area ZIP Code areas which have Median Household Income:


Code for calculating spatial weights martrix for ZIP codes which have Median Household Income
nb_q1 <- poly2nb(bayarea_zip_vars1, queen = TRUE) # shapefile used, have no NA values of Median Household Income variable

w_queen1 <- nb2listw(nb_q1, style = "B", zero.policy=TRUE) # queen-contiguity based Weights for list of neighbors for all observations 
isolates1 <- which(w_queen1$neighbours == "0")
bayarea_zip_vars1_NoZero <- bayarea_zip_vars1[-c(isolates1),] # shapefile where there are no observation with zero neighbours based on queen-contiguity


Calculating list of neighbors(Neighborhoods) and Queen-based Spatial Weights Matrix for Bay Area ZIP Code areas which have Internet Usage:


Code for calculating spatial weights martrix for ZIP codes which have Internet Use
nb_q2 <- poly2nb(bayarea_zip_vars, queen = TRUE) # shapefile used, have no NA values of Broadband Internet Use

w_queen2 <- nb2listw(nb_q2, style = "B", zero.policy=TRUE)
isolates2 <- which(w_queen2$neighbours == "0")

bayarea_zip_vars_NoZero <- bayarea_zip_vars[-c(isolates2),] # shapefile where there are no observation with zero neighbours based on queen-contiguity



3.4.1 Global Spatial Auto-Correlation:
Calculating list of neighbors(Neighborhoods) and Queen-based Standardized Spatial Weights Matrix for Bay Area ZIP Code areas which have Median Household Income or/and Internet Usage(People) :


Code for calculating spatial weights martrix for ZIP codes which have Median Household Income or Internet Use
nb_q1 <- poly2nb(bayarea_zip_vars1_NoZero, queen = TRUE) # Constructing neighbours list from filtering observations which have no zero neighbours and no NA values of Median Household Income
w_queen_std1 <- nb2listw(nb_q1, style = "W") # creating spatial weights matrix using queen contiguity and row-standardardised weights

nb_q2 <- poly2nb(bayarea_zip_vars_NoZero, queen = TRUE) # Constructing neighbours list from filtering out observations which have zero neighbours and no NA values of Broadband Internet Use
w_queen_std2 <- nb2listw(nb_q2, style = "W") # creating spatial weights matrix using queen contiguity and row-standardardised weights


Calculating Spatial Lag for Median Household Income and Internet Usage(People):


Code for calculating spatial lag for ZIP codes
bayarea_zip_vars1_NoZero$sl_MedianHhI <- lag.listw(w_queen_std1, bayarea_zip_vars1_NoZero$estimate_MedianHhI) # calculating spatial lag for Medain Household Income Variable in Bay Area 

bayarea_zip_vars_NoZero$sl_InternetUse <-  lag.listw(w_queen_std2, bayarea_zip_vars_NoZero$estimate_InternetUse) # calculating spatial lag for Internet Use Variable in Bay Area 


Moran I’s for Median Household Income in Bay Area ZIP Code Areas:


Code for calculating Moran’s I statitstic for Median Household Income
set.seed(42)
moran.mc(bayarea_zip_vars1_NoZero$estimate_MedianHhI, w_queen_std1, nsim=1000, alternative="greater") # Moran's I statistic for Median Household Income Variable in Bay Area



    Monte-Carlo simulation of Moran I

data:  bayarea_zip_vars1_NoZero$estimate_MedianHhI 
weights: w_queen_std1  
number of simulations + 1: 1001 

statistic = 0.39557, observed rank = 1001, p-value = 0.000999
alternative hypothesis: greater


Moran I’s for Median Household Income in Bay Area is 0.396 and p-value is 0.000999. So, Observed Spatial Pattern is statistically Significant. P-value means chances of obtaining Moran I’s value greater than original, given random spatial distribution. If it is less than 0.05, We reject Null Hypothesis i.e, observed spatial pattern is due to random chance. Moran I’s is analogous to Chi-Square Statistic. Spatial distribution of Median Household Income is spatially concentrated than random spatial distribution.
Moran I’s for Internet Usage(People) in Bay Area ZIP Code Areas:


Code for calculating Moran’s I statitstic for Internet Use
set.seed(42)
moran.mc(bayarea_zip_vars_NoZero$estimate_InternetUse, w_queen_std2, nsim=1000, alternative="greater") # Moran's I statistic for Interent Use Variable in Bay Area



    Monte-Carlo simulation of Moran I

data:  bayarea_zip_vars_NoZero$estimate_InternetUse 
weights: w_queen_std2  
number of simulations + 1: 1001 

statistic = 0.23313, observed rank = 1001, p-value = 0.000999
alternative hypothesis: greater


Moran I’s for Internet Usage (People) in Bay Area is 0.23313 and p-value is 0.000999. So, Observed Spatial Pattern is statistically Significant. Spatial distribution of Internet Usage (People) is mild spatially concentrated than random spatial distribution.

Calculating LISAs for Bay Area ZIP COde Areas for both Median Household Income and Internet Usage(People):

1.1 Analysis of Spatial Datasets through APIs
In the rapidly evolving field of Geoinforamtics to address complex scientific questions, the ability to access, analyze, and inference from spatial datasets stands as a cornerstone of research and development. Scientists around the world, trying to gain deeper understanding of many complex geographical phenomena, the dependence on accurate, latest and real-time spatial data has never been more critical. This Assignment uses richness of APIs (Application Programming Interfaces) to access different spatial datasets, offering opportunity to explore satellites/ objects patterns over geographic area.
APIs work as gatekeepers for programmatically retrieving data from remote servers, enabling researchers to tap into a vast amount of spatial data resources maintained by governments, non-profits, and private organizations. There are many types of APIs, but we are going to use RESTful API which is an type of API that relies on HTTP protocol to retrieve information from remote databases. Not all APIs which use HTTP protocol are RESTful.
RESTful APIs means APIs which adheres to principles and constraints of REST, stands for Representational State Transfer, starting with Null style, which are client-server architecture, statelessness, cacheability, uniform interface, layered system and Code-On-Demand(optional) (Fielding, 2000). Terms ‘REST APIs’ and ‘RESTful APIs’ are often used interchangeably in context of web services, saying an APIs is RESTful typically implies strict compliance with REST principles or to REST Architectural Constraints. By leveraging API technology,
Finally, This assignment aims to analyze active satellites overhead for each country, same methodology can be implemented to track space objects overhead. It also outlines methodology used in accessing and utilizing various spatial datasets for analysis through APIs.

3.1 Rationale for CRS
As this assignment covered, satellites overhead per country, which involves calculating coordinates of satellites i.e. Latitude and Longitude. We are going to use EPSG:4326-WGS84 as CRS for our spatial analyses, also for its compatibility with global positioning systems (GPS) and web mapping services. WGS84 is cordinate reference system for GPS satellites (GISGeography, 2023).

title: Real-Time Orbital Tracking and Country-Level Satellite Density Analysis
text:
4.1 Map Projection Problem
The issue of map projections where geography of countries extending into the International Date Line presents a challenge in plotting latitude and longitude on 2D maps, particularly for areas like east russia near the 180-degree meridian. This problem arises due to the representation of the Earth’s surface on a two-dimensional plane which requires distortions, and the International Date Line acts as a discontinuity for spatial datasets. As a result, geographical features that span across this meridian may appear fragmented or inaccurately placed on either side of the map. Below code rectifies this issue and adds geometry back to Geo dataframe(countries_gdf).


Code
def shift_geom(geometry, offset):
    """
    For coordinates with longitude < 0, increase by 2 * offset.
    For longitude >= 0, keep as is.
    Latitude remains unchanged.
    """
    if geometry is None:
        return None

    def shift_special(x, y, z=None):
        if x < 0:
            new_x = x + 2 * offset
        else:
            new_x = x
        return new_x, y

    return transform(shift_special, geometry)

def plot_classifications(df, col):
    if df[col].nunique() <= 1:
        print(f"Skipping classification plots: all values in '{col}' are identical (Value: {df[col].unique()[0]}). This is usually caused by an upstream API failure (like Celestrak or OpenDataSoft) resulting in empty spatial joins.")
        return
        
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 1, figsize=(15, 20))
    
    # 1. Equal Interval
    ei = EqualInterval(df[col], k=5)
    sns.kdeplot(df[col], fill=True, color='lightblue', ax=axes[0])
    sns.rugplot(df[col], ax=axes[0], color='lightblue')
    for b in ei.bins:
        axes[0].axvline(b, color='red', lw=1)
    axes[0].set_title('equal_interval classification')
    
    # 2. Quantiles
    qu = Quantiles(df[col], k=5)
    sns.kdeplot(df[col], fill=True, color='lightblue', ax=axes[1])
    sns.rugplot(df[col], ax=axes[1], color='lightblue')
    for b in qu.bins:
        axes[1].axvline(b, color='red', lw=1)
    axes[1].set_title('quantiles classification')
    
    # 3. Fisher Jenks
    fj = FisherJenks(df[col], k=5)
    sns.kdeplot(df[col], fill=True, color='lightblue', ax=axes[2])
    sns.rugplot(df[col], ax=axes[2], color='lightblue')
    for b in fj.bins:
        axes[2].axvline(b, color='red', lw=1)
    axes[2].set_title('fisher_jenks classification')
    
    # 4. Natural Breaks
    nb = NaturalBreaks(df[col], k=5)
    sns.kdeplot(df[col], fill=True, color='lightblue', ax=axes[3])
    sns.rugplot(df[col], ax=axes[3], color='lightblue')
    for b in nb.bins:
        axes[3].axvline(b, color='red', lw=1)
    axes[3].set_title('natural_breaks classification')
    
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

def add_scalebar(ax, length, location=(0.05, 0.05), linewidth=3,
                 units='km', fontsize=10, color='black'):
    """
    Add a scale bar to a matplotlib Axes object.
    
    Parameters:
    - ax: The Axes object to draw the scale bar on.
    - length: The length of the scale bar in units.
    - location: A tuple indicating the location of the scale bar (x, y) in axis coordinates (0 to 1).
    - linewidth: The thickness of the scale bar line.
    - units: The units of the scale bar length ('km', 'miles', etc.).
    - fontsize: The font size of the scale bar label.
    - color: The color of the scale bar and text.
    """
    # Calculate the end point of the scale bar
    x = location[0]
    y = location[1]
    xend = x + length / 44448 # Example scale; you may need to adjust this
    
    # Draw the scale bar
    ax.plot([x, xend], [y, y], color=color, linewidth=linewidth, transform=ax.transAxes)
    
    # Label the scale bar
    ax.text((x + xend) / 1.35, y - 0.01, f'{length} {units}',
            horizontalalignment='center', verticalalignment='top',
            transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=fontsize, color=color)

def add_scalebar(ax, length, location=(0.05, 0.05), linewidth=3,
                 units='km', fontsize=10, color='black'):
    """
    Add a scale bar to a matplotlib Axes object.
    
    Parameters:
    - ax: The Axes object to draw the scale bar on.
    - length: The length of the scale bar in units.
    - location: A tuple indicating the location of the scale bar (x, y) in axis coordinates (0 to 1).
    - linewidth: The thickness of the scale bar line.
    - units: The units of the scale bar length ('km', 'miles', etc.).
    - fontsize: The font size of the scale bar label.
    - color: The color of the scale bar and text.
    """
    # Calculate the end point of the scale bar
    x = location[0]
    y = location[1]
    xend = x + length / 44448 # Example scale; you may need to adjust this
    
    # Draw the scale bar
    ax.plot([x, xend], [y, y], color=color, linewidth=linewidth, transform=ax.transAxes)
    
    # Label the scale bar
    ax.text((x + xend) / 1.35, y - 0.01, f'{length} {units}',
            horizontalalignment='center', verticalalignment='top',

title: Big Data Trajectory Analysis: Microsoft GeoLife GPS Dataset
text: This project analyzes a sample of the Microsoft GeoLife GPS Trajectory Dataset (originally completed for the Big Data Analytics COMP 336/529 module at the University of Liverpool)[cite: 1, 8]. Using Apache Spark (PySpark), the pipeline cleans raw trajectory logs, performs timezone standardization, and executes distributed window and aggregation operations to extract user mobility metrics—including activity frequency, spatial extremes, altitude spans, geodesic travel distances, and peak velocities[cite: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9].

# Define function to calculate geodesic distance between two coordinates in km
def calculate_distance(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2):
    if None in [lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2]:
        return 0.0
    from geopy.distance import geodesic
    coord_1 = (lat1, lon1)
    coord_2 = (lat2, lon2)
    return geodesic(coord_1, coord_2).km

title: Big Data Trajectory Analysis: Microsoft GeoLife GPS Dataset
section: 3 Part 1: Data Cleaning & Timezone Conversion (GMT to GMT+8)
text:
3 Part 1: Data Cleaning & Timezone Conversion (GMT to GMT+8)

Precision Formatting: Latitude and Longitude are rounded to 4 decimal places, while Altitude and Timestamp (DelphiDate) are rounded to 9–10 decimal places[cite: 2, 10, 11].
Delphi Timestamp Conversion: The raw Timestamp represents the number of days passed since 1899-12-30 00:00:00 GMT[cite: 2]. To shift from GMT to China Standard Time (\text{GMT}+8), we add \frac{8\text{ hours}}{24\text{ hours}} = \frac{1}{3}\text{ day} to each record, storing the result as DelphiDateChina[cite: 2, 11].
Calendar Date & Time Conversion: The Date and Time columns are concatenated into a unified timestamp (OgTimeStamp), converted to Unix epoch seconds, shifted forward by 28,800\text{ seconds} (8\text{ hours}), and converted back into ChinaTimestamp and ChinaDate[cite: 2, 11, 12].



Code
# Standardize coordinate and metric precision
data = data.withColumn("Longitude", round(col("Longitude"), 4))
data = data.withColumn("Latitude", round(col("Latitude"), 4))
data = data.withColumn("Altitude", round(col("Altitude"), 9))
data = data.withColumn("Timestamp", round(col("Timestamp"), 9))

# Shift DelphiDate (+1/3 day) and Unix Timestamp (+8 hours) to GMT+8
data = data.withColumn("DelphiDate", col("Timestamp"))
data = data.withColumn("combinedDate", concat_ws(" ", col("Date"), col("Time")))
data = data.withColumn("OgTimeStamp", col("combinedDate").cast("timestamp"))
data = data.withColumn("ChinaTimestamp", from_unixtime(unix_timestamp("OgTimeStamp") + (8 * 60 * 60)))
data = data.withColumn("DelphiDateChina", round(col("DelphiDate") + (1 / 3), 10))

# Drop intermediate columns
data = data.drop("combinedDate", "Timestamp", "OgTimeStamp", "DelphiDate")
data.show(5)

section: 4 Part 2: User Consistency (Days with \ge 5 Data Points)
text:
4 Part 2: User Consistency (Days with \ge 5 Data Points)
We extract ChinaDate from ChinaTimestamp and group by UserID and ChinaDate to count daily records (DataPointsPerEachDay)[cite: 3, 12]. After filtering for days with at least 5 records, we count the qualifying days per user and output the Top 5 users, breaking ties by preferring smaller UserID values[cite: 3, 12, 13, 14].


Code
data = data.withColumn("ChinaDate", to_date(col("ChinaTimestamp")))

User_Daily_Activity = data.groupBy("UserID", "ChinaDate").agg(
    count("ChinaDate").alias("DataPointsPerEachDay")
)

Day_at_least_five_points = User_Daily_Activity.filter(col("DataPointsPerEachDay") >= 5)

user_DayCounts_AtleastFive = Day_at_least_five_points.groupBy("UserID").agg(
    count("ChinaDate").alias("DaysWithAtleastFivePerUser")
)

Top_Five_users = user_DayCounts_AtleastFive.orderBy(
    col("DaysWithAtleastFivePerUser").desc(), col("UserID")

5 Part 3: Weekly Tracking Volume (> 100 Data Points per Week)

We filter for high-volume weeks exceeding 100 data points and aggregate the total number of qualifying weeks per user[cite: 4, 13].

data = data.withColumn("Year", year(col("ChinaDate")))
data = data.withColumn("WeekNo", weekofyear(col("ChinaDate")))

More_than_hundred = weekly_Activity_No.filter(col("DataPointsPerWeek") > 100)

text:
6 Part 4: Southernmost Reach (Minimum Latitude per User)
To find the southernmost point reached by each user and the earliest date it occurred, we aggregate min("Latitude") per user and join the result back to the main dataset[cite: 5, 14]. A Window specification partitioned by UserID and Latitude ordered chronologically by ChinaDate extracts the first date (first("ChinaDate")) in the event of ties[cite: 5, 14].

min_latitude = data.groupBy("UserID").agg(_min("Latitude").alias("MinLatitude"))

dataset_with_min_latitude = data.join(min_latitude, "UserID").filter(

windowSpec = Window.partitionBy("UserID", "Latitude").orderBy("ChinaDate")

dataset_with_min_latitude = dataset_with_min_latitude.withColumn(
    "DayOrFirstDayAtMinLatitude", first("ChinaDate").over(windowSpec)
)

output = dataset_with_min_latitude.select(

7 Part 5: Maximum Daily Altitude Span
For every user and date, we compute the vertical elevation span: \text{DailyAltitudeSpan} = \max(\text{Altitude}) - \min(\text{Altitude}) We then aggregate by UserID to find each user’s maximum single-day elevation change and rank the Top 5 users[cite: 6, 15, 16].

title: Big Data Trajectory Analysis: Microsoft GeoLife GPS Dataset
section: 8 Part 6: Geodesic Distance Traveled (Daily Peak & Cumulative Total)
text:
8 Part 6: Geodesic Distance Traveled (Daily Peak & Cumulative Total)
Using a Window partitioned by UserID and ordered by ChinaTimestamp, we lag Latitude and Longitude to pair each observation with its preceding coordinate[cite: 6, 16]. Initial NULL values per user are coalesced with the current coordinate so the starting point distance evaluates to 0.0 km[cite: 9, 16]. Segment distances are computed via distance_udf, summed by day, and aggregated to identify each user’s highest-mileage day alongside the cumulative distance across all users[cite: 7, 17].


Code
windowAbstract = Window.partitionBy("UserID").orderBy("ChinaTimestamp")

data = data.withColumn(
    "prevLatitude", coalesce(lag("Latitude").over(windowAbstract), col("Latitude"))
)
data = data.withColumn(
    "prevLongitude", coalesce(lag("Longitude").over(windowAbstract), col("Longitude"))
)

# Calculate point-to-point geodesic distance in km
data = data.withColumn(
    "Distance", distance_udf("prevLatitude", "prevLongitude", "Latitude", "Longitude")
)

# Daily total distance per user
daily_distances = data.groupBy("UserID", "ChinaDate").agg(
    _sum("Distance").alias("DailyTotalDistancesPerUser")
)

# Maximum single-day distance per user
max_distances = daily_distances.groupBy("UserID").agg(
    _max("DailyTotalDistancesPerUser").alias("MaxDistanceForEachUser")
)

max_distance_day = daily_distances.join(max_distances, "UserID").filter(
    col("DailyTotalDistancesPerUser") == col("MaxDistanceForEachUser")
)

max_distance_output = max_distance_day.select(
    "UserID", "ChinaDate", "MaxDistanceForEachUser"
)
max_distance_output.show()

# Total distance traveled across all users and days
total_distance = daily_distances.agg(
    _sum("DailyTotalDistancesPerUser").alias("TotalDistanceByAllUsers")
)
total_distance.show()

section: 9 Part 7: Peak Travel Speed (km/hr) & Earliest Occurrence
text:
9 Part 7: Peak Travel Speed (km/hr) & Earliest Occurrence
To compute segment velocities, ChinaTimestamp is lagged across the user-ordered window (prevChinaTimestamp), with initial nulls defaulted to 2001-01-15 00:00:00 to prevent division-by-zero errors[cite: 7, 8, 18]. Elapsed time in seconds (TimeDiffSecs) is converted to hours, and speed is calculated as: \text{SpeedKmHour} = \frac{\text{Distance}}{\text{TimeDiffSecs} / 3600} After joining each user’s maximum speed back to the main DataFrame, row_number() over a ChinaDate-ordered window isolates the earliest date (rank == 1) that peak speed was achieved[cite: 8, 19].


Code
null_timestamp = to_timestamp(lit("2001-01-15 00:00:00"))
windowAbstractN = Window.partitionBy("UserID").orderBy("ChinaTimestamp")

data = data.withColumn(
    "prevChinaTimestamp",
    coalesce(lag("ChinaTimestamp").over(windowAbstractN), null_timestamp)
)

data = data.withColumn(
    "TimeDiffSecs",
    unix_timestamp("ChinaTimestamp") - unix_timestamp("prevChinaTimestamp")
)

data = data.withColumn(
    "SpeedKmHour",
    when(col("TimeDiffSecs") > 0, col("Distance") / (col("TimeDiffSecs") / 3600)).otherwise(0.0)
)

max_speeds = data.groupBy("UserID").agg(
    _max("SpeedKmHour").alias("MaxSpeedKmHour")
)

max_speed_day = data.join(max_speeds, "UserID").filter(
    col("SpeedKmHour") == col("MaxSpeedKmHour")
)

# Rank by ChinaDate to extract the earliest date in case of ties
windowAbstractNew = Window.partitionBy("UserID").orderBy("ChinaDate")
max_speed_day = max_speed_day.withColumn("rank", row_number().over(windowAbstractNew))

max_speed_day = max_speed_day.filter(col("rank") == 1).select(
    "UserID", "MaxSpeedKmHour", "ChinaDate"
)

max_speed_day.show()

title: S&P 500 Market Mode & Factor Analysis: Dimensionality Reduction with PCA
text:
Modern financial markets generate massive, high-dimensional time-series datasets. Analyzing the joint behavior of hundreds of equities—such as the constituents of the S&P 500 Index—poses a classic high-dimensional statistical challenge: estimating and interpreting an N \times N covariance matrix where the number of assets (N \approx 500) is of the same order of magnitude as the number of historical trading days (T \approx 750).
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is an unsupervised linear dimensionality reduction technique that transforms a high-dimensional set of correlated variables into a smaller set of orthogonal (mutually uncorrelated) latent variables called Principal Components (PCs).








NoteCore Mathematical & Statistical Concepts in PCA




Variance (\sigma^2): In statistics, variance measures how far a set of observations is spread out from their average value: \sigma^2 = \frac{1}{T-1} \sum_{t=1}^{T} (r_t - \bar{r})^2 In quantitative finance, the variance of daily asset returns directly measures total return volatility (risk). Directions of maximum variance in a multi-asset return space correspond to the most significant sources of collective price movement.
Covariance (\Sigma): While variance measures the dispersion of a single asset, covariance measures the degree to which two assets move together over time. A positive covariance indicates that two stocks tend to rise and fall simultaneously.
Principal Components (Eigenvectors, v_k): Principal components are orthogonal axes constructed as linear combinations of the original asset returns: \text{PC}_k = \sum_{i=1}^{N} w_{ki} r_i Geometrically, the first principal component (\text{PC}_1) points in the direction of maximum variance across the entire dataset. Each subsequent component (\text{PC}_2, \text{PC}_3, \dots) maximizes the remaining variance subject to being strictly orthogonal (uncorrelated) to all preceding components. In finance, the weight vector v_k = [w_{k1}, w_{k2}, \dots, w_{kN}]^\top is often interpreted as an eigenportfolio.
Eigenvalues (\lambda_k) & Explained Variance Ratio: Performing eigendecomposition on the return covariance matrix \Sigma yields \Sigma v_k = \lambda_k v_k. Each eigenvalue \lambda_k equals the exact variance of the data projected onto the k-th principal component. The Explained Variance Ratio measures the proportion of total market variance captured by component k: \text{Explained Variance Ratio}_k = \frac{\lambda_k}{\sum_{i=1}^{N} \lambda_i}






When applied to daily equity returns across a broad index like the S&P 500, the eigenvalue spectrum naturally separates into three distinct regimes:

The Dominant “Market Mode” (\text{PC}_1): The first principal component typically captures between 25\% and 40\% of the total variance across all stocks. Its loadings (w_{1i}) almost uniformly share the same sign, reflecting systematic macroeconomic risk—interest rate shifts, GDP growth expectations, and broad market sentiment—that moves the entire equity market in tandem.
Sector & Style Factors (\text{PC}_2 to \text{PC}_K): The next several components capture mesoscopic co-movements across specific industries (e.g., Financials vs. Utilities, Energy vs. Airlines, High-Growth Tech vs. Defensive Consumer Staples).
Idiosyncratic Noise (Higher-Order PCs): The long tail of remaining components accounts for firm-specific events (e.g., earnings surprises, litigation, product launches) and random microstructure noise that cannot be compressed into low-dimensional systematic factors.




A critical modeling decision in financial PCA is whether to decompose the sample covariance matrix (unnormalized returns) or the sample correlation matrix (standardized returns):

Covariance-Based PCA (Unnormalized): Operates directly on mean-centered daily percentage returns. Because variance scales quadratically with return magnitude, highly volatile stocks (such as Biotech, Semiconductor, or Energy firms) exert a disproportionate influence on the leading eigenvectors.
Correlation-Based PCA (Normalized via StandardScaler): Standardizes each stock’s return series to zero mean (\mu = 0) and unit variance (\sigma = 1) prior to fitting PCA: z_{i,t} = \frac{r_{i,t} - \mu_i}{\sigma_i} Decomposing the covariance matrix of Z-scores is mathematically equivalent to decomposing the correlation matrix of raw returns. Every stock contributes exactly 1.0 unit of variance to the total system (\sum \lambda_i = N), placing low-beta defensive stocks and high-beta growth stocks on an equal footing.

title: S&P 500 Market Mode & Factor Analysis: Dimensionality Reduction with PCA
text:
2 Data Cleaning & Pipeline (Parts 1 – 6)
To perform a valid spectral decomposition on a panel of asset returns, the input matrix must be a strictly balanced, non-missing time-series matrix of dimension T \times N. Any missing values (NaN) or misaligned trading dates would distort pairwise covariance estimates. In Parts 1 through 6, we build a reproducible preprocessing pipeline to transform the raw transaction log into a clean wide return matrix.

2.1 Environment Setup


Code
import pandas as pan
from datetime import date
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler




2.2 Part 1: Data Ingestion & Schema Exploration
We begin by loading stock_data.csv into a Pandas DataFrame and inspecting its schema and initial records.


Code
# Load S&P 500 index dataset from CSV into a pandas DataFrame
data = pan.read_csv('/Users/jay/Desktop/websiteV02/data/data_python/SP500_comp/stock_data.csv')
print(data.head())

Schema Analysis:
The raw dataset is structured in long (stacked) format with seven columns:

date: Trading date string (YYYY-MM-DD).
open, high, low, close: Daily intraday price extrema and official closing price (in USD).
volume: Total number of shares traded during the session.
Name: Official S&P 500 stock ticker symbol (e.g., AAL for American Airlines Group).



2.3 Part 2: Constituents Profiling
Next, we extract the unique set of stock tickers present in the dataset, sort them alphabetically, and inspect the boundary tickers.


Code
# Identify unique stock tickers and sort alphabetically
list_alpha = sorted(data['Name'].unique())
first_four = list_alpha[:4]
display_list = first_four + ['........... remaining stocks']

print("Identifying the set of names in S&P index:", display_list)
print(f"Total No. of unique stocks listed over course of time in the given dataset: {len(list_alpha)}")
print("First 5 names in that set: ", list_alpha[:5])
print("Last  5 names in that set: ", list_alpha[-5:])


Identifying the set of names in S&P index: ['A', 'AAL', 'AAP', 'AAPL', '........... remaining stocks']
Total No. of unique stocks listed over course of time in the given dataset: 505
First 5 names in that set:  ['A', 'AAL', 'AAP', 'AAPL', 'ABBV']
Last  5 names in that set:  ['XYL', 'YUM', 'ZBH', 'ZION', 'ZTS']


Analysis of Constituents:
Although the index is nominally the “S&P 500”, the historical dataset contains 505 unique stock tickers ranging alphabetically from ['A', 'AAL', 'AAP', 'AAPL', 'ABBV'] to ['XYL', 'YUM', 'ZBH', 'ZION', 'ZTS']. This occurs because dual-class share structures (such as Alphabet’s GOOG/GOOGL or Under Armour’s UA/UAA) and periodic index rebalancings result in slightly more than 500 symbols appearing over a multi-year window.


2.4 Part 3: Active Trading Filter (3-Year Continuous Coverage)
Stocks that were added to the index late (via IPOs or corporate spin-offs) or delisted early create structural missingness across a multi-year panel. Rather than imputing synthetic prices—which would introduce artificial zero-volatility periods and bias our covariance matrix—we filter for constituents that actively traded across the entire 3-year target window from 2014-07-01 to 2017-06-30.


Code
# Convert 'date' column to Python date objects
data['date'] = pan.to_datetime(data['date']).dt.date

# Define the 3-year evaluation window boundaries
first_date = date(2014, 7, 1)
last_date = date(2017, 6, 30)

# Retain only stocks whose trading history spans at least 2014-07-01 through 2017-06-30
filtered_names = data.groupby('Name').filter(
    lambda x: x['date'].min() <= first_date and x['date'].max() >= last_date
)['Name'].unique()

removed_names = set(list_alpha) - set(filtered_names)

print(f"Stocks removed from the dataset based on given condition: {sorted(list(removed_names))}")
print(f"No. of stocks remaining: {len(filtered_names)}")

No. of stocks remaining: 486


Analysis of Filtered Constituents:
Exactly 19 incomplete stocks (APTV, BHF, BHGE, CFG, CSRA, DWDP, DXC, EVHC, FTV, HLT, HPE, HPQ, KHC, PYPL, QRVO, SYF, UA, WLTW, WRK) are excluded because they lack full coverage across the 2014-07-01 to 2017-06-30 window (for example, PayPal PYPL and Hewlett Packard Enterprise HPE spun off in 2015, and Kraft Heinz KHC merged in 2015). This leaves 486 continuously traded stocks for analysis.


2.5 Part 4: Date Alignment Across Constituents
Even among the 486 continuously active stocks, occasional exchange halts or data recording gaps can cause a ticker to miss a single trading day. To guarantee a complete rectangular matrix without missing entries, we retain only trading dates within [2014-07-01, 2017-06-30] that are common to all 486 stocks.


Code
# Filter dataset to the 486 continuously active stocks
data_filtered_names = data[data['Name'].isin(filtered_names)]

# Keep only dates where all 486 stocks have a recorded observation
data_common_dates = data_filtered_names.groupby('date').filter(
    lambda x: x['Name'].nunique() == len(filtered_names)
)
common_dates_unique = data_common_dates['date'].unique()

# Restrict common dates to the target 3-year window (2014-07-01 to 2017-06-30)
common_dates_unique_between_750days = common_dates_unique[
    (common_dates_unique >= first_date) & (common_dates_unique <= last_date)
]

first_few_dates_str = [str(d) for d in common_dates_unique_between_750days[:5]]
last_few_dates_str = [str(d) for d in common_dates_unique_between_750days[-5:]]

print(f"No. of dates remaining after filtering: {len(common_dates_unique_between_750days)}")
print("First 5 dates after filtering:", first_few_dates_str)
print("Last  5 dates after filtering:", last_few_dates_str)

Last  5 dates after filtering: ['2017-06-26', '2017-06-27', '2017-06-28', '2017-06-29', '2017-06-30']


Date Alignment Results:
Filtering for strict cross-sectional completeness across the 3-year window yields 745 common trading days, beginning on 2014-07-01 and ending on 2017-06-30 (approx. 248 trading days per year after accounting for weekends, U.S. market holidays such as July 4th on 2014-07-04, and occasional missing ticker records).


2.6 Part 5: Panel Reshaping (Wide Price Matrix)
With both the cross-sectional dimension (N = 486 stocks) and temporal dimension (T = 745 trading days) aligned, we pivot the long table into a wide closing-price matrix where rows represent trading dates and columns represent individual stock tickers.


Code
# Filter for valid stocks and aligned trading dates, then pivot into a wide matrix
data_new = data[
    data['Name'].isin(filtered_names) &
    data['date'].isin(common_dates_unique_between_750days)
]

close_table = data_new.pivot(index='date', columns='Name', values='close')
print(f"Close Price Matrix Shape: {close_table.shape}")
print(close_table.head())

2.7 Part 6: Daily Percentage Return Calculation
Raw stock prices are non-stationary (I(1) processes) and depend on arbitrary share nominal values (e.g., a $15 stock vs. a $500 stock). # Fit unnormalized PCA on the raw daily returns matrix

Dominance of \lambda_1: The first eigenvalue (\lambda_1 \approx 0.039797) is more than 4.5\times larger than the second eigenvalue (\lambda_2 \approx 0.008720), and nearly 15\times larger than the fourth and fifth eigenvalues (\lambda_4 \approx 0.002795, \lambda_5 \approx 0.002541).
Uniform Sign of \text{PC}_1 Loadings: Inspecting the eigenvector weights of \text{PC}_1 reveals that all loadings share the same negative sign (ranging around -0.03 to -0.06). Because eigenvector signs are arbitrary up to multiplication by -1, this confirms that \text{PC}_1 is a long-only market portfolio where all 486 S&P 500 stocks move in the same direction in response to aggregate market shocks.



3.2 Part 8: Scree Plot Analysis & The Systematic Market Factor
A Scree Plot graphs the Explained Variance Ratio against the component index k, allowing us to visually separate high-signal systematic factors from low-variance idiosyncratic noise. The Elbow Point is the inflection point where the steep initial drop flattens into a gradual tail.


Code
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.plot(range(1, 21), pca.explained_variance_ratio_[:20], marker='o', label='Explained Variance Ratio')

# Identify and mark the Elbow Point at PC 4 (index 3)
elbow_point = 3
plt.plot(elbow_point + 1, pca.explained_variance_ratio_[elbow_point], 'ro', markersize=8, label='Elbow Point')
plt.annotate(
    'Elbow Point (PC 4)',
    (elbow_point + 1, pca.explained_variance_ratio_[elbow_point]),
    textcoords="offset points", xytext=(-10, 10), ha='left', fontsize=12, color='red'
)

plt.title('Explained Variance Ratios of the First 20 Principal Components')
plt.xlabel('Principal Component')
plt.ylabel('Explained Variance Ratio')
plt.text(0.5, -0.15, 'Source: Calculations are based on given Stocks Dataset', ha='center', va='center', transform=plt.gca().transAxes)
plt.grid(True)
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

pov = pca.explained_variance_ratio_[0] * 100
print(f"Percentage of variance explained by the First Principal Component is: {pov:.2f} %")









Percentage of variance explained by the First Principal Component is: 28.81 %








TipFinancial Interpretation: Why \text{PC}_1 Captures 28.81% of Variance & Elbow at \text{PC}_4




The Market Mode (\text{PC}_1 = 28.81\%): Nearly one-third of all daily return variance across 486 diverse corporations is driven by a single latent variable. In Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) terms, \text{PC}_1 empirically recovers the systematic market factor (\beta_{\text{market}}). When macroeconomic news hits the market, correlations across all equities spike, causing a single dimension to account for 28.81\% of total volatility.
The Elbow Point at \text{PC}_4: Components 2 and 3 capture major cross-sector rotations (explaining \sim 6.3\% and \sim 3.7\% of variance, respectively, such as energy/commodity sensitivity and interest-rate sensitivity). By \text{PC}_4 (\sim 2.0\% of variance), the marginal explanatory power of additional components levels off dramatically. Thus, the top 3–4 components represent the primary systematic macro and sector factors, while components beyond \text{PC}_4 transition into granular industry and firm-specific risk.





3.3 Part 9: Cumulative Variance & The 95% Reconstruction Threshold
To evaluate how effectively PCA compresses the 486-dimensional stock universe while preserving almost all information, we compute the Cumulative Explained Variance Ratio: C_K = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \frac{\lambda_k}{\sum_{i=1}^{N} \lambda_i} We then identify the minimum number of components K_{0.95} required to surpass 95\% of total variance.


Code
# Compute cumulative variance ratios across all principal components
cumulative_variance_ratios = np.cumsum(pca.explained_variance_ratio_)

# Find the minimum number of components explaining at least 95% of variance
num_of_req_pc_95 = np.where(cumulative_variance_ratios >= 0.95)[0][0] + 1
print(f"No. of principal components required to explain 95% of the variance: {num_of_req_pc_95}")

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.plot(cumulative_variance_ratios, marker='o', markersize=3, label='Cumulative Variance Ratio')
plt.title('Cumulative Variance Ratios of Principal Components')
plt.xlabel('No. of Principal Components')
plt.ylabel('Cumulative Variance Ratio')
plt.text(0.5, -0.15, 'Source: Calculations are based on given Stocks Dataset', ha='center', va='center', transform=plt.gca().transAxes)
plt.grid(True)

# Draw horizontal threshold line at 95%
plt.axhline(y=0.95, color='r', linestyle='--', label='95% Variance Line')

# Annotate the exact component count where cumulative variance reaches 95%
plt.annotate(
    f'Principal component {num_of_req_pc_95}',
    xy=(num_of_req_pc_95 - 1, 0.95),
    xytext=(num_of_req_pc_95 - 1, 0.82),
    arrowprops=dict(facecolor='black', arrowstyle='->'),
    ha='center'
)

plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


No. of principal components required to explain 95% of the variance: 226









Why 226 Components Are Required for 95% Variance:
While the first 4 components capture roughly 40.8\% of total market variance, reaching the strict 95% threshold requires 226 principal components (out of 486—a dimensionality reduction of \sim 53.5\%). In financial markets, once the broad market mode and major sector factors are extracted, the remaining \sim 55\% of variance is idiosyncratic (stock-specific) risk distributed thinly across hundreds of individual companies. Because idiosyncratic shocks are largely uncorrelated across firms, no small set of linear factors can compress them; hundreds of dimensions are needed to reconstruct 95% of every individual stock’s daily fluctuations.

title: S&P 500 Market Mode & Factor Analysis: Dimensionality Reduction with PCA
text:
4 Normalized PCA & Comparative Analysis (Part 10)

4.1 The Role of StandardScaler in Financial Factor Extraction
In Parts 7–9, PCA was fitted on raw returns. However, individual S&P 500 stocks exhibit vastly different baseline volatilities: high-beta stocks (e.g., airlines, energy exploration, semiconductors) experience much larger daily percentage swings than low-beta defensive utilities or consumer staples.
By applying StandardScaler, we normalize each stock i to have zero mean and unit variance (\sigma_i^2 = 1). This transforms our analysis from Covariance-based PCA to Correlation-based PCA, ensuring that every constituent has an equal voice in determining the principal components.


Code
# Initialize StandardScaler and normalize the returns matrix (mean=0, std=1 per stock)
scaler = StandardScaler()
normalized_returns = scaler.fit_transform(returns_table)

normalized_returns_table = pan.DataFrame(
    normalized_returns,
    columns=returns_table.columns,
    index=returns_table.index
)

# Fit PCA on the standardized returns matrix
pca_normalized = PCA()
pca_normalized.fit(normalized_returns_table)

# Display the top 5 principal components and eigenvalues for normalized returns
for i in range(5):
    print(f"Principal Component {i+1} with Eigenvalue: {pca_normalized.explained_variance_[i]:.6f}")
    print("First 10 Stock Loadings:", np.round(pca_normalized.components_[i][:10], 6))
    print()

NoteWhy Normalization Increases Both \text{PC}_1 Share (31.82%) and the 95% Threshold (253 PCs)



Comparing the normalized results against the unnormalized baseline reveals an intriguing dual shift:

Higher \text{PC}_1 Explained Variance (31.82\% vs. 28.81\%): In unnormalized PCA, a handful of ultra-volatile stocks with large idiosyncratic swings inflate the total variance denominator and pull early components toward specific high-volatility sub-sectors. Once StandardScaler equalizes volatility across all 486 stocks, the underlying co-movement (correlation) of low-volatility blue-chip stocks with the broader market becomes fully visible, strengthening the dominant Market Mode by +3.01 percentage points.
More Components Required for 95% Variance (253 vs. 226): Without normalization, total variance is concentrated in the most volatile stocks; capturing their movements allows fewer components (226) to reach 95\% of total raw variance. After standardization, every single stock—including quiet, low-volatility firms with unique idiosyncratic patterns—contributes an equal 1/486 share of total variance. Consequently, the residual variance tail is more evenly spread out, requiring 27 additional principal components (253 total) to reach the 95\% cumulative threshold.

5.2 Key Financial & Big Data Takeaways






TipPortfolio Risk & Dimensionality Reduction Insights




Limits of Naive Diversification: Because the first principal component alone explains 28.81\% to 31.82\% of total return variance, holding a large number of S&P 500 stocks does not eliminate systematic risk. Approximately one-third of portfolio volatility is tied to the undiversifiable “Market Mode” (\text{PC}_1). True market-neutral hedging requires constructing portfolios that are orthogonal to \text{PC}_1 (\sum w_i v_{1i} = 0).
Low-Rank Factor Structure (The Top 4 PCs): Both unnormalized and normalized Scree Plots exhibit a clear Elbow Point at \text{PC}_4. This confirms the core premise of Arbitrage Pricing Theory (APT) and multi-factor risk models: systematic co-movement across hundreds of equities is governed by a compact set of 3 to 4 dominant macroeconomic and sector factors.
High Idiosyncratic Dimensionality in the Tail: While the systematic signal is low-dimensional, achieving 95\% reconstruction accuracy requires 226 to 253 components. In financial big data, noise is not negligible—over half of total return variance stems from firm-specific events, meaning aggressive dimensionality reduction (e.g., keeping only 10–20 PCs) acts as a denoising filter that strips away idiosyncratic stock risk while retaining core systematic drivers.

title: Relationship between Standard Occupational Classification (SOC) and Address Duration in APS 2021 Survey
text:
Residential mobility—how frequently individuals and households relocate—is closely intertwined with labour market structure, socioeconomic status, and life-course dynamics. Higher-skilled professionals often participate in national or regional labour markets that reward geographic flexibility and career-driven relocation, whereas lower-skilled and routine occupations are more frequently anchored to local labour markets and longer-term residential stability.
This notebook reconstructs and documents the empirical analysis submitted for ENVS450 (Social Survey Analysis) coursework at the Department of Geography and Planning, School of Environmental Sciences, University of Liverpool (Module Leader: Dr. Paul Williamson). The study investigates a core empirical question:

Research Question: Does occupational skill level, as measured by the UK Office for National Statistics (ONS) Standard Occupational Classification (SOC 2020), relate to how long individuals have resided at their current address (Address_Duration) in the 2021 Annual Population Survey (APS)?



The analysis uses the Annual Population Survey (APS) 2021 teaching extract (APS), which comprises N = 249,997 individual survey respondents across 60 demographic, socioeconomic, and housing variables, accompanied by a structured variable dictionary (meta_data) and UK Mid-Year Population Estimates (MYE_UK_wide) across seven age bands.
The analytical workflow proceeds through seven stages:

Univariate Description & Recoding: Collapsing the 28-category nominal SOC_Sub_Major variable into 4 ordinal ONS occupational skill levels (L1–L4) and the 8-category ordinal Address_Duration variable into 4 duration intervals (0-2 Years, 2-5 Years, 5-10 Years, 10 years or longer), evaluating central tendency via the Median and categorical dispersion via the Standardised Reciprocal Diversity Index (SRDI).
Bivariate Cross-Tabulation: Examining conditional row percentages in both directions (N = 108,964 complete cases) to distinguish how residential tenure distributes within skill levels versus how occupational skill levels compose each tenure band.
Graphical Visualisation: Constructing 100% stacked bar charts with exact percentage annotations to visualise the bivariate distributions.
Statistical Significance Testing: Testing the null hypothesis of statistical independence in the population using Pearson’s Chi-Square (\chi^2) test and evaluating substantive effect size via Cramér’s V.
Quantifying Random Sampling Error: Computing 95% Confidence Intervals (CIs) for every cell percentage to assess sampling precision.
Addressing Non-Random Response Bias: Implementing post-stratification survey reweighting calibrated against ONS Mid-Year Population Estimates by age group (Age_Count_Ratio) and comparing the results against both unweighted estimates and official ONS survey weights (Weight_APS).
Multivariate Extension (Subgroup Analysis): Discretising numeric household size (Hhold_Size) into tertiles (Low, Medium, High) to test whether household composition moderates the relationship between occupational skill level and residential tenure.

title: Relationship between Standard Occupational Classification (SOC) and Address Duration in APS 2021 Survey
text:
2.1 Standard Occupational Classification (SOC 2020) Sub-Major Group
In the raw APS 2021 extract, SOC_Sub_Major is a nominal categorical variable with 28 levels (26 substantive occupational sub-major groups plus "Does not apply" and "No answer"). Each category represents a grouping of job titles and occupational roles.

2.1.1 Rationale and Recoding into ONS Skill Levels
Following the official Office for National Statistics (ONS, 2023) SOC 2020 Volume 1 taxonomy, occupational groups are structured around the concept of Skill Level—defined by the duration of formal education, training, and work experience required for competent performance of the job tasks. We reclassify the 26 occupational sub-major groups into 4 ordinal skill levels (L1 through L4 in ascending order of skill), while mapping "Does not apply" and "No answer" to "Ineligible or unknown" and converting that level to NA:

Level 1 (L1 — Elementary occupations): Competence associated with compulsory general education and short periods of on-the-job induction (2 sub-major groups).
Level 2 (L2 — Administrative, caring, sales, and operative occupations): Competence requiring general education typically up to GCSE/O-level standard plus longer periods of work-related training or experience (9 sub-major groups).
Level 3 (L3 — Associate professional and skilled trade occupations): Competence requiring post-compulsory education (A-levels, vocational awards, apprenticeships) or substantial technical experience (10 sub-major groups).
Level 4 (L4 — Professional and higher managerial occupations): Competence requiring a degree-level qualification or equivalent extensive professional experience (5 sub-major groups).

Transforming SOC_Sub_Major from a 28-level nominal variable into a 4-level ordered factor (L1 < L2 < L3 < L4) reduces table sparsity and enables direct ordinal testing of whether higher occupational skill levels are associated with greater residential mobility.

    "Corporate managers and directors",
    "Science, research, engineering and technology professionals",
    "Health professionals",
    "Teaching and other educational professionals",
    "Business, media and public service professionals"
  ),
  "L3" = c(
    "Other managers and proprietors",
    "Science, engineering and technology associate professionals",
    "Health and social care associate professionals",
    "Protective service occupations",
    "Culture, media and sports occupations",
    "Business and public service associate professionals",
    "Skilled agricultural and related trades",
    "Skilled metal, electrical and electronic trades",
    "Skilled construction and building trades",
    "Textiles, printing and other skilled trades"
  ),
  "L2" = c(
    "Administrative occupations",
    "Secretarial and related occupations",
    "Caring personal service occupations",
    "Leisure, travel and related personal service occupations",
    "Community and civil enforcement occupations",
    "Sales occupations",
    "Customer service occupations",

)

# Order levels explicitly and convert "Ineligible or unknown" to NA
APScopy$SOC_Skill_Level_order <- ordered(
  fct_relevel(APScopy$SOC_Skill_Level, c("Ineligible or unknown", "L1", "L2", "L3", "L4")),

text:
2.2 Length of Time at Current Address (Address Duration)
The Address_Duration variable records how long each respondent has lived at their current residential address. In the raw APS extract, it is an ordinal categorical variable with 8 levels (6 duration bands plus "Does not apply" and "No answer").

2.2.1 Rationale and Recoding into 4 Duration Intervals
Before reclassification, the 8-level raw variable has a very low dispersion index (\text{SRDI} = 32.81) because nearly half of all respondents are concentrated in the "10 years or longer" category while the shorter duration categories ("Less than 12 months", "12 months, less than 24", "2 years, less than 3", "3 years, less than 5") each hold relatively small proportions. Retaining fine-grained short intervals alongside a massive 10+ year category can produce sparse cells in multi-way cross-tabulations.
We therefore collapse the valid responses into 4 ordinal duration intervals:

0-2 Years: "Less than 12 months" and "12 months, less than 24" (recent movers).
2-5 Years: "2 years, less than 3" and "3 years, less than 5" (short-to-medium tenure).
5-10 Years: "5 years, less than 10" (medium-to-long tenure).
10 years or longer (10-Inf): "10 years or longer" (long-term settled residents).
Missing (NA): "Does not apply" and "No answer" mapped to "Ineligible or unknown" and converted to NA.



Code
# Collapse 8 Address_Duration levels into 4 duration intervals + Ineligible/unknown
APScopy$Address_Duration_recode <- fct_collapse(
  APScopy$Address_Duration,
  "0-2 Years"             = c("Less than 12 months", "12 months, less than 24"),
  "2-5 Years"             = c("2 years, less than 3", "3 years, less than 5"),
  "5-10 Years"            = "5 years, less than 10",
  "10 years or longer"    = "10 years or longer",
  "Ineligible or unknown" = c("Does not apply", "No answer")
)

# Convert "Ineligible or unknown" to NA

title: Relationship between Standard Occupational Classification (SOC) and Address Duration in APS 2021 Survey
text:
3.3 Discussion of Bivariate Patterns
Comparing Table 1 and Table 2 reveals a clear, monotonic relationship between occupational skill level and residential mobility:

Long-term residential stability decreases as occupational skill level increases (Table 1): Across all skill levels, the modal duration category is "10 years or longer", indicating that a large share of the workforce is residentially settled. However, the proportion residing at the same address for 10+ years declines steadily from 53.5\% (0.54) among elementary workers (L1) and 51.2\% (0.51) in L2, to 48.4\% (0.48) in L3, and down to 42.9\% (0.43) among higher managerial and professional workers (L4).
Recent mobility increases with skill level (Table 1): Conversely, the share of respondents who moved within the last 0\text{--}2 years is lowest in L1 (11.9\%, 0.12) and L2 (12.2\%, 0.12), slightly higher in L3 (12.8\%, 0.13), and highest in L4 (14.7\%, 0.15). A similar gradient holds in the 2\text{--}5 year band (17.0\% in L1 vs. 21.3\% in L4) and the 5\text{--}10 year band (17.6\% in L1 vs. 21.1\% in L4).
Occupational composition shifts across tenure bands (Table 2): Conditioning on address duration (Ross, 2009, p. 73), respondents who have lived at their current address for less than 2 years, 2 to 5 years, or 5 to 10 years are most likely to belong to the highest skill level L4 (36.8\%, 35.7\%, and 35.9\% respectively, compared to the overall L4 share of 32.9\%). By contrast, among those who have stayed at their current address for 10 years or longer, L2 is the largest occupational group (33.5\%, vs. 29.4\% for L4). Across all duration bands, L1 constitutes the smallest share of the workforce (7.9\%, 7.5\%, 7.9\%, and 9.7\%).

Together, these two cross-tabulations demonstrate that higher-skilled professionals (L4) experience substantially higher residential turnover than routine and elementary workers (L1 and L2).

6.2.1 1. Copy-Paste Variable Bug in assignment_1_practice.R (Line 307)
When calculating the L1 column of Table 4 in assignment_1_practice.R (lines 299–309), the lower bound correctly used pct_s1 (pct_s[, "L1"]), but the upper bound on line 307 accidentally referenced pct_a1 (pct_a[, "0-2 Years"] from Table 3) instead of pct_s1:

6.2.2 2. Frequentist Interpretation of Confidence Intervals
In the original report (page 9), the 95% CI was first correctly introduced (“sample estimate will be population representative in 95 out of every 100 samples”), followed by the phrasing “there is probability of 0.95 that % of people staying for 10 or more years who has SOC Skill Level L2 in the population lies within the range of 33.1% to 33.9%.”
In strict frequentist inference, the true population parameter \pi is a fixed (non-random) constant, while the interval endpoints are random variables across repeated samples. Thus, a 95% CI means that if we repeated the survey sampling procedure many times, 95% of the resulting confidence intervals would contain the true population percentage. Regardless of phrasing, because the subgroup sample sizes are large (n \ge 9,486), the confidence intervals in Tables 3 and 4 are narrow (\pm 0.4\% to \pm 1.0\%) and non-overlapping across key skill categories, confirming that the observed differences between L1–L2 and L4 cannot be attributed to random sampling error.

7.1 Deriving Age-Group Survey Weights (Age_Count_Ratio)
We reshape MYE_UK_wide from wide to long format, tabulate the observed age distribution in APScopy, and join the two tables to compute Age_Count_Ratio for each of the seven age groups (0-15, 16-29, 30-44, 45-64, 65-69, 70-74, 75+):

# Reshape ONS Mid-Year Population Estimates to long format
MYE_UK_long <- pivot_longer(
  MYE_UK_wide,
  cols = c("0-15":"75+"),
  names_to = "Age_Group",
  values_to = "MYE_Count"
)

# Tabulate APS sample counts by Age_Group for the United Kingdom
APScopy$Nation <- factor("United Kingdom")
APScopy_UK_long <- tally(Age_Group ~ Nation, data = APScopy, format = "count") %>%
  data.frame() %>%
  relocate(Nation) %>%
  rename(Area = Nation, APS_Count = Freq)

# Join population benchmarks with APS sample counts and compute weights

  mutate(
    MYE_Pct = MYE_Count / sum(MYE_Count) * 100,
    APS_Pct = APS_Count / sum(APS_Count) * 100,
    Age_Count_Ratio = MYE_Count / APS_Count

7.4.1 Interpretation of Weighting Results

Impact of Age Reweighting on Table 5 vs. Table 1: In Table 5, most cells shift by more than \pm 1 percentage point relative to the unweighted Table 1. Specifically, because younger adults (16-29 and 30-44) were under-represented in the raw sample and receive the largest weights (371.8 and 321.8), up-weighting younger cohorts increases the estimated proportion of recent movers (0-2 Years rises by +1.3 to +1.9 percentage points across skill levels, and 2-5 Years rises by +0.8 to +1.7 percentage points) while reducing the proportion in the 10 years or longer category by -2.3 to -3.9 percentage points (falling from 47.9\% to 44.5\% overall, and from 42.9\% to 38.96\% in L4).
Impact on Table 6 vs. Table 2: By contrast, in Table 6 (skill composition within each address duration band), the age-weighted percentages change very little compared to the unweighted Table 2 (most differences are < 0.8 percentage points). This indicates that Address_Duration is much more strongly confounded by age than SOC_Skill_Level is within a given tenure band.
Comparison with Official ONS Weights (Weight_APS): The official ONS weight (Weight_APS) calibrates simultaneously across age, sex, and sub-national region/local authority. Despite incorporating these additional demographic dimensions, the cell percentages produced by Weight_APS (e.g., L4: 16.57\%, 23.14\%, 21.62\%, 38.67\%) are remarkably close to our single-variable age-weighted estimates in Table 5 (L4: 16.54\%, 22.96\%, 21.53\%, 38.96\%). This confirms that age structure is the dominant source of non-response bias affecting residential duration in the APS 2021 sample.

title: Ordinary Least Squares Regression for modelling Green Central Heating in Census 2021
text:
The focal point of this report centres around the research question: “What are the key determinants impacting the implementation of green central heating in the districts of the UK?” This question is highly relevant in the context of rising environmental awareness, residential decarbonisation targets, and the transition toward a sustainable energy future. Domestic heating accounts for a substantial share of national greenhouse gas emissions, meaning that the adoption of green central heating systems—such as heat pumps, biomass boilers, solar thermal, and district or communal heat networks—stands as a crucial pillar in reducing residential carbon footprints and promoting energy-efficient practices.
Understanding the socio-economic, demographic, and housing-stock factors that shape the uptake of green central heating technologies provides actionable insight for both public policymakers and private-sector energy markets. Effective decarbonisation policy requires more than technological availability; it requires identifying how lifestyle patterns, housing tenure, dwelling structure, and local heating infrastructure interact across different local authorities.
This report is systematically organised to follow the end-to-end statistical modelling workflow required by ENVS450 Assignment 2:

Literature Review and Variables Selection Rationale summarises existing empirical research on sustainable household technology adoption and motivates our candidate predictors.
Methodology & Setup introduces the 2021 Census district-level dataset (\(N = 331\) local authority districts across \(55\) variables) and outlines the quantitative modelling strategy.
Univariate Description of Outcome Variable examines the distribution, skewness, central tendency, and dispersion of Green_Central_Heating.
Correlation Analysis of Outcome Variable screens bivariate associations between Green_Central_Heating and all other continuous and categorical variables in the dataset (excluding the identifier District) using rank-based correlation (Table 1).
Selection of Predictor Variables justifies the five chosen candidate predictors (four continuous and one newly constructed binary categorical variable, Age_Profile).
Regression Model Fitting Strategy & Initial ‘Best’ Model Identification applies the Narrative approach across three sequential Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) models (model1, model2, model3) to assess confounding (“explained away” effects) and identify the initial ‘best’ main-effects specification (Tables 2 & 3).
Interaction Effect Evaluation tests all two-way multiplicative interactions among the main predictors (model2i_first, Table 4) and uses backwards elimination to retain statistically significant interactions (model2i, Table 5 and Figures 1–3).
Enhancing the ‘Best’ Model (Polynomials) evaluates non-linear quadratic terms across the continuous predictors (Table 6) to arrive at the final preferred model (M2, Table 7).
Assessment of the Final Model conducts regression diagnostics—residual normality (Figure 4), homoscedasticity (Figure 5), multicollinearity (\(\text{VIF}\)), and error independence (Durbin-Watson)—evaluates the relative importance of predictors via Adequacy (Figure 6), and synthesises what the model reveals about the UK housing landscape.
