section: 2 Literature Review and Variables Selection Rationale
text:
2 Literature Review and Variables Selection Rationale
Recent studies in environmental sciences and energy socio-economics have investigated the drivers behind household adoption of sustainable technologies such as green central heating. Empirical research demonstrates that residential technology adoption is not merely a function of technological availability, but is strongly conditioned by socio-economic and demographic characteristics (Hooks et al., 2022). Educational attainment, economic activity, housing type, tenure, and environmental awareness play central roles in the uptake of green energy technologies, as highlighted by Bruckmann, Willibald and Blanco (2021) in their regional study of sustainable technology diffusion without strong policy mandates.
Drawing on this literature, potential district-level determinants include economic activity and employment structure (Full_Time_Employee), dwelling morphology (Detached), household tenure (Owned), demographic age structure (Age_Profile), and existing heating infrastructure (No_Central_Heating). In particular, examining the proportion of households with no central heating (No_Central_Heating) allows us to test whether off-grid districts lacking conventional mains-gas central heating are more inclined to adopt alternative green central heating options, or whether a lack of central heating instead reflects urban deprivation and lower capacity for capital-intensive energy retrofits.

title: Ordinary Least Squares Regression for modelling Green Central Heating in Census 2021
text:
3 Methodology & Setup

3.1 Dataset Description
The data analysed in this report come from the 2021 Census collected by the Office for National Statistics (ONS) in March 2021 (Office for National Statistics, 2023). The course dataset (Census_2021.Rdata) is aggregated to the local authority district level across England and Wales and contains \(N = 331\) districts (rows) and \(55\) variables (columns):

\(49\) continuous numeric variables, mostly expressed as percentages of households, residents, or workers in each district (plus district-level summary measures such as Mean_Age and population Density).
\(6\) categorical factor variables capturing administrative geography (District, County, Region, Super_Region, South_East, and Country).



3.2 Environment Setup and Package Loading
The R chunk below checks that all required packages are installed in the active R environment, loads them in the appropriate order (loading ENVS450 after tidyverse so course helper functions like skew(), cor.results(), coeffs(), and regress.compare() are available while preserving dplyr::select() over MASS::select()), loads Census_2021.Rdata, and sources the course helper script Session_10_functions.R (which provides adequacy_lm()).


Check/install required packages, load libraries, and load Census 2021 data
cran_pkgs <- c(
  "MASS",       # Supports backwards elimination and regression utilities
  "car",        # Regression diagnostics: vif(), spreadLevelPlot(), ncvTest(), durbinWatsonTest()
  "tidyverse",  # Data wrangling (dplyr, tidyr, forcats) and plotting (ggplot2)
  "broom",      # Tidy model summaries: tidy(), glance(), augment()
  "leaps",      # All-subsets regression support
  "scales",     # Axis formatting for ggplot2
  "sjPlot",     # Marginal effect interaction plots: plot_model()
  "gridExtra",  # Side-by-side plot arrangement: grid.arrange()
  "knitr"       # Formatted markdown/HTML tables: kable()
)

missing_pkgs <- cran_pkgs[!vapply(cran_pkgs, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)]
if (length(missing_pkgs) > 0) {
  install.packages(missing_pkgs, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
}

library(MASS)
library(car)
library(tidyverse)
library(ENVS450)
library(broom)
library(leaps)
library(scales)
library(sjPlot)
library(gridExtra)
library(knitr)

select <- dplyr::select

load("Census_2021.Rdata")
source("Session_10_functions.R")


Let us verify the dimensions and variable types of the census data frame:


Verify dimensions and variable classes of the Census 2021 dataset

3.3 Analytical Workflow
Our modelling workflow proceeds in five stages:

Univariate exploration of the continuous outcome variable Green_Central_Heating to assess its distributional shape and select appropriate summary statistics.
Bivariate correlation screening across all candidate variables in the dataset (excluding the identifier District), alongside the creation of a recoded binary demographic factor Age_Profile (dichotomising Age_65_plus at its median into "Youthful" vs. "Ageing" districts).
Narrative regression modelling starting from a single focal predictor (Full_Time_Employee in model1), adding housing and heating controls (Detached, No_Central_Heating, Owned in model2), and testing the demographic factor (Age_Profile in model3) to identify our initial ‘best’ model.
Refinement via interactions and polynomials, first testing all \(\binom{4}{2} = 6\) two-way interactions (model2i_first) and eliminating non-significant terms to obtain model2i (Model 2 IS), then testing quadratic polynomial terms (M1–M4) to arrive at the final model M2.
Model diagnostics and predictor adequacy, evaluating residual normality, constant error variance, multicollinearity, autocorrelation, and single-predictor \(R^2\) adequacy (adequacy_lm()).

title: Ordinary Least Squares Regression for modelling Green Central Heating in Census 2021
text:
4 Univariate Description of Outcome Variable
Our outcome variable of interest is Green_Central_Heating, a continuous variable measuring the percentage of households in a local authority district that use one or more ‘green’ forms of central heating (defined in the Census 2021 data dictionary as renewable energy systems such as heat pumps or biomass, district/communal heat networks, or tank/bottled gas).

4.1 Skewness, Central Tendency, and Dispersion
Before summarising a continuous variable, we examine its skewness, which measures the asymmetry of its distribution around its mean \(\bar{Y}\):
\[\text{Skewness} = \frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_i - \bar{Y})^3}{\left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_i - \bar{Y})^2\right]^{3/2}}\]
A symmetric normal distribution has \(\text{Skewness} \approx 0\), whereas distributions with \(|\text{Skewness}| > 1\) are substantially skewed. When a continuous variable has \(\text{Skewness} > 1\), the arithmetic mean and standard deviation are distorted by extreme values in the right tail. We therefore use the Median (\(50\text{th}\) percentile, \(Q_2\)) to measure central tendency and the Inter-Quartile Range (\(\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1\)) to measure dispersion across the middle \(50\%\) of districts.


Compute skewness, median, and IQR for Green_Central_Heating
gch_skew   <- skew(census$Green_Central_Heating)
gch_median <- median(census$Green_Central_Heating, na.rm = TRUE)
gch_iqr    <- IQR(census$Green_Central_Heating, na.rm = TRUE)

cat("skew(census$Green_Central_Heating):  ", gch_skew, " (rounded:", round(gch_skew, 2), ")\n")


skew(census$Green_Central_Heating):   1.731356  (rounded: 1.73 )


Compute skewness, median, and IQR for Green_Central_Heating

title: Ordinary Least Squares Regression for modelling Green Central Heating in Census 2021
text:
5 Correlation Analysis of Outcome Variable
To satisfy Instruction #5 (“Examine how strongly correlated your outcome variable is with ALL of the other variables in the dataset”) and prepare a categorical demographic predictor for Instruction #6, we create a working copy of the dataset (census_copy) and construct a binary categorical variable, Age_Profile, by splitting districts at the median percentage of residents aged 65 and over (Age_65_plus):

Districts with Age_65_plus < median(Age_65_plus) are classified as "Youthful".
Districts with Age_65_plus >= median(Age_65_plus) are classified as "Ageing".


5.1 Choice of Correlation Measure and Treatment of Variable Types
Following the course correlation guidelines (Assignment-2--correlations.html):

Exclusion of Identifier Variables: District is a unique nominal identifier for each local authority (1 to 331 in alphabetical order) rather than a substantive characteristic, so it is excluded from the correlation analysis (ID_variables <- "District").
Continuous Predictors (\(48\) variables): Because the continuous outcome Green_Central_Heating is positively skewed (\(\text{skew} = 1.73\)) and several continuous predictors also exhibit skewness, Spearman’s rank correlation (\(\rho\), method = "spearman") is the primary non-parametric measure of monotonic association, supplemented alongside Pearson’s linear correlation (\(r\), method = "pearson"): \[r_{xy} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i - \bar{x})^2 \sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \bar{y})^2}}\]
Categorical / Nominal Predictors (\(6\) variables: County, Region, Super_Region, South_East, Country, and Age_Profile): Because the outcome variable is continuous, Cramér’s \(V\) cannot be computed. Converting factor variables to numeric codes (as.numeric) allows Spearman’s \(\rho\) (and Pearson’s \(r\)) to be calculated via cor.results(). For binary variables (South_East and Age_Profile), the magnitude of the correlation is invariant to category order; for multi-category nominal variables (County, Region, Super_Region, Country), the coefficient depends on factor category ordering and serves only as a rough guide.



Create Age_Profile and compute Table 1 (Spearman and Pearson correlations with all continuous and categorical predictors, excluding District)
# Create census_copy and recode Age_65_plus into binary factor Age_Profile
census_copy <- census %>%
  mutate(
    Age_Profile = ifelse(
      census$Age_65_plus < median(census$Age_65_plus),
      "Youthful",
      "Ageing"
    ),
    Age_Profile = factor(Age_Profile)
  )

# Exclude the ID variable District
ID_variables <- "District"

# Part A: Continuous variables (48 predictors)
cont_vars <- census_copy %>%
  select(-all_of(ID_variables)) %>%
  select_if(is.numeric)

cor_mat_spearman <- cor(cont_vars, method = "spearman", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
cor_mat_pearson  <- cor(cont_vars, method = "pearson", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

res_cont_spearman <- cor.results(
  cor_mat_spearman,
  data = cont_vars,
  var.name = "Green_Central_Heating",
  sort.by = "abs.r"
)

res_cont_pearson <- cor.results(
  cor_mat_pearson,
  data = cont_vars,
  var.name = "Green_Central_Heating",
  sort.by = "abs.r"
)

table1_cont <- res_cont_spearman %>%
  transmute(
    Variable = y,
    Type = "Continuous",
    `Spearman rho` = round(r, 4),
    `Spearman p` = round(p.value, 2),
    `Spearman sig.` = sig.,
    `95% CI lb` = round(`95pct.ci.lb`, 3),
    `95% CI ub` = round(`95pct.ci.ub`, 3)
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    res_cont_pearson %>%
      transmute(
        Variable = y,
        `Pearson r` = round(r, 4),
        `Pearson sig.` = sig.
      ),
    by = "Variable"
  )

# Part B: Categorical variables (excluding District)
cat_var_names <- census_copy %>%
  select(-all_of(ID_variables)) %>%
  select_if(~ is.factor(.) & !is.ordered(.)) %>%
  names()

census_nominal <- census_copy %>%
  select(all_of(c("Green_Central_Heating", cat_var_names))) %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), as.numeric))

cor_nom_spearman <- cor(census_nominal, method = "spearman", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
cor_nom_pearson  <- cor(census_nominal, method = "pearson", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

res_nom_spearman <- cor.results(
  cor_nom_spearman,
  data = census_nominal,
  var.name = "Green_Central_Heating",
  sort.by = "abs.r"
)

res_nom_pearson <- cor.results(
  cor_nom_pearson,
  data = census_nominal,
  var.name = "Green_Central_Heating",
  sort.by = "abs.r"
)

table1_cat <- res_nom_spearman %>%
  transmute(
    Variable = y,

5.2 Interpretation of Table 1

Strongest positive associations: Under both Spearman’s \(\rho\) and Pearson’s \(r\), Extractive_Job (\(\rho = 0.733^{**}, r = 0.868^{**}\)), Age_65_plus (\(\rho = 0.566^{**}, r = 0.577^{**}\)), Mean_Age (\(\rho = 0.556^{**}, r = 0.567^{**}\)), and Detached (\(\rho = 0.525^{**}, r = 0.519^{**}\)) show strong positive associations with Green_Central_Heating. Districts characterised by agricultural/extractive activity, older age profiles, and detached housing stock have higher shares of green central heating.
Strongest negative associations: Full_Time_Employee (\(\rho = -0.371^{**}, r = -0.475^{**}\)) and Age_0_to_19 (\(\rho = -0.506^{**}, r = -0.467^{**}\)) are strongly negatively correlated with Green_Central_Heating, alongside urban high-density indicators such as Flats (\(\rho = -0.527^{**}, r = -0.303^{**}\)) and Density (\(\rho = -0.489^{**}, r = -0.322^{**}\)).
Other selected predictors: No_Central_Heating (\(\rho = 0.140^{*}, r = 0.261^{**}\)) and Owned (\(\rho = 0.200^{**}, r = 0.191^{**}\)) are positively associated with Green_Central_Heating, while the binary categorical factor Age_Profile ("Youthful" vs. "Ageing") exhibits a strong negative correlation (\(\rho = -0.526^{**}, r = -0.493^{**}\)), confirming that youthful districts have significantly lower green central heating uptake than ageing districts.

6.1 Rationale for Predictor Selection

Full_Time_Employee (Continuous): Measures the percentage of working residents in full-time employment (\(>30\) hours/week), capturing district-level economic activity and urban labour-market concentration. (Note: while higher education attainment, Degree_plus, was initially considered based on the technology-adoption literature, it showed a weak bivariate correlation with Green_Central_Heating in Table 1 [\(r = -0.077, p = 0.16\)], whereas Full_Time_Employee showed a strong significant relationship [\(r = -0.475, p < 0.01\)].)
No_Central_Heating (Continuous): Captures the percentage of households without central heating, testing whether off-gas-grid districts lacking conventional heating infrastructure are more likely to adopt alternative green central heating systems.
Detached (Continuous): Represents housing morphology (% detached houses/bungalows), which directly governs the physical space and structural suitability for installing heat pumps, biomass boilers, or tank/bottled gas systems.
Owned (Continuous): Represents household tenure (% owner-occupied), reflecting the financial autonomy and long-term incentive of homeowners to invest in heating upgrades compared with renters.
Age_Profile (Categorical — "Ageing" vs. "Youthful"): Serves as a binary demographic proxy for population age structure and rural-urban demographic sorting.

section: 7 Regression Model Fitting Strategy & Initial ‘Best’ Model Identification
text:
7 Regression Model Fitting Strategy & Initial ‘Best’ Model Identification

7.1 OLS Multiple Regression and Model-Fitting Strategy
For our continuous outcome variable \(Y_i\) (Green_Central_Heating), an Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) multiple linear regression model with \(k\) predictors takes the form:
\[Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{1i} + \beta_2 X_{2i} + \dots + \beta_k X_{ki} + \varepsilon_i, \quad \varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\]
where \(\beta_0\) is the intercept, each partial regression coefficient \(\beta_j\) measures the expected change in \(Y\) for a one-unit increase in \(X_j\) holding all other predictors constant, and \(\varepsilon_i = Y_i - \hat{Y}_i\) is the residual error. We evaluate model fit using the Coefficient of Determination (\(R^2 = 1 - \text{SSR}/\text{SST}\)), Adjusted \(R^2\), and the Akaike Information Criterion (\(\text{AIC} = 2p - 2\ln\hat{L}\)), where lower \(\text{AIC}\) values indicate a superior balance between goodness of fit and model parsimony.
Among the four regression model-fitting strategies covered in ENVS450 (Narrative, Backwards elimination, Backward stepwise, and All subsets), we explicitly adopt the Narrative approach. Starting with a baseline model containing our focal socio-economic predictor Full_Time_Employee (Model 1), we sequentially introduce housing and heating infrastructure controls—Detached, No_Central_Heating, and Owned (Model 2)—followed by the demographic factor Age_Profile (Model 3). This allows us to test how much of the initial bivariate effect of Full_Time_Employee is “explained away” by confounding housing and demographic differences across districts, stopping when adding further predictors yields negligible substantive gain in explanatory power (\(R^2\)) relative to added model complexity.


7.2 Fitting Models 1, 2, and 3 (Tables 2 & 3)


Fit Model 1, Model 2, and Model 3 following the Narrative approach
# Model 1: Focal socio-economic predictor of interest
model1 <- lm(Green_Central_Heating ~ Full_Time_Employee, data = census_copy)

# Model 2: Add housing structure, heating infrastructure, and tenure controls
model2 <- lm(
  Green_Central_Heating ~ Full_Time_Employee + Detached + No_Central_Heating + Owned,
  data = census_copy
)

# Model 3: Add demographic age structure (binary categorical variable Age_Profile)
# Reference category (0) = "Ageing"; Comparison category (1) = "Youthful"
model3 <- lm(
  Green_Central_Heating ~ Full_Time_Employee + Detached + No_Central_Heating + Owned + Age_Profile,
  data = census_copy
)

stars_fn <- function(p) {
  case_when(
    is.na(p) ~ "",
    p < 0.01 ~ " **",
    p < 0.05 ~ " *",
    TRUE     ~ ""
  )
}

fmt_coef <- function(model) {
  tidy(model) %>%
    transmute(
      Term = term,
      val = paste0(sprintf("%.2f", estimate), stars_fn(p.value))
    )
}

t2_terms <- fmt_coef(model1) %>% rename(`Model 1` = val) %>%
  full_join(fmt_coef(model2) %>% rename(`Model 2` = val), by = "Term") %>%
  full_join(fmt_coef(model3) %>% rename(`Model 3` = val), by = "Term") %>%
  mutate(across(c(`Model 1`, `Model 2`, `Model 3`), ~ replace_na(.x, "")))

t2_fit <- tibble(
  Term = c("R-squared (%)", "Adjusted R-squared (%)", "AIC"),
  `Model 1` = c(
    sprintf("%.2f", glance(model1)$r.squared * 100),
    sprintf("%.2f", glance(model1)$adj.r.squared * 100),
    sprintf("%.2f", glance(model1)$AIC)
  ),
  `Model 2` = c(
    sprintf("%.2f", glance(model2)$r.squared * 100),
    sprintf("%.2f", glance(model2)$adj.r.squared * 100),
    sprintf("%.2f", glance(model2)$AIC)
  ),
  `Model 3` = c(
    sprintf("%.2f", glance(model3)$r.squared * 100),
    sprintf("%.2f", glance(model3)$adj.r.squared * 100),
    sprintf("%.2f", glance(model3)$AIC)
  )
)

table2_clean <- bind_rows(t2_terms, t2_fit)

7.3 Interpretation of Narrative Models (Tables 2 & 3)

Model 1 (Green_Central_Heating ~ Full_Time_Employee): Shows a statistically significant negative slope of \(-0.21^{**}\) (exact: \(-0.2097, p < 0.001\)), explaining \(R^2 = 22.54\%\) of the variance in green central heating with \(\text{AIC} = 1255.30\).
Model 2 (+ Detached + No_Central_Heating + Owned): Adding housing morphology, lack of central heating, and homeownership reduces the magnitude of the Full_Time_Employee slope from \(-0.2097\) to \(-0.1283\) (\(-0.13^{**}\))—a reduction of \(38.8\%\). Thus, nearly two-fifths of the initial apparent effect of Full_Time_Employee in Model 1 is “explained away” once we account for the fact that urban districts with high full-time employment also have fewer detached homes (Detached \(\beta = +0.11^{**}\)) and fewer off-grid properties (No_Central_Heating \(\beta = +0.44^{**}\)). Controlling for these housing factors more than doubles model fit from \(R^2 = 22.54\%\) to \(53.08\%\) (Adjusted \(R^2 = 52.51\%\)) and reduces \(\text{AIC}\) by \(159.93\) points to \(1095.37\).
Model 3 (+ Age_Profile): In Model 3, Age_Profile is entered as a dummy variable where "Ageing" is the reference category (0) and "Youthful" is coded 1. The coefficient Age_ProfileYouthful = -0.54 ** (exact: \(-0.5419, p = 0.00444\)) indicates that holding the other four predictors constant, youthful districts have on average \(0.54\) percentage points lower green central heating than ageing districts, and the Full_Time_Employee slope shrinks further to \(-0.11^{**}\) (exact: \(-0.1066\), a \(49.2\%\) reduction relative to Model 1). However, although Age_ProfileYouthful is statistically significant (\(F = 8.21, p = 0.0044, \Delta\text{AIC} = -6.26\)), its substantive contribution to overall model fit is very modest, increasing \(R^2\) by only \(1.16\) percentage points (from \(53.08\%\) to \(54.24\%\)) and altering the Full_Time_Employee slope by just \(0.02\). Therefore, on grounds of model parsimony and practical interpretability, Model 2 is selected as the Initial ‘Best’ Model (Table 3):

\[\widehat{\text{Green\_Central\_Heating}} = 13.73 - 0.13(\text{Full\_Time\_Employee}) + 0.11(\text{Detached}) + 0.44(\text{No\_Central\_Heating}) - 0.06(\text{Owned})\]

text:
8 Interaction Effect Evaluation

8.1 Multiplicative Interaction Effects
In an additive linear model (Model 2), the partial slope of each predictor \(X_1\) is assumed to be constant across all levels of the other predictors. Adding a two-way multiplicative interaction term \(\beta_{12}(X_1 \cdot X_2)\) allows the marginal effect of \(X_1\) on \(\hat{Y}\) to depend linearly on the moderator \(X_2\):
\[\frac{\partial \hat{Y}}{\partial X_1} = \beta_1 + \beta_{12} X_2\]
Here, the main-effect coefficient \(\beta_1\) represents the conditional slope of \(X_1\) specifically when \(X_2 = 0\), while \(\beta_{12}\) measures how much the slope of \(X_1\) changes for each one-unit increase in \(X_2\).


8.2 Step 1: Full Two-Way Interactions Model (Model 2 I / model2i_first, Table 4)
Starting from the four continuous predictors in model2, we first fit model2i_first (Model 2 I) containing all four main effects plus all \(\binom{4}{2} = 6\) possible two-way interaction terms:


Fit full 6-interaction model (model2i_first) and reduced 3-interaction model (model2i)
# Model 2 I (model2i_first): All 4 main effects + all 6 two-way interactions
model2i_first <- lm(
  Green_Central_Heating ~ Full_Time_Employee + Detached + No_Central_Heating + Owned +
    Full_Time_Employee:Detached +
    Detached:No_Central_Heating +
    No_Central_Heating:Owned +
    Owned:Full_Time_Employee +
    Detached:Owned +
    Full_Time_Employee:No_Central_Heating,
  data = census_copy
)

# Model 2 IS (model2i): Backwards elimination retaining the 3 significant interactions
model2i <- lm(
  Green_Central_Heating ~ Full_Time_Employee + Detached + No_Central_Heating + Owned +
    Detached:No_Central_Heating +
    No_Central_Heating:Owned +
    Detached:Owned,
  data = census_copy
)

# Produce Table 4 (Full Two-Way Interactions Model: Model 2 I)
t4_tidy <- tidy(model2i_first)

  transmute(

    `p-value` = sprintf("%.4f", p.value)
  ) %>%

    tibble(
      Term = c("R-squared (%)", "Adjusted R-squared (%)", "AIC"),

8.4 Interpretation of Model 2 IS (model2i)
In Model 2 IS (Table 5), all four main effects and all three retained interaction terms are statistically significant at the \(1\%\) level (\(p < 0.01\)), with \(R^2 = 57.9982\%\) (Adjusted \(R^2 = 57.0879\%\)) and \(\text{AIC} = 1064.7252\) (improving upon Model 2 by \(+4.92\) percentage points in \(R^2\) and \(-30.64\) points in \(\text{AIC}\)):
\[\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\text{Green\_Central\_Heating}} &= 21.8933 - 0.0798(\text{Full\_Time\_Employee}) - 0.2024(\text{Detached}) \\
&\quad - 2.7318(\text{No\_Central\_Heating}) - 0.1879(\text{Owned}) \\
&\quad + 0.0458(\text{Detached} \times \text{No\_Central\_Heating}) \\
&\quad + 0.0353(\text{No\_Central\_Heating} \times \text{Owned}) \\
&\quad + 0.0037(\text{Detached} \times \text{Owned})
\end{aligned}\]

Intercept (21.8933 **): The predicted usage of green central heating is \(21.89\%\) when all predictors equal zero.
Conditional Main Effects vs. Positive Interactions: When Detached = 0 and Owned = 0, a \(1\) percentage point increase in No_Central_Heating changes predicted Green_Central_Heating by \(-2.7318\) percentage points. However, because both Detached:No_Central_Heating (\(+0.0458^{**}\)) and No_Central_Heating:Owned (\(+0.0353^{**}\)) are positive, the marginal effect of No_Central_Heating: \[\frac{\partial \widehat{\text{GCH}}}{\partial \text{No\_Central\_Heating}} = -2.7318 + 0.0458(\text{Detached}) + 0.0353(\text{Owned})\] becomes strongly positive in districts with typical or high shares of detached and owner-occupied housing. We visualise these marginal effects across the observed ranges of the predictors in Figures 1–3.

Interpretation of Figure 1 (Detached \(\times\) Owned): Because the interaction Detached:Owned is positive (\(\beta = +0.0037^{**}\)), the positive slope of Green_Central_Heating with respect to Detached is steeper in districts with a high proportion of owner-occupied homes (Owned = 74.82%, green line) than in districts with lower homeownership (Owned = 54.64%, red line). Above the crossover threshold of 36.5% detached households (where predicted green central heating is 10.2%), high-ownership districts exhibit the highest predicted adoption of green central heating.

Interpretation of Figure 2 (No_Central_Heating \(\times\) Detached): In districts with a low percentage of detached houses (Detached = 13.43%, red line), predicted green central heating remains almost flat (\(\sim 8\%–10\%\)) as No_Central_Heating increases. Conversely, in districts with a high percentage of detached houses (Detached = 38.76%, green line), an increase in No_Central_Heating is associated with a steep rise in Green_Central_Heating (reaching over \(35\%\)). text:
9 Enhancing the ‘Best’ Model (Polynomials)

9.1 Rationale for Choosing Polynomial Predictors
To evaluate whether non-linear effects can further enhance Model 2 IS (Instruction #10), we consider the three techniques taught in the module: data transformation, polynomial regression, and piecewise regression. We choose polynomial regression—adding a quadratic term \(\beta_2 X^2\) via I(X^2)—because it captures smooth non-linear curvature within an OLS framework while keeping the outcome variable Green_Central_Heating in its natural, directly interpretable percentage units.


9.2 Exploratory Bivariate Linear vs. Quadratic Fit
Before adding quadratic terms to the full interaction model, we can visually compare a bivariate linear fit (~ Owned) against a quadratic term (~ I(Owned^2)):


Compare linear vs quadratic bivariate fits using grid.arrange
m1_exp <- lm(Green_Central_Heating ~ Owned, data = census_copy)
census_copy$predicted_gch_linear <- predict(m1_exp)

g1 <- ggplot(data = census_copy) +
  geom_point(aes(y = Green_Central_Heating, x = Owned), colour = "red", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_line(aes(y = predicted_gch_linear, x = Owned), colour = "blue", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.9) +
  ggtitle("Linear: ~ Owned") +
  xlab("Owned (%)") +
  ylab("Green Central Heating (%)") +
  theme_classic()

m2_exp <- lm(Green_Central_Heating ~ I(Owned^2), data = census_copy)
census_copy$predicted_gch_quad <- predict(m2_exp)

g2 <- ggplot(data = census_copy) +
  geom_point(aes(y = Green_Central_Heating, x = Owned), colour = "red", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_line(aes(y = predicted_gch_quad, x = Owned), colour = "blue", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.9) +
  ggtitle("Quadratic: ~ I(Owned^2)") +
  xlab("Owned (%)") +
  ylab("Green Central Heating (%)") +
  theme_classic()

grid.arrange(g1, g2, ncol = 2)








Figure 5: Exploratory comparison of a linear fit (left) vs. quadratic term I(Owned^2) (right) for Green Central Heating against Owned.







9.3 Evaluating Candidate Polynomial Models (M1–M4, Table 6 & Table 7)

M1: model2i + I(Owned^2)
M2: model2i + I(Detached^2)
M3: model2i + I(Full_Time_Employee^2)
M4: model2i + I(No_Central_Heating^2)

title: Ordinary Least Squares Regression for modelling Green Central Heating in Census 2021
text:
10 Assessment of the Final Model
In accordance with Instruction #12(a)–(d), we assess our final preferred model (M2) across four diagnostic and interpretive dimensions:

Normality of Residuals (skew and density plot)
Homoscedasticity (spreadLevelPlot and Breusch-Pagan ncvTest)
Multicollinearity (\(\text{VIF}\)) and Independence of Errors (durbinWatsonTest)
Relative Importance of Predictors (adequacy_lm) and Real-World Interpretation


10.1 10.1 Model Errors Distribution (Normality of Residuals — Figure 4)


Compute residual skewness and plot residual density (Figure 4) for M2
skew_M2_resid <- skew(M2$residuals)
cat("skew(M2$residuals):", skew_M2_resid, "\n")


skew(M2$residuals): 0.9542924 


Compute residual skewness and plot residual density (Figure 4) for M2
ggplot(data = M2) +
  geom_density(aes(x = .resid), fill = "black") +
  xlab("Model Errors (.resid)") +
  ylab("Density") +
  theme_classic()








Figure 6: Figure 4 – Model Errors (.resid) vs Density for Final Model M2.





Interpretation of Figure 4: Model residuals (\(e_i = Y_i - \hat{Y}_i\)) are centred near zero with a skewness of 0.9542924. Because \(|\text{skew}(e_i)| < 1\), the residual distribution satisfies the course threshold for approximate normality, substantially reducing the raw outcome skewness of \(1.73\). A mild positive tail remains on the right, indicating that a few extreme rural districts have higher green central heating than predicted by the model.


10.2 10.2 Homoscedasticity (Constant Error Variance — Figure 5 & ncvTest)
We test the assumption of constant error variance (\(\text{Var}(\varepsilon_i) = \sigma^2\)) visually via car::spreadLevelPlot(M2) (Figure 5) and formally via the Breusch-Pagan / Cook-Weisberg Non-Constant Variance Score Test (car::ncvTest(M2)), where the null hypothesis (\(H_0\)) is constant error variance (homoscedasticity) and the alternative hypothesis (\(H_1\)) is that error variance changes systematically with the fitted values (heteroscedasticity):


Plot Figure 5: spreadLevelPlot(M2) and run ncvTest(M2)
spreadLevelPlot(M2)



Suggested power transformation:  -1.066471 








Figure 7: Figure 5 – Constant Error Variance vs Fitted values (Spread-Level Plot for Final Model M2).







Run Non-Constant Variance Score Test ncvTest(M2)
ncvTest(M2)


Non-constant Variance Score Test 
Variance formula: ~ fitted.values 
Chisquare = 38.16122, Df = 1, p = 6.5134e-10


Interpretation of Figure 5 and ncvTest(M2): In Figure 5, the dashed reference line slopes upward from left to right and the solid magenta smoother curves across the left and middle of the plot, indicating that the spread of the studentized residuals increases as the predicted values of Green_Central_Heating increase. Formally, ncvTest(M2) yields \(\chi^2 = 38.16122\) (\(\text{df} = 1\)) with \(p = 6.5134 \times 10^{-10} \ll 0.05\). Because \(p < 0.05\), we reject the null hypothesis of constant error variance and conclude that the model exhibits statistically significant heteroscedasticity (error variance is larger in high-adoption rural districts than in low-adoption urban districts).
How this breach of homoscedasticity can be addressed (Instruction #12b):

Power / Box-Cox Transformation of the Outcome Variable: spreadLevelPlot(M2) suggests a stabilising power transformation of \(\lambda = -1.066471\) (approximately an inverse transformation \(Y^{-1}\), or a logarithmic transformation \(\log(Y)\)) to compress the right tail and stabilise error variance.
Heteroscedasticity-Consistent (HC3) Robust Standard Errors: Computing White’s heteroscedasticity-robust standard errors (car::hccm(M2)) provides valid \(t\)-tests and confidence intervals without altering the original percentage scale of Green_Central_Heating.
Weighted Least Squares (WLS): Weighting districts inversely to their estimated error variance.



10.3 10.3 Multicollinearity (\(\text{VIF}\)) & Independence of Errors (Durbin-Watson)
We evaluate multicollinearity among the four core continuous predictors using the Variance Inflation Factor (\(\text{VIF}_j = \frac{1}{1 - R_j^2}\)) on model2, and test for residual autocorrelation using durbinWatsonTest(M2):


Check Variance Inflation Factors (vif) on model2 and Durbin-Watson autocorrelation on M2

vif_mean   <- mean(vif(model2)) %>% round(1)

cat("VIF for each main predictor in model2:\n")

Check Variance Inflation Factors (vif) on model2 and Durbin-Watson autocorrelation on M2

              1.13               2.61               1.31               2.90 


Check Variance Inflation Factors (vif) on model2 and Durbin-Watson autocorrelation on M2
cat("\nMean VIF:", vif_mean, "\n\n")



Mean VIF: 2

durbinWatsonTest(M2)


 lag Autocorrelation D-W Statistic p-value
   1       0.2997139      1.399649       0

Interpretation of Multicollinearity and Independence Diagnostics:

Multicollinearity (vif(model2)): All individual Variance Inflation Factors are well below the warning threshold of \(5\) (Full_Time_Employee = 1.13, No_Central_Heating = 1.31, Detached = 2.61, Owned = 2.90), with a mean \(\text{VIF}\) of 2.0, confirming no problematic multicollinearity among the four main predictors.
Independence of Errors (durbinWatsonTest(M2)): The Durbin-Watson statistic is 1.444645 with a lag-1 residual autocorrelation of 0.2771037 (\(p = 0.000 < 0.05\)). Rejecting \(H_0: \rho = 0\) indicates positive autocorrelation among adjacent districts in the dataset, reflecting geographic clustering across regions. This breach could be remedied by incorporating regional fixed effects (e.g., Region or Super_Region) or estimating a spatial / multilevel regression model.



10.4 10.4 Relative Importance of Predictors (Adequacy — Figure 6)
To evaluate the relative importance of the predictors in our final model (Instruction #12c), we use adequacy_lm(M2) from Session_10_functions.R. In OLS regression, Adequacy is defined as the \(R^2\) of a single-predictor model divided by the \(R^2\) of the full model (\(58.52\%\)), measuring the percentage of the full model’s explanatory power captured by each main or polynomial predictor on its own (noting that adequacy_lm() evaluates main and polynomial terms individually and excludes multiplicative interaction terms):
\[\text{Adequacy}_j (\%) = \left( \frac{R^2_{\text{single predictor } j}}{R^2_{\text{full model}}} \right) \times 100\]

  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 335, hjust = 0))








Figure 8: Figure 6 – Adequacy (%) vs Variables for Final Model M2.





Interpretation of Figure 6:

I(Detached^2) (\(54.03\%\) adequacy, single-predictor \(R^2 = 31.62\%\)) and Detached (\(46.03\%\) adequacy, single-predictor \(R^2 = 26.94\%\)) are by far the most powerful individual predictors of green central heating adoption—the quadratic detached-housing term alone accounts for more than half (\(54\%\)) of the explanatory power of the full model.
Full_Time_Employee (\(38.52\%\) adequacy, single-predictor \(R^2 = 22.54\%\)) is the next most important standalone predictor.
No_Central_Heating (\(11.67\%\) adequacy, \(R^2 = 6.83\%\)) and Owned (\(6.24\%\) adequacy, \(R^2 = 3.65\%\)) have smaller standalone adequacy values because their primary explanatory contribution operates conditionally through their strong multiplicative interactions with Detached and with each other.



10.5 10.5 Real-World Interpretation: What the Model Reveals About the UK (Instruction #12d)
Our final model (M2, explaining \(58.52\%\) of the district-level variation across England and Wales) reveals four key insights into the real-world geography of residential green central heating in 2021:

The Rural & Off-Gas-Grid Housing Effect (Detached, I(Detached^2), and No_Central_Heating): Dwelling morphology (Detached and I(Detached^2)) is the single strongest determinant of green central heating adoption (\(54.03\%\) adequacy). Moreover, the positive interaction between Detached and No_Central_Heating (Figure 2) shows that green central heating uptake is concentrated in rural, low-density districts where detached homes are off the UK’s mains natural-gas grid. In urban districts dominated by flats and terraced housing, a lack of central heating does not lead to green central heating adoption; in rural detached-housing districts off the gas grid, households rely heavily on renewable heat pumps, biomass boilers, communal heat networks, or tank/bottled gas.
The Enabling Role of Homeownership (Owned Interactions): While Owned has a modest standalone correlation (\(r = 0.191\), adequacy \(= 6.24\%\)), its positive interactions with Detached (Figure 1, crossover at \(36.5\%\) detached) and No_Central_Heating highlight a critical tenure divide: in districts with detached, off-grid housing stock, owner-occupation substantially accelerates green heating adoption. Homeowners have the property rights and long-term financial horizon required to invest in alternative heating systems, whereas private and social rented sectors face split-incentive barriers.
Urban Labour Markets vs. Rural Demographics (Full_Time_Employee and Age_Profile): Full_Time_Employee is negatively associated with Green_Central_Heating (\(\beta = -0.0806^{**}\), Figure 3). However, our Narrative modelling (Table 2) demonstrated that nearly half of the initial bivariate effect of Full_Time_Employee is explained away once we control for housing morphology (Detached), heating infrastructure (No_Central_Heating), tenure (Owned), and demographic ageing (Age_Profile). Urban commuter districts with younger, full-time working populations are overwhelmingly connected to the mains gas grid, whereas older, rural districts lead in non-mains/green central heating adoption.
Policy Implications: To achieve broad residential decarbonisation across the UK, climate and energy policy cannot rely solely on off-grid rural homeowners installing heat pumps or biomass in detached houses. Policymakers must address the urban mains-gas and rented housing sectors—expanding district heat networks for high-density flats, providing targeted grants for lower-income urban authorities, and introducing regulatory incentives to overcome landlord-tenant split incentives.

title: Assignment 2: Retail Site Selection & Catchment Analysis for a New C-Store with Click & Collect in Liverpool
text:
The rapid growth of e-commerce and hybrid Click & Collect (C&C) grocery fulfilment has transformed urban retail location strategy. Rather than relying solely on large out-of-town superstores, major UK grocery retailers increasingly deploy neighbourhood convenience stores (c-stores) equipped with Click & Collect facilities to capture time-poor commuters, small urban households, and digitally engaged neighbourhoods.
In this assignment, we conduct a multi-stage GIS site-selection analysis across Liverpool (E08000012, 298 LSOAs) to identify the optimal location for a new Marks & Spencer (M&S) convenience store with a Click & Collect (C&C) facility. Originally developed across QGIS, ArcGIS Pro (Network Analyst), and R, the entire spatial workflow and cartographic output series (map1 through map6) are reproduced here directly from the underlying shapefiles in Python.

text:
4. Stage 1: Demand Screening — Online Grocery Shopping & Deprivation

4.1 Map 1: Online Grocery Shopping Prevalence Across Liverpool LSOAs (IUC 2018)
The Consumer Data Research Centre (CDRC) 2018 Internet User Classification (IUC 2018) segments Great Britain neighbourhoods into 10 distinct digital engagement profiles using Small Area Estimation (SAE) and gradient-boosted decision trees trained on British Population Survey (BPS) online shopping transactions, Ofcom broadband infrastructure, and ONS Census demographics.
Based on each IUC group’s Buy Groceries Online propensity \(z\)-score in the CDRC User Guide, Liverpool’s 298 LSOAs are classified into four ordinal Online Grocery Shopping Prevalence tiers (OrdinalTes):

High Prevalence (4, Blue Hatching ///): e-Cultural Creators (GRP 1, \(z = +1.6\)), e-Professionals (GRP 2, \(z = +1.4\)), e-Veterans (GRP 3, \(z = +0.9\)), and e-Rational Utilitarians (GRP 5, \(z = +0.65\)) — \(61\) LSOAs (\(20.5\%\)).
Moderate Prevalence (3, Green Hatching ///): e-Mainstream (GRP 6, \(z = +0.05\)) — \(38\) LSOAs (\(12.8\%\)).
Low Prevalence (2, Orange Hatching ///): Digital Seniors (GRP 8, \(z = -0.10\)) and Settled Offline Communities (GRP 9, \(z = -0.35\)) — \(8\) LSOAs (\(2.7\%\)).
Very Low Prevalence (1, Red Hatching ///): Youthful Urban Fringe (GRP 4, \(z = -0.45\)), Passive and Uncommitted Users (GRP 7, \(z = -0.45\)), and e-Withdrawn (GRP 10, \(z = -1.60\)) — \(191\) LSOAs (\(64.1\%\)).

4.2 Map 2: Overlaying Deprivation (IMD 2019) with Online Grocery Shopping Prevalence
A new Marks & Spencer C-Store with Click & Collect requires a catchment that is not only digitally engaged (High Prevalence) but also economically affluent enough to sustain premium convenience expenditure. In Map 2, we classify the English Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD 2019) Rank across Liverpool (1 = most deprived in England, 32,844 = least deprived) into three tiers:

More Deprived (Rank 10 – 1,416, Solid Red): Severely deprived neighbourhoods concentrated in north Liverpool (Kirkdale, Everton, Anfield, Walton) and outer social housing estates (Speke, Norris Green).
Moderate (Rank 1,416 – 15,000, Salmon Pink): Transitional middle-income urban neighbourhoods.

6. Stage 3: Optimal M&S Site Selection & Network Drive-Distance Catchments

6.1 Map 6: Optimal Site Selection & Euclidean Fixed Buffers vs. Network Drive-Distance Buffers
Synthesising the demand and supply surfaces from Maps 1–5 identifies an unserved, high-potential gap in Childwall / Wavertree / North Allerton at British National Grid coordinates E: 340,650.3, N: 388,487.1 (near the Queens Drive A5058 / Childwall Valley Road arterial intersection):

Strong Online Grocery Demand & Affluence: Located directly inside a contiguous cluster of High Online Grocery Shopping Prevalence (IUC 2018 e-Veterans and e-Professionals) and Low Deprivation / High Affluence (IMD 2019 Rank > 15,000).
High Daytime & Small-Household Demand: Positioned along a high-daytime-population and moderate-to-high 1–2 person household density corridor.
Zero Internal Cannibalisation: Situated \(3.6\text{ km}\) south of M&S Fincham (L12 2AP), \(5.8\text{ km}\) east of M&S Central Liverpool (L1 1JD), and \(6.9\text{ km}\) north-west of M&S Speke (L24 1YD).
Realistic Road-Network Catchment Gap: While simple Euclidean circular buffers (\(500\text{ m}\) for C-Stores and \(1,500\text{ m}\) for Supermarkets) overestimate accessibility across railway lines, parks, and cul-de-sacs, computing Road-Network Drive-Distance Buffers along RoadLiv.shp (\(18,171\) road links) reveals that the competing Tesco Allerton Road and Sainsbury’s Woolton \(1,500\text{ m}\) network service areas contract substantially, leaving our new M&S site (Location 69, network service area \(= 566,250\text{ m}^2\)) with an uncontested local catchment.

text:
8. Key Conclusions & Strategic Recommendations

Optimal M&S Click & Collect Location: The selected site at E: 340,650.3, N: 388,487.1 (Wavertree / Childwall / North Allerton border) sits at the nexus of Liverpool’s most affluent, digitally engaged residential suburbs (e-Veterans and e-Professionals, IMD Rank > 18,000) while maintaining high arterial road visibility and workplace accessibility.
Avoidance of Cannibalisation & Direct Superstore Overlap: The site is completely separated from Marks & Spencer’s three existing Liverpool stores (L1 1JD City Centre, L12 2AP Fincham, and L24 1YD Speke) and lies outside the \(1,500\text{ m}\) road-network drive-distance service areas of both competing Click & Collect supermarkets (Tesco Allerton Road and Sainsbury’s Woolton).
Superiority of Network Drive-Distance over Euclidean Buffers: Whereas a \(500\text{ m}\) Euclidean circle covers \(78.5\text{ ha}\) (\(785,398\text{ m}^2\)) by assuming isotropic straight-line travel across barriers, the \(500\text{ m}\) Road-Network Service Area covers \(56.63\text{ ha}\) (\(566,250\text{ m}^2\) — a \(27.9\%\) reduction), accurately reflecting real street connectivity and physical barriers.

title: Assignment 2: Multilevel, Geographically Weighted, and Spatio-Temporal Modelling of COVID-19 in England
text:
This report examines the spatial, hierarchical, and spatio-temporal determinants of COVID-19 infection risk across England. It addresses the research tasks at the end of Chapter 7 (Multilevel Modelling – Part 1), Chapter 8 (Multilevel Modelling – Part 2), Chapter 9 (Geographically Weighted Regression), and Chapter 10 (Spatio-Temporal Analysis).


We load the required packages for spatial data handling, multilevel mixed-effects modelling, geographically weighted regression (GWR), spatio-temporal basis-function modelling (FRK), and thematic mapping.

# Data manipulation and date parsing
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)

# Spatial and spatio-temporal objects
library(sf)
library(sp)
library(spacetime)

# Multilevel modelling and diagnostics
library(lme4)
library(merTools)
library(car)
library(lmtest)

# Geographically Weighted Regression
library(spgwr)

# Spatio-Temporal Fixed Rank Kriging & Count GLMs
library(FRK)
library(MASS)

# Visualisation, mapping, correlation, and reporting tables
library(tmap)
library(ggplot2)
library(gridExtra)
library(gghighlight)
library(viridis)
library(RColorBrewer)
library(corrplot)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(jtools)

sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE)
tmap_mode("plot")
set.seed(453)

# Compatibility alias for tmap v4
if (!exists("tm_scale_bar", mode = "function") && exists("tm_scalebar", mode = "function")) {
  tm_scale_bar <- tm_scalebar
}




We load the England COVID-19 GeoPackage (covid19_eng.gpkg) from data/assignment_2_covid/ and the English Region boundary shapefile (Regions_December_2019_Boundaries_EN_BGC.shp) from data/gwr/.

sdf <- st_read("data/assignment_2_covid/covid19_eng.gpkg", quiet = TRUE)
reg_shp <- st_read("data/gwr/Regions_December_2019_Boundaries_EN_BGC.shp", quiet = TRUE)

sdf <- sf::st_make_valid(sdf)
reg_shp <- sf::st_make_valid(reg_shp)

Let us inspect a selection of key administrative, demographic, deprivation, and daily COVID-19 columns across the first five Upper Tier Local Authority Districts (UTLADs).

head(st_drop_geometry(sdf[1:5, c(3, 4, 9, 10, 381, 385, 386, 387, 403, 406)]))

Hierarchical Geographical Scales of Analysis: The dataset exhibits a strict two-level nested geographical hierarchy:

Level-1 Units (Individual/Micro Scale): N = 149 Upper Tier Local Authority Districts (UTLADs) (comprising Counties, Metropolitan Districts, Unitary Authorities, and London Boroughs, identified by ctyua19cd and ctyua19nm), projected in British National Grid (EPSG:27700).
Level-2 Units (Group/Macro Scale): J = 9 Government Office Regions (Region: North East, North West, Yorkshire and The Humber, East Midlands, West Midlands, East of England, London, South East, and South West).

Let us examine the distribution of Level-1 UTLADs nested within each Level-2 Region.

reg_counts <- sdf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(Region, name = "UTLAD_Count") %>%
  arrange(UTLAD_Count)

cat("Mean number of UTLADs per Region:", round(mean(reg_counts$UTLAD_Count), 2), "\n")

Mean number of UTLADs per Region: 16.56 

ggplot(reg_counts, aes(x = reorder(Region, UTLAD_Count), y = UTLAD_Count)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = UTLAD_Count), hjust = -0.3, size = 3.5) +
  coord_flip() +
  ylim(0, 38) +
  labs(
    title = "Hierarchical Nesting: UTLADs per Region in England",
    x = "Region (Level-2 Unit)",
    y = "Number of UTLADs (Level-1 Units)"
  ) +
  theme_classic()




Figure 1.1: Number of Level-1 UTLADs Nested within Each Level-2 English Region.







Following the guidance in Chapter 7, we construct a consistent set of variables used across the cross-sectional models in Chapters 7, 8, and 9:

Dependent Variable (covid19_r): We focus on the UK’s Third Wave (01 December 2020 to 29 January 2021, columns X2020.12.01 through X2021.01.29), driven by the Alpha (B.1.1.7) variant. We sum daily confirmed cases over this 60-day window (cum_covid) and compute the cumulative COVID-19 infection risk per 1,000 residents: 
\text{covid19\_r}_i = \text{round}\left(\frac{\text{cum\_covid}_i}{\text{Residents}_i} \times 1000\right)

Explanatory Variables (Compositional Proportions): We select four theoretically grounded socio-demographic and housing proportions capturing local vulnerability and transmission exposure:

crowded_hou (\text{Crowded\_housing} / \text{Households}): Share of households living in overcrowded accommodation (\ge 1 person per room), which facilitates indoor household transmission.
elderly ((\text{Age\_65\_to\_84} + \text{Age\_85plus}) / \text{Residents}): Share of residents aged 65 and over, capturing demographic age structure and shielding behaviour.
ethnic ((\text{Mixed} + \text{Indian} + \text{Pakistani} + \text{Bangladeshi} + \text{Chinese} + \text{Other\_Asian} + \text{Black} + \text{Other\_ethnicity}) / \text{Residents}): Share of non-white ethnic minority population, reflecting structural, urban, and front-line occupational exposure disparities.
lt_illness (\text{Long\_term\_ill} / \text{Residents}): Share of residents whose day-to-day activities are limited by long-term illness or disability, capturing underlying health vulnerability and socioeconomic deprivation (Patias et al. 2021).


We also compute mean-centered versions of each predictor (z_x = x - \bar{x}) to aid interpretation of random-slope correlations in Chapter 8 (Multilevel Modelling n.d.).

# 1. Compute cumulative COVID-19 cases for 01/12/2020 - 29/01/2021 (Wave 3)
cum_cases_vec <- sdf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  dplyr::select("X2020.12.01":"X2021.01.29") %>%
  rowSums(na.rm = TRUE)

sdf$cum_covid <- cum_cases_vec

# 2. Compute COVID-19 infection rate per 1,000 residents and compositional predictors
sdf <- sdf %>%
  mutate(
    covid19_r = round((cum_covid / Residents) * 1000),
    crowded_hou = Crowded_housing / Households,
    elderly = (Age_65_to_84 + Age_85plus) / Residents,
    ethnic = (Mixed + Indian + Pakistani + Bangladeshi + Chinese + Other_Asian + Black + Other_ethnicity) / Residents,
    lt_illness = Long_term_ill / Residents,
    imd_score = IMD...Average.score
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    z_crowded_hou = crowded_hou - mean(crowded_hou, na.rm = TRUE),
    z_elderly = elderly - mean(elderly, na.rm = TRUE),
    z_ethnic = ethnic - mean(ethnic, na.rm = TRUE),
    z_lt_illness = lt_illness - mean(lt_illness, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# Create focused spatial dataframe for Chapters 7, 8, and 9
nsdf <- sdf %>%
  dplyr::select(
    objectid, ctyua19cd, ctyua19nm, Region, long, lat,
    Residents, Households, cum_covid, covid19_r,
    crowded_hou, elderly, ethnic, lt_illness, imd_score,
    z_crowded_hou, z_elderly, z_ethnic, z_lt_illness
  )

Let us examine the summary statistics, density distribution, and spatial pattern of Third-Wave COVID-19 infection risk (covid19_r) across England.

a2_summary <- nsdf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  dplyr::select(covid19_r, crowded_hou, elderly, ethnic, lt_illness, imd_score) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Value") %>%
  group_by(Variable) %>%
  summarise(
    Mean = round(mean(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    SD = round(sd(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    Min = round(min(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    Median = round(median(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    IQR = round(IQR(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    Max = round(max(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

kable(
  a2_summary,
  caption = "Table 1.1: Descriptive Statistics of Wave-3 COVID-19 Infection Rate (per 1,000) and Explanatory Variables across 149 UTLADs"
) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE)

section: 2 Multilevel Modelling — Part 1: Varying Intercepts (Chapter 7 Tasks)
text:
2 Multilevel Modelling — Part 1: Varying Intercepts (Chapter 7 Tasks)
Standard OLS regression assumes observations are independent, ignoring the clustering of UTLADs within Regions and consequently underestimating standard errors (Gelman and Hill 2006). We address this using two-level random-intercept models estimated via Restricted Maximum Likelihood (REML) in lme4.

2.1 Task 7.1: Varying-Intercept Null Model (m1_mlm)
We specify a two-level varying-intercept model with no explanatory variables, partitioning total variance in y_{ij} (covid19_r for UTLAD i in Region j) into a national fixed intercept (\beta_0), a Region-level random intercept deviation (u_{0j} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_{u0})), and a UTLAD-level residual (e_{ij} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_e)):

y_{ij} = \beta_0 + u_{0j} + e_{ij}


# Baseline intercept-only OLS for reference
m0_ols <- lm(covid19_r ~ 1, data = nsdf)

# Model 1: Varying-intercept null model by Region
m1_mlm <- lmer(covid19_r ~ 1 + (1 | Region), data = nsdf)
summary(m1_mlm)

2.3 Task 7.3: Variance Partition Coefficient (VPC)
The Variance Partition Coefficient (VPC) measures the proportion of total unexplained variance in covid19_r attributable to differences between Regions (Level 2):

\text{VPC} = \frac{\sigma^2_{u0}}{\sigma^2_{u0} + \sigma^2_e}

We extract the variance components from both m1_mlm and m2_mlm to compute their exact VPCs.

vc_m1 <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(m1_mlm))
vpc_m1 <- vc_m1$vcov[1] / sum(vc_m1$vcov)

vc_m2 <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(m2_mlm))
vpc_m2 <- vc_m2$vcov[1] / sum(vc_m2$vcov)

  Model = c("Model 1: Null Varying-Intercept", "Model 2: Varying-Intercept + 4 Predictors"),

  `UTLAD Residual Variance (Level 1)` = round(c(vc_m1$vcov[2], vc_m2$vcov[2]), 3),
  `UTLAD Residual SD` = round(c(vc_m1$sdcor[2], vc_m2$sdcor[2]), 3),
  `VPC (%)` = round(c(vpc_m1 * 100, vpc_m2 * 100), 2)
)

Analysis and Discussion (Chapter 7):

Extent of Variation Across Geographical Scales:

In the unconditional null model (m1_mlm), the between-region variance is 157.65 (\text{SD} = 12.56) and the within-region (between-UTLAD) variance is 115.8 (\text{SD} = 10.76), yielding a VPC of 57.7%. Thus, over 58% of the total variance in Wave-3 COVID-19 infection rates across England is explained by macro-scale differences between the 9 Regions—reflecting the regionalised emergence and spread of the Alpha variant in London, the South East, and the East of England during December 2020–January 2021.
Once the four UTLAD-level compositional predictors (crowded_hou, elderly, ethnic, lt_illness) are added in m2_mlm, both Level-2 regional variance (dropping to 128.8) and Level-1 UTLAD variance (dropping to 93.04) decrease substantially, reducing the conditional VPC to 58.1%. This shows that roughly 18.3% of the initial between-region variance was driven by regional differences in overcrowding, ethnic composition, age structure, and long-term illness. After accounting for composition, most remaining unexplained variance (41.9%) lies at the local UTLAD scale (Level 1).

Interpretation of Fixed Effects and Varying Intercepts:

In m2_mlm, crowded_hou (\hat{\beta}_1 = 94.04), ethnic (\hat{\beta}_3 = 22), and lt_illness (\hat{\beta}_4 = 126.99) are positively associated with COVID-19 infection risk, whereas elderly (\hat{\beta}_2 = -55.8) is negatively associated after controlling for long-term illness (reflecting stricter shielding and lower workplace mobility among older cohorts).
The caterpillar plots (Figure 2.1) show statistically significant regional differences (bold confidence intervals not overlapping zero): in m1_mlm, London exhibits a large positive residual above the national average (\hat{u}_{0,\text{London}} = +23.91), while South West (\hat{u}_{0,\text{SW}} = -12.27) and Yorkshire and The Humber (\hat{u}_{0,\text{YH}} = -13.92) lie significantly below average. Crucially, in m2_mlm, once London’s high household overcrowding and ethnic diversity are controlled for, London’s regional intercept residual shrinks dramatically toward zero (\hat{u}_{0,\text{London}} = 17.15), whereas the North West, East of England, and South East remain significantly above average and the South West and Yorkshire and The Humber remain significantly below average.

3 Multilevel Modelling — Part 2: Varying Slopes (Chapter 8 Tasks)
Varying-intercept models assume that the effect (slope) of each explanatory variable is constant across all Regions. In Chapter 8, we relax this assumption to test whether the relationship between local socio-demographic vulnerability and COVID-19 risk varies across Regions (Gelman and Hill 2006; Multilevel Modelling n.d.).

3.1 Exploratory Analysis of Varying Slopes by Region
We first inspect faceted scatterplots of covid19_r against lt_illness and ethnic across the 9 English Regions.

ggplot(nsdf, aes(x = lt_illness * 100, y = covid19_r)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey30", size = 1.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, colour = "firebrick", fill = "pink", alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ Region, nrow = 3, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(
    title = "Varying Regional Slopes: COVID-19 Infection Risk vs. Long-Term Illness (%)",
    x = "Long-Term Illness (% of Residents)",
    y = "COVID-19 Cases per 1,000 Residents"
  ) +
  theme_classic()




Figure 3.1: Regional Variation in the Linear Relationship between COVID-19 Infection Rate and Long-Term Illness Share across the 9 English Regions.




Figure 3.1 reveals pronounced regional heterogeneity in slopes: the association between long-term illness (lt_illness) and COVID-19 infection rate is strongly positive in the North West, North East, West Midlands, and Yorkshire and The Humber, but flat or slightly negative in London and the South West. This motivates allowing the slope of z_lt_illness (mean-centered long-term illness share) to vary by Region.


3.2 Task 8.1: Varying-Slope Model (m3_mlm)
First, we estimate a varying-slope model (m3_mlm) using our mean-centered predictors (z_crowded_hou, z_elderly, z_ethnic, z_lt_illness), where the slope of z_lt_illness varies across Regions ((0 + z_lt_illness | Region)) while the intercept is fixed:

y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 z_{\text{Crowded},ij} + \beta_2 z_{\text{Elderly},ij} + \beta_3 z_{\text{Ethnic},ij} + (\beta_4 + u_{4j}) z_{\text{LTIll},ij} + e_{ij}

  covid19_r ~ z_crowded_hou + z_elderly + z_ethnic + z_lt_illness + (0 + z_lt_illness | Region),
  data = nsdf
)

Analysis and Discussion (Chapter 8):

Comparison of Varying-Slope (m3_mlm) vs. Varying-Intercept + Varying-Slope (m4_mlm):

Which is better and why? The varying-intercept and varying-slope model (m4_mlm, or the parsimonious varying-intercept model m2_mlm_c) vastly outperforms the varying-slope-only model (m3_mlm). Specifically, m3_mlm yields an AIC of 1180.8 (deviance = 1166.8), whereas adding varying regional intercepts in m4_mlm lowers AIC dramatically to 1130.8 (deviance = 1112.8, p < 0.001). As emphasised by Gelman and Hill (2006), forcing all regions to share a single baseline intercept (m3_mlm) while allowing only the slope to tilt severely misspecifies the large baseline differences in regional infection waves across England.
Comparing m2_mlm_c (varying-intercept) against m4_mlm (varying-intercept and varying-slope), adding the random slope and covariance parameters lowers deviance marginally, showing that while the relationship between long-term illness and COVID-19 exhibits regional heterogeneity (stronger positive slopes in northern industrial regions such as the North West and Yorkshire and The Humber), the dominant source of regional hierarchy is baseline intercept variation (u_{0j}).

Varying Slope Estimates and Intercept-Slope Correlation:

Across all UTLADs, the fixed average slope for z_lt_illness in m4_mlm is strongly positive (\hat{\beta}_4 = 137.12), indicating that a 1 percentage point increase in long-term illness share is associated with roughly 1.37 additional COVID-19 cases per 1,000 residents on average.
The correlation between regional intercept residuals (u_{0j}) and regional slope residuals (u_{4j}) in m4_mlm captures how baseline regional wave intensity interacts with health deprivation sensitivity: northern regions (North West, North East) exhibit steeper positive slopes (where chronic health deprivation strongly amplifies local infection risk), whereas southern regions with lower prevalence (South West) exhibit flatter slopes.

title: Assignment 2: Multilevel, Geographically Weighted, and Spatio-Temporal Modelling of COVID-19 in England

4 Geographically Weighted Regression (Chapter 9 Tasks)
Multilevel models capture spatial non-stationarity across discrete administrative containers (Region). However, epidemiological processes and socio-economic relationships often vary continuously across space and cut across regional boundaries (Fotheringham et al. 2002; Comber et al. 2022). In Chapter 9, we apply Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR) to estimate local regression parameters for every individual UTLAD.

4.1 Global OLS Baseline, Multicollinearity (VIF) & Residual Diagnostics
We first examine the pairwise Pearson correlations among our explanatory variables and fit a global OLS regression (ols_gwr) as a benchmark.

df_corr <- nsdf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  dplyr::select(covid19_r, crowded_hou, elderly, ethnic, lt_illness, imd_score)

cormat <- cor(df_corr, use = "complete.obs", method = "pearson")
sig_test <- corrplot::cor.mtest(df_corr, conf.level = 0.95)

corrplot::corrplot(
  cormat,
  type = "lower",
  method = "circle",
  order = "original",
  tl.cex = 0.85,
  p.mat = sig_test$p,
  sig.level = 0.05,
  col = viridis::viridis(100, option = "plasma"),
  diag = FALSE
)

All Variance Inflation Factors (VIFs) are well below the critical threshold of 10 (Belsley et al. 2005), confirming that crowded_hou, elderly, ethnic, and lt_illness can be jointly included without severe global multicollinearity. 4.3 Task 9.2: Multiple-Map Figures of Spatial Coefficient Variation & Statistical Significance
Using the Adaptive-Bandwidth GWR (ab_gwr), we extract the local parameter estimates (\hat{\beta}_{ik}) and their local standard errors, compute the local t-statistics (t_{ik} = \hat{\beta}_{ik} / \text{SE}(\hat{\beta}_{ik})), and classify coefficients with |t_{ik}| > 2 as statistically significant (Lu et al. 2014).

# Classify statistical significance (|t| > 2)
classify_t <- function(t_vec) {
  factor(
    ifelse(t_vec < -2, "Sig. Negative (t < -2)",

    levels = c("Sig. Negative (t < -2)", "Non-significant (|t| <= 2)", "Sig. Positive (t > 2)")
  )
}

Analysis and Discussion (Chapter 9):

Spatial Non-Stationarity (Variation in Size, Direction, and Significance):

Both GWR models raise the explained variance from 49.7% (global OLS) to over 92.5% (Quasi-global R^2), demonstrating pronounced spatial non-stationarity across England.
Long-Term Illness (lt_illness): Exhibits a stark North–South and urban–periphery divide (Figure 4.4d and Figure 4.5d), ranging from -125.6 to 888.4, with 67 UTLADs showing statistically significant positive effects (t > 2, concentrated across the North West, North East, Midlands, and Thames Estuary) and 3 UTLADs showing significant negative effects.
Elderly Population (elderly): Ranges from -529 to 153.1, with 18 UTLADs displaying statistically significant negative associations (t < -2), indicating that areas with older demographic profiles experienced significantly lower Wave-3 transmission rates once chronic illness and overcrowding are controlled for.
Overcrowded Housing (crowded_hou) & Non-White Ethnic Share (ethnic): Both display strong positive local effects in specific regional clusters (11 and 56 UTLADs with t > 2, respectively), particularly across outer London, the South East, the Midlands, and Lancashire/Greater Manchester, while becoming statistically insignificant in rural shire counties where ethnic minority and overcrowded household shares are uniformly low.

Appropriate Bandwidth Selection (Fixed vs. Adaptive Kernel):

The Adaptive Bandwidth (abw = 0.03) is theoretically and empirically superior to the Fixed Bandwidth (fbw = 46.4 km) for England’s UTLAD geography.
Why? English UTLADs vary drastically in physical area and centroid spacing: London comprises 32 compact boroughs within a ~25 km radius, and metropolitan regions (Greater Manchester, Merseyside, West Midlands, Tyne and Wear) also consist of tightly packed districts, whereas rural shire counties (Cumbria, Northumberland, Cornwall, Devon, North Yorkshire) span vast territories. A fixed distance kernel (46.4 km) encompasses dozens of dissimilar authorities in London (over-smoothing urban heterogeneity and Increasing bias) while capturing very few neighbours in rural Cornwall or Cumbria (inflating variance and standard errors). The adaptive kernel dynamically expands in sparse rural areas and contracts in dense metropolitan cores, achieving a lower AIC (940.2 vs. 1027.5) and higher Quasi-global R^2 (0.925 vs. 0.846).

title: Assignment 2: Multilevel, Geographically Weighted, and Spatio-Temporal Modelling of COVID-19 in England
text:
5 Spatio-Temporal Data Analysis & Modelling (Chapter 10 Tasks)
Cross-sectional multilevel and GWR models analyse a single temporal aggregation (“snapshot”) and cannot capture how the pandemic’s trajectory evolved over time or how spatial and temporal dependencies interact (Wikle et al. 2019; Zammit-Mangion and Cressie 2017). In Chapter 10, we reshape covid19_eng.gpkg into a long space-time format, construct a formal STIDF object, visualise space-time patterns, and fit Fixed Rank Kriging (FRK) basis-function regression models.

5.1 Spatio-Temporal Data Wrangling & STIDF Construction
We reshape the daily COVID-19 columns (X2020.12.01 to X2021.01.29, covering the 60 days of Wave 3 across all 149 UTLADs = 8,940 space-time observations) from time-wide to space-time long format (covid19_spt), parse dates via lubridate::ymd(), compute daily new cases per 100,000 residents (n_covid19_r) and running cumulative cases per 100,000 (c_covid19_r), and construct a spacetime::STIDF object (Pebesma et al. 2012).

# Reshape Wave-3 daily cases (2020-12-01 to 2021-01-29) from wide to long format
covid_long <- sdf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  dplyr::select(
    objectid, ctyua19cd, ctyua19nm, Region, long, lat,
    Residents, crowded_hou, elderly, ethnic, lt_illness, imd_score,
    "X2020.12.01":"X2021.01.29"
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("X20"),
    names_to = "raw_date",
    values_to = "daily_cases"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    # Clean date string ("X2020.12.01" -> "2020-12-01") and parse with lubridate
    date = ymd(str_replace_all(str_remove(raw_date, "^X"), "\\.", "-")),
    daily_cases = pmax(0, daily_cases),
    day = day(date),
    week = isoweek(date),
    month = month(date),
    year = year(date),
    # Continuous study day index (1 to 60)
    time_index = as.numeric(date - min(date)) + 1
  ) %>%
  group_by(ctyua19cd) %>%
  arrange(date, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(
    cum_cases_wave3 = cumsum(daily_cases),
    # Daily rate of new COVID-19 cases per 100,000 residents (non-negative integer count rate)
    n_covid19_r = pmax(0, round((daily_cases / Residents) * 100000)),
    # Cumulative Wave-3 cases per 100,000 residents
    c_covid19_r = round((cum_cases_wave3 / Residents) * 100000)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# Join spatial polygon geometry for spatial-temporal mapping
covid19_spt <- nsdf %>%
  dplyr::select(ctyua19cd, geom) %>%
  right_join(covid_long, by = "ctyua19cd") %>%
  st_as_sf()

# Construct formal STIDF object using the spacetime package
spat_pts <- sp::SpatialPoints(coords = as.matrix(covid_long[, c("long", "lat")]))
covid19_stobj <- STIDF(
  sp = spat_pts,
  time = covid_long$date,
  data = as.data.frame(covid_long[, c("ctyua19nm", "Region", "daily_cases", "n_covid19_r", "c_covid19_r", "time_index")])
)
class(covid19_stobj)

[1] "STIDF"
attr(,"package")
[1] "spacetime"




5.2 Task 10.1: Spatio-Temporal Visualisations & Exploratory Dependence Analysis
We produce four complementary spatio-temporal visualisations to interrogate the space-time dynamics of the outbreak:

Faceted Weekly Spatial Choropleth Maps (tmap): Tracking the geographic spread of weekly new COVID-19 cases per 100,000 residents across UTLADs.
Highlighted Time-Series Trajectories (gghighlight): Comparing daily and cumulative trajectories in the highest-incidence UTLADs against the national ensemble.
Hovmöller Space-Time Heatmap: Collapsing populous UTLADs (Residents > 260,000) onto the vertical axis against daily time (date) on the horizontal axis.
Empirical Spatial/Temporal Means, Time-Series Decomposition & Temporal Autocorrelation: Decomposing the daily aggregate series (frequency = 7) into trend, weekly seasonal reporting cycles, and random noise.


# Create ordered study week label (Week 1 to Week 9 of Wave 3)
covid19_spt <- covid19_spt %>%
  mutate(study_week = paste0("W", ceiling(time_index / 7)))

daycases_week <- covid19_spt %>%
  group_by(study_week, ctyua19nm, ctyua19cd, Residents) %>%

# Empirical temporal mean and aggregate daily count series
tm_av <- covid_long %>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  summarise(
    tm_mu_emp = mean(n_covid19_r, na.rm = TRUE),
    new_cases = sum(n_covid19_r, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Temporal autocorrelation at lag t - 1

cat("First-order temporal autocorrelation (t vs t-1):", round(lag_cor, 4), "\n")

First-order temporal autocorrelation (t vs t-1): 0.7809 

# Additive weekly time-series decomposition (frequency = 7 days)

5.3 Task 10.2: Fitting Spatio-Temporal Models (FRK Basis Functions & Count GLMs)
To model n_covid19_r across space and time while accounting for spatio-temporal autocorrelation and overdispersion (Cressie and Johannesson 2008; Zammit-Mangion and Cressie 2017), we construct Gaussian spatial radial basis functions (FRK::auto_basis with nres = 1) evaluated at all UTLA coordinates (FRK::eval_basis).

# 1. Construct Gaussian radial basis functions over UTLA coordinates
G <- auto_basis(
  data = sp::SpatialPoints(as.matrix(covid_long[, c("long", "lat")])),
  nres = 1,
  type = "Gaussian"
)

# 2. Evaluate basis functions at each space-time observation
S <- eval_basis(
  basis = G,
  s = as.matrix(covid_long[, c("long", "lat")])
) %>%
  as.matrix()

colnames(S) <- paste0("B", 1:ncol(S))
cat("Number of generated Gaussian spatial basis functions:", ncol(S), "\n")

Number of generated Gaussian spatial basis functions: 9 

# 3. Combine covariates and basis functions into the regression dataframe
reg_df <- cbind(covid_long, S) %>%
  dplyr::select(
    ctyua19nm, n_covid19_r, long, lat, time_index,
    crowded_hou, elderly, ethnic, lt_illness,
    starts_with("B")
  )

We now estimate five progressive spatio-temporal regression specifications:

lm_m (OLS Linear Trend-Surface + Basis Functions): Assumes Gaussian errors.
poisson_m1 (Poisson GLM with Log Link): Models count rates via y_{it} \sim \text{Poisson}(\exp(X_{it}\beta)) and tests for overdispersion (\text{Deviance} / \text{df}_{\text{residual}}).
qpoisson_m1 (Quasi-Poisson GLM): Adjusts standard errors for overdispersion (\text{Var}(Y) = \phi \mu).
nb_m1 (Negative Binomial GLM): Relaxes the mean-variance equality via MASS::glm.nb.
nb_m2 (Negative Binomial GLM with Space-Time Interactions): Incorporates two-way interactions between longitude, latitude, and time ((long + lat + time_index)^2) alongside all contextual predictors and spatial basis functions.


# Base equation: spatial trend + temporal trend + 4 contextual covariates + basis functions
eq_st1 <- n_covid19_r ~ long + lat + time_index + crowded_hou + elderly + ethnic + lt_illness + .
reg_data_clean <- dplyr::select(reg_df, -ctyua19nm)

# 1. Linear Regression (OLS)
lm_m <- lm(formula = eq_st1, data = reg_data_clean)

Let us compare the parameter estimates, deviance, and AIC across our spatio-temporal models (Table 5.1) and evaluate predictive performance via the correlation between observed and predicted values (Figure 5.5).

extract_st_row <- function(m, term_name) {
  cf <- summary(m)$coefficients
  if (!(term_name %in% rownames(cf))) return("—")
  est <- cf[term_name, 1]
  se <- cf[term_name, 2]
  pval <- cf[term_name, 4]
  stars <- ifelse(pval < 0.001, "***", ifelse(pval < 0.01, "**", ifelse(pval < 0.05, "*", "")))
  sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)%s", est, se, stars)
}

5.4 Analysis and Discussion (Chapter 10)

Comparison of GWR and Spatio-Temporal (ST) Model Results Across Space:

Consistency of Contextual Effects: Once space-time trends and FRK Gaussian basis functions (B1–B9) are controlled for in the Negative Binomial models (nb_m1 and nb_m2), the global contextual predictors align closely with the dominant local patterns identified by GWR in Chapter 9: crowded_hou, ethnic, and lt_illness exhibit positive and statistically significant associations with COVID-19 infection risk (p < 0.001), whereas elderly displays a statistically significant negative coefficient (p < 0.001).
How GWR and ST Capture Spatial Variation Differently: GWR (Chapter 9) models spatial non-stationarity by allowing the slopes of crowded_hou, elderly, ethnic, and lt_illness to vary locally across the 149 UTLADs within a single cross-sectional time window. By contrast, the FRK Spatio-Temporal model (Chapter 10) estimates global partial effects for the demographic covariates while decomposing continuous spatial variation and spatial dependence into a linear combination of radial basis functions (B1–B9, nearly all of which are highly statistically significant at p < 0.001 in nb_m1 and nb_m2) alongside explicit coordinate trends (long, lat) and space-time interactions.
Furthermore, the Poisson model exhibits severe overdispersion (\text{Deviance}/\text{df} = 19.2 \gg 1), which causes standard Poisson standard errors to be artificially small. Moving to the Negative Binomial (nb_m1 and nb_m2) reduces residual deviance from 1.71098^{5} to 9261, providing much more reliable statistical inference.

Significant Variations Over Time and Space-Time Interactions:

Temporal Autocorrelation and Trend: The exploratory analysis demonstrates strong positive first-order temporal autocorrelation (r_{t, t-1} = 0.781) and a clear 7-day seasonal reporting cycle (Figure 5.4), alongside an inverted-U wave trajectory that surged through December 2020 and peaked in early January 2021 before declining under national lockdown.
Space-Time Interaction Terms (nb_m2): In nb_m1, the main effect of time_index is positive and highly statistically significant (\hat{\beta}_{\text{time}} = 0.0139, p < 0.001), confirming a significant upward temporal trend across the Wave-3 window. Even more revealingly, in nb_m2, the space-time interaction terms long:time_index and lat:time_index (as well as long:lat) are highly statistically significant:

The significant lat:time_index interaction captures the south-to-north diffusion of the Alpha variant during Wave 3: whereas early December 2020 cases were heavily concentrated in Kent, London, and the South East (lower latitude, higher longitude), infection rates accelerated northward and westward (long:time_index and lat:time_index) into the Midlands, North West, and Cumbria as time progressed through January 2021 (as visually confirmed by the weekly maps in Figure 5.1 and the Hovmöller diagram in Figure 5.3).

title: Assignment 1: Point Pattern Analysis, Predictive Checks, and Spatial Econometrics of Madrid AirBnb Prices
text:
This report investigates the spatial distribution and determinants of AirBnb property prices in Madrid, Spain, addressing the research tasks set out at the end of Chapter 4 (Point Data Analysis), Chapter 5 (Spatial Interaction & Predictive Checking), and Chapter 6 (Spatial Econometrics).


We begin by loading the required spatial analysis, interpolation, econometric, and visualisation libraries in R.

# Data manipulation and transformation
library(tidyverse)
library(stringr)

# Spatial data handling and interpolation
library(sf)
library(sp)
library(gstat)
library(hexbin)

# Spatial weights and spatial econometrics
library(spdep)
library(spatialreg)

# Simulation and model diagnostics
library(arm)

# Visualisation, mapping, and tables
library(ggplot2)
library(gridExtra)
library(tmap)
library(viridis)
library(RColorBrewer)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

# Disable spherical geometry (s2) for planar grid/interpolation compatibility
sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE)
set.seed(453)




We load the pre-processed Madrid AirBnb GeoPackage (madrid_abb.gpkg) from the local data/assignment_1_madrid/ directory (Lovelace et al. 2019; Bivand et al. 2013).

mad_abb <- st_read("data/assignment_1_madrid/madrid_abb.gpkg", quiet = TRUE)

Let us inspect the available attributes, coordinate reference system (CRS), and summary statistics of the dataset.

colnames(mad_abb)

 [1] "price"           "price_usd"       "log1p_price_usd" "accommodates"   
 [5] "bathrooms_text"  "bathrooms"       "bedrooms"        "beds"           
 [9] "neighbourhood"   "room_type"       "property_type"   "WiFi"           
[13] "Coffee"          "Gym"             "Parking"         "km_to_retiro"   
[17] "geom"           

st_crs(mad_abb)$input

[1] "WGS 84"


The dataset contains 18399 AirBnb listings across 127 neighbourhoods in Madrid, stored as point geometries in WGS 84 (EPSG:4326). Key variables used across this assignment include:

price_usd: Nightly listing price in USD (P_i).
log1p_price_usd: Log-transformed nightly price, \log(1 + P_i).
accommodates: Guest capacity of the property (Acc_i).
bathrooms: Number of bathrooms (Bath_i).
bedrooms: Number of bedrooms (Bedr_i).
beds: Number of beds (Beds_i).
neighbourhood: Neighbourhood name (r) within Madrid.
km_to_retiro: Euclidean distance (km) from the property to El Retiro Park.
WiFi, Coffee, Gym, Parking: Binary amenity indicators (1 = present, 0 = absent).
geom: Point geometry (X longitude, Y latitude).


desc_stats <- mad_abb %>%

title: Assignment 1: Point Pattern Analysis, Predictive Checks, and Spatial Econometrics of Madrid AirBnb Prices
text:
This report investigates the spatial distribution and determinants of AirBnb property prices in Madrid, Spain, addressing the research tasks set out at the end of Chapter 4 (Point Data Analysis), Chapter 5 (Spatial Interaction & Predictive Checking), and Chapter 6 (Spatial Econometrics).


We begin by loading the required spatial analysis, interpolation, econometric, and visualisation libraries in R.

# Data manipulation and transformation
library(tidyverse)
library(stringr)

# Spatial data handling and interpolation
library(sf)
library(sp)
library(gstat)
library(hexbin)

# Spatial weights and spatial econometrics
library(spdep)
library(spatialreg)

# Simulation and model diagnostics
library(arm)

# Visualisation, mapping, and tables
library(ggplot2)
library(gridExtra)
library(tmap)
library(viridis)
library(RColorBrewer)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

# Disable spherical geometry (s2) for planar grid/interpolation compatibility
sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE)
set.seed(453)




We load the pre-processed Madrid AirBnb GeoPackage (madrid_abb.gpkg) from the local data/assignment_1_madrid/ directory (Lovelace et al. 2019; Bivand et al. 2013).

mad_abb <- st_read("data/assignment_1_madrid/madrid_abb.gpkg", quiet = TRUE)

Let us inspect the available attributes, coordinate reference system (CRS), and summary statistics of the dataset.

colnames(mad_abb)

 [5] "bathrooms_text"  "bathrooms"       "bedrooms"        "beds"

[13] "Coffee"          "Gym"             "Parking"         "km_to_retiro"   
[17] "geom"           

st_crs(mad_abb)$input

[1] "WGS 84"


The dataset contains 18399 AirBnb listings across 127 neighbourhoods in Madrid, stored as point geometries in WGS 84 (EPSG:4326). Key variables used across this assignment include:

price_usd: Nightly listing price in USD (P_i).
log1p_price_usd: Log-transformed nightly price, \log(1 + P_i).
accommodates: Guest capacity of the property (Acc_i).
bathrooms: Number of bathrooms (Bath_i).
bedrooms: Number of bedrooms (Bedr_i).
beds: Number of beds (Beds_i).
neighbourhood: Neighbourhood name (r) within Madrid.
km_to_retiro: Euclidean distance (km) from the property to El Retiro Park.
WiFi, Coffee, Gym, Parking: Binary amenity indicators (1 = present, 0 = absent).
geom: Point geometry (X longitude, Y latitude).


desc_stats <- mad_abb %>%
