title: Assignment 1: Point Pattern Analysis, Predictive Checks, and Spatial Econometrics of Madrid AirBnb Prices
text:
2 Point Data Analysis (Chapter 4 Tasks)
Chapter 4 focuses on visualising dense spatial point patterns and interpolating continuous attribute surfaces from point samples (Brunsdon and Comber 2015).

2.1 Exploratory Price Distribution & Spatial Binning
Before constructing the spatial Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) and Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) surfaces, we examine the non-spatial distribution of raw (price_usd) versus log-transformed (log1p_price_usd) prices, alongside 2D spatial binning of listing coordinates.

# Histogram + 1D KDE of raw price_usd
p_raw_hist <- ggplot(mad_abb, aes(x = price_usd)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, aes(y = after_stat(density)), fill = "grey35", colour = "white") +
  geom_density(fill = "#FF6666", alpha = 0.45, colour = "#FF6666", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Raw AirBnb Price (USD)",
    x = "Price (USD)",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Histogram + 1D KDE of log1p_price_usd
p_log_hist <- ggplot(mad_abb, aes(x = log1p_price_usd)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, aes(y = after_stat(density)), fill = "grey35", colour = "white") +
  geom_density(fill = "#FF6666", alpha = 0.45, colour = "#FF6666", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Log-Transformed AirBnb Price",
    x = "log(1 + Price USD)",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

grid.arrange(p_raw_hist, p_log_hist, ncol = 2)




Figure 1.1: Distribution and 1D KDE of Raw USD Prices (left) vs. Log-Transformed Prices (right) in Madrid.




Raw AirBnb prices are heavily right-skewed (mean = $118.98, median = $60, maximum = $9999), with most properties clustered below $150 per night and a thin tail of luxury listings. Taking the natural logarithm (log1p_price_usd) compresses extreme values and yields a near-symmetric, bell-shaped distribution centered around 4.19.
To address point overplotting across the 18399 locations, we first compare raw point plotting with two-dimensional square binning (geom_bin2d) and hexagonal binning (geom_hex).

mad_coords <- as.data.frame(st_coordinates(mad_abb))

# Square 2D binning
sqbin <- ggplot() +
  geom_bin2d(data = mad_coords, aes(x = X, y = Y), bins = 40) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "viridis", name = "Count") +
  labs(title = "2D Square Binning", x = "Longitude (X)", y = "Latitude (Y)") +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_minimal()

# Hexagonal 2D binning
hexbin_plot <- ggplot() +
  geom_hex(data = mad_coords, aes(x = X, y = Y), bins = 40) +
  scale_fill_continuous(type = "viridis", name = "Count") +
  labs(title = "2D Hexagonal Binning", x = "Longitude (X)", y = "Latitude (Y)") +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_minimal()

grid.arrange(sqbin, hexbin_plot, ncol = 2)




Figure 1.2: Spatial Distribution of Madrid AirBnb Listings using Square Binning (left) and Hexagonal Binning (right).






2.2 Task 4.1: Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) of AirBnb Locations in Madrid
To obtain a smooth, continuous surface representing the spatial intensity (probability density) of AirBnb property locations across Madrid, we apply two-dimensional Kernel Density Estimation (stat_density2d_filled).

kde_surface <- ggplot(data = mad_abb) +
  stat_density2d_filled(
    data = mad_coords,
    aes(x = X, y = Y),
    alpha = 0.85,
    n = 100
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "viridis", name = "Density Level") +
  geom_sf(alpha = 0) +
  labs(
    title = "Spatial Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) of AirBnb Locations in Madrid",
    subtitle = "Continuous probability surface of listing concentration (WGS 84)",
    x = "Longitude",
    y = "Latitude"
  ) +
  theme_bw()

kde_surface




Figure 1.3: Two-Dimensional Spatial Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) of AirBnb Property Locations in Madrid.




Interpretation of the KDE Surface: The spatial KDE reveals an intense, monocentric concentration of AirBnb properties in the historic and tourist core of Madrid (Centro district, around longitudes -3.71^\circ to -3.69^\circ and latitudes 40.41^\circ to 40.43^\circ, covering neighbourhoods such as Sol, Embajadores, Palacio, Cortes, Justicia, and Universidad). Density decays radially outward into surrounding residential districts (Chamberí, Salamanca, Arganzuela, Retiro, and Tetuán), with peripheral suburban districts exhibiting very sparse listing density.


2.3 Task 4.2: Spatial Interpolation of AirBnb Prices via Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW)
While KDE estimates the density of point occurrences, it does not show how property values vary across space. To construct a continuous surface of AirBnb prices (\hat{z}(x) = \sum_i w_i z_i / \sum_i w_i), we apply Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) interpolation (Brunsdon and Comber 2015; Cressie 2015):

Create a regular target grid (mad.grid): A 100 \times 100 grid (10,000 evenly spaced prediction centres) spanning the bounding box of mad_abb.
Compute IDW predictions: Use gstat::idw() with nmax = 150 nearest neighbours for both raw USD prices (price_usd ~ 1) and log-transformed prices (log1p_price_usd ~ 1).
Render the interpolated raster surfaces: Map the predicted values (var1.pred) across the grid.


# 1. Create a 100 x 100 regular grid of cell centres over Madrid
mad.grid <- mad_abb %>%
  st_bbox() %>%
  st_as_sfc() %>%
  st_make_grid(
    n = 100,
    what = "centers"
  ) %>%
  st_as_sf() %>%
  cbind(., st_coordinates(.))

# Ensure identical CRS between source locations and target grid
st_crs(mad.grid) <- st_crs(mad_abb)

# 2. Fit IDW for raw price_usd (nmax = 150 nearest neighbours)
idw.raw <- idw(
  price_usd ~ 1,
  locations = mad_abb,
  newdata = mad.grid,
  nmax = 150
) %>%
  cbind(st_coordinates(.))

# 3. Fit IDW for log1p_price_usd (nmax = 150 nearest neighbours)
idw.log <- idw(
  log1p_price_usd ~ 1,
  locations = mad_abb,
  newdata = mad.grid,
  nmax = 150
) %>%
  cbind(st_coordinates(.))

Let us inspect the first rows of the interpolated IDW spatial object and plot both the raw price surface and the log-price surface.

head(st_drop_geometry(idw.raw), 5)

  var1.pred var1.var         X        Y
1  80.35464       NA -3.862370 40.33358
2  82.20369       NA -3.859291 40.33358
3  82.24160       NA -3.856212 40.33358
4  82.26039       NA -3.853133 40.33358
5  82.30258       NA -3.850054 40.33358



p_idw_raw <- ggplot(idw.raw, aes(x = X, y = Y, fill = var1.pred)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_viridis_b(option = "viridis", name = "Pred. USD ($)") +
  theme_void() +
  geom_sf(alpha = 0) +
  labs(
    title = "IDW Surface: Raw Price (USD)",
    subtitle = "Binned Viridis scale (nmax = 150)"
  ) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

p_idw_log <- ggplot(idw.log, aes(x = X, y = Y, fill = var1.pred)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", name = "Pred. log(Price)") +
  theme_void() +
  geom_sf(alpha = 0) +
  labs(
    title = "IDW Surface: Log Price",
    subtitle = "Continuous Magma scale (nmax = 150)"
  ) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

grid.arrange(p_idw_raw, p_idw_log, ncol = 2)




Figure 1.4: Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) Interpolated Surfaces of Madrid AirBnb Prices: Raw USD Price (left) and Log Price (right), using nmax = 150.




We can also use the IDW model to predict the nightly price of a single hypothetical property located near El Retiro Park (X = -3.6830, Y = 40.4153):

pt_retiro <- c(X = -3.6830, Y = 40.4153) %>%
  st_point() %>%
  st_sfc(crs = st_crs(mad_abb)) %>%
  st_sf()

idw.one <- idw(price_usd ~ 1, locations = mad_abb, newdata = pt_retiro, nmax = 150)


cat("Predicted nightly price near El Retiro Park: $", round(idw.one$var1.pred[1], 2), "USD\n")

Predicted nightly price near El Retiro Park: $ 166.67 USD


Interpretation of the IDW Price Surface: Unlike the KDE map—where intensity peaks strictly in the historic center—the IDW price surface highlights distinct high-price corridors extending into affluent districts such as Salamanca, Chamberí, Chamartín (north-central Madrid), and the eastern perimeter near San Blas-Canillejas (around the Wanda Metropolitano stadium and IFEMA exhibition centre), while southern districts (Usera, Villaverde, Puente de Vallecas, Carabanchel) form a persistent low-price belt.

title: Assignment 1: Point Pattern Analysis, Predictive Checks, and Spatial Econometrics of Madrid AirBnb Prices
text:
3 Regression Modelling & Predictive Checks (Chapter 5 Tasks)
Chapter 5 focuses on building regression models of property prices and evaluating their adequacy through Predictive Performance Checks (PPC) that account for both point predictions and inferential/predictive simulation uncertainty (Gelman and Hill 2006).

3.1 Task 5.1: Baseline Linear Regression Model for Raw Price (P_i)
We first estimate the baseline Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) model explaining raw price in USD (price_usd) as a linear function of four core structural property characteristics:

P_i = \alpha + \beta_1 Acc_i + \beta_2 Bath_i + \beta_3 Bedr_i + \beta_4 Beds_i + \epsilon_i


ba.price <- lm(price_usd ~ accommodates + bathrooms + bedrooms + beds, data = mad_abb)
summary(ba.price)

3.3 Task 5.3: Predictive Check Analysis & Model Comparison
To evaluate how well each model captures the true data-generating process, we perform two levels of Predictive Performance Checks (PPC) following Gelman and Hill (2006):

Point-Estimate Predictive Check: Comparing the empirical kernel density of the deterministic fitted values (\hat{y}_i = X_i\hat{\beta}) against the observed outcome distribution (y_i).
Simulated Predictive Check (Inferential + Predictive Uncertainty): Using arm::sim() to draw posterior parameter realisations (\tilde{\beta}, \tilde{\sigma}) and simulating 250 synthetic outcome vectors \tilde{y} \sim \mathcal{N}(X\tilde{\beta}, \tilde{\sigma}^2).


par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 3, 1))

# 1. Point-estimate check for Raw Price model
plot(
  density(ba.price$fitted.values),
  xlim = c(-50, 600),
  ylim = c(0, max(max(density(ba.price$fitted.values)$y), max(density(mad_abb$price_usd)$y)) * 1.05),
  col = "black",
  lwd = 2,
  xlab = "Price (USD)",
  ylab = "Density",
  main = "Point Check: Raw Price Model"
)
lines(density(mad_abb$price_usd), col = "red", lwd = 2)
legend("topright", legend = c("Predicted (Fitted)", "Actual"), col = c("black", "red"), lwd = 2, bty = "n")

# 2. Point-estimate check for Log Price model
plot(
  density(ba.log_price$fitted.values),
  xlim = c(1.5, 8.5),
  ylim = c(0, max(max(density(ba.log_price$fitted.values)$y), max(density(mad_abb$log1p_price_usd)$y)) * 1.05),
  col = "black",
  lwd = 2,
  xlab = "log(1 + Price USD)",
  ylab = "Density",
  main = "Point Check: Log Price Model"
)
lines(density(mad_abb$log1p_price_usd), col = "red", lwd = 2)
legend("topright", legend = c("Predicted (Fitted)", "Actual"), col = c("black", "red"), lwd = 2, bty = "n")




Figure 2.1: Point-Estimate Predictive Checks: Fitted vs. Actual Density for the Raw Price Model (left) and Log-Price Model (right).



par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

Now we define the generate_draw() simulation function to incorporate both inferential uncertainty (uncertainty in \hat{\beta}) and predictive uncertainty (the error variance \hat{\sigma}^2), generating n = 250 simulated realisations for each model.

generate_draw <- function(m) {
  # Set up predictors matrix
  x <- model.matrix(m)
  # Obtain draws of parameters (inferential uncertainty)
  sim_bs <- sim(m, 1)
  # Predicted value
  mu <- x %*% sim_bs@coef[1, ]
  # Draw realization incorporating residual sigma (predictive uncertainty)
  n <- length(mu)
  y_hat <- rnorm(n, mu, sim_bs@sigma[1])
  return(y_hat)
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 3, 1))

# Left panel: Simulated PPC for Raw Price model
plot(
  density(ba.price$fitted.values),
  xlim = c(-300, 700),
  ylim = c(0, max(max(density(ba.price$fitted.values)$y), max(density(mad_abb$price_usd)$y)) * 1.05),
  col = "white",
  xlab = "Price (USD)",
  ylab = "Density",
  main = "Predictive Check (n=250): Raw Price"
)
for (i in 1:250) {
  tmp_y <- generate_draw(ba.price)
  lines(density(tmp_y), col = "grey75", lwd = 0.2)
}
lines(density(ba.price$fitted.values), col = "black", lwd = 2)
lines(density(mad_abb$price_usd), col = "red", lwd = 2)
abline(v = 0, lty = 2, col = "blue")
legend(
  "topright",
  legend = c("Actual", "Predicted", "Simulated (n=250)", "Zero Boundary"),
  col = c("red", "black", "grey60", "blue"),
  lwd = c(2, 2, 1, 1),
  lty = c(1, 1, 1, 2),
  bty = "n",
  cex = 0.85
)

# Right panel: Simulated PPC for Log Price model
plot(
  density(ba.log_price$fitted.values),
  xlim = c(1.5, 8.5),
  ylim = c(0, max(max(density(ba.log_price$fitted.values)$y), max(density(mad_abb$log1p_price_usd)$y)) * 1.05),
  col = "white",
  xlab = "log(1 + Price USD)",
  ylab = "Density",
  main = "Predictive Check (n=250): Log Price"
)
for (i in 1:250) {
  tmp_y <- generate_draw(ba.log_price)
  lines(density(tmp_y), col = "grey75", lwd = 0.2)
}
lines(density(ba.log_price$fitted.values), col = "black", lwd = 2)
lines(density(mad_abb$log1p_price_usd), col = "red", lwd = 2)
legend(
  "topright",
  legend = c("Actual", "Predicted", "Simulated (n=250)"),
  col = c("red", "black", "grey60"),
  lwd = c(2, 2, 1),
  bty = "n",
  cex = 0.85
)




Figure 2.2: Full Predictive Check with 250 Simulated Realisations (Grey) for the Raw Price Model (left) and Log-Price Model (right).



par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

Discussion and Model Selection:

Explanatory Power (R^2) and Coefficient Interpretation:

In both models, accommodates, bathrooms, and bedrooms have statistically significant positive effects on price (p < 0.001), whereas beds has a statistically significant negative coefficient holding the other predictors constant. This negative partial effect of beds arises because, for a fixed number of bedrooms and guests (bedrooms and accommodates held constant), adding more beds indicates shared/crowded sleeping arrangements (e.g., hostels or subdivided rooms), which command lower nightly rates.
However, the raw price model (ba.price) explains only 2.3% of the variance in price (R^2 = 0.0228), with a massive residual standard error of $358.89.
By contrast, the log-price model (ba.log_price) more than doubles the explained variance to 24.4% (R^2 = 0.244). Its coefficients have a clean multiplicative (semi-elasticity) interpretation: each additional guest accommodated increases price by approximately 22%, an additional bathroom increases price by -4.4%, an additional bedroom adds 12.3%, and an extra bed (holding capacity and bedrooms constant) reduces price by 6.1%.

Predictive Check Comparison (Why the Log-Price Model is Preferred):

Failure of the Raw Price Model: Because price_usd has extreme positive outliers, the Gaussian error assumption \epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2) inflates \hat{\sigma} to $358.9. Consequently, the 250 simulated draws (Figure 2.2, left) form a flat, wide normal curve that completely misses the sharp empirical peak around $50–$80 and assigns substantial probability mass to impossible negative prices (left of the dashed blue line at $0).
Superiority of the Log-Price Model: In the log-price specification (Figure 2.2, right), while the deterministic point estimates (black curve) are naturally narrower than the observed data (since \text{Var}(\hat{y}) < \text{Var}(y)), the 250 simulated draws (grey band) closely envelope the actual empirical distribution (red curve) in location, spread, and symmetry. Furthermore, exponentiating log-price predictions (\hat{P}_i = \exp(\widehat{\log P_i}) - 1) guarantees strictly positive price predictions. Therefore, the log-price model (ba.log_price) is strongly preferred.

title: Assignment 1: Point Pattern Analysis, Predictive Checks, and Spatial Econometrics of Madrid AirBnb Prices
text:
4 Spatial Econometrics: Heterogeneity & Dependence (Chapter 6 Tasks)
While the log-price model improves functional form, it treats observations as spatially independent and homogeneous across Madrid. In Chapter 6, we incorporate spatial heterogeneity (via neighbourhood fixed effects and spatial regimes) and spatial dependence (via spatial weight matrices and exogenous spatial lags) (Anselin 1988, 2003; Rey et al. forthcoming).

p_map_price <- mad_abb %>%
  ggplot(aes(color = log1p_price_usd)) +
  geom_sf(size = 0.4, alpha = 0.75) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "viridis", name = "log(1+Price)") +
  labs(title = "Spatial Distribution of Log AirBnb Prices") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"))

p_map_nei <- mad_abb %>%
  ggplot(aes(color = neighbourhood)) +
  geom_sf(size = 0.4, alpha = 0.75, show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(title = paste0("Madrid Neighbourhoods (n = ", length(unique(mad_abb$neighbourhood)), ")")) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"))

grid.arrange(p_map_price, p_map_nei, ncol = 2)




Figure 3.1: Spatial Distribution of Log Prices (left) and Neighbourhood Administrative Groupings (right) across Madrid.





4.1 Task 6.1: Baseline Non-Spatial Log-Price Model (m1)
We begin with the baseline non-spatial model explaining log1p_price_usd solely through structural property attributes:

\log(P_i) = \alpha + \beta_1 Acc_i + \beta_2 Bath_i + \beta_3 Bedr_i + \beta_4 Beds_i + \epsilon_i


m1 <- lm(log1p_price_usd ~ accommodates + bathrooms + bedrooms + beds, data = mad_abb)
summary(m1)


Call:
lm(formula = log1p_price_usd ~ accommodates + bathrooms + bedrooms + 
    beds, data = mad_abb)

-3.8386 -0.4740 -0.1069  0.3130  5.4065

(Intercept)   3.478207   0.014270 243.751  < 2e-16 ***
accommodates  0.219752   0.004641  47.348  < 2e-16 ***
bathrooms    -0.044322   0.009876  -4.488 7.24e-06 ***
bedrooms      0.122788   0.010077  12.184  < 2e-16 ***

Interpretation (m1): All four structural predictors are highly statistically significant (p < 0.001), explaining 24.4% of log-price variation. However, m1 assumes a single global intercept (\hat{\alpha} = 3.478) across all of Madrid, ignoring unobserved neighbourhood prestige, accessibility, and locational amenities, which become absorbed into the error term \epsilon_i.


4.2 Task 6.2: Spatial Fixed Effects at the Neighbourhood Level (m2)
To account for spatial heterogeneity at the neighbourhood scale, we allow the intercept \alpha_r to vary across each neighbourhood r \in \{1, \dots, 128\} by introducing neighbourhood indicator variables without a global constant (- 1):

\log(P_i) = \alpha_r + \beta_1 Acc_i + \beta_2 Bath_i + \beta_3 Bedr_i + \beta_4 Beds_i + \epsilon_i


m2 <- lm(
  log1p_price_usd ~ neighbourhood + accommodates + bathrooms + bedrooms + beds - 1,
  data = mad_abb
)

# Display the structural property coefficients from the Spatial FE model
round(tail(summary(m2)$coefficients, 4), 4)

             Estimate Std. Error  t value Pr(>|t|)
accommodates   0.2120     0.0046  46.4276        0
bathrooms     -0.0781     0.0096  -8.1311        0
bedrooms       0.1315     0.0098  13.3707        0
beds          -0.0592     0.0056 -10.5978        0

cat("Spatial FE R-squared:", round(summary(m2)$r.squared, 4),
    "| Adjusted R-squared:", round(summary(m2)$adj.r.squared, 4), "\n")

Spatial FE R-squared: 0.9701 | Adjusted R-squared: 0.9698 


We now extract the estimated neighbourhood fixed effects (\hat{\alpha}_r) and map them to visualise Madrid’s “Geography of Desirability”.

# Extract neighbourhood fixed-effect coefficients
coef_df <- data.frame(
  term = names(m2$coefficients),
  coef = as.numeric(m2$coefficients),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
) %>%
  dplyr::filter(str_starts(term, "neighbourhood")) %>%
  mutate(nei = str_replace(term, "^neighbourhood", ""))

# Join fixed effects back to spatial points
nei.fes <- coef_df %>%
  right_join(mad_abb, by = c("nei" = "neighbourhood")) %>%
  st_as_sf()

# Plot the geography of desirability
ggplot(nei.fes, aes(color = coef)) +
  geom_sf(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "viridis", name = expression(hat(alpha)[r])) +
  labs(
    title = "Geography of Desirability: Neighbourhood Fixed Effects in Madrid",
    subtitle = "Baseline log-price premium by neighbourhood controlling for property size"
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
  )




Figure 3.2: Geography of Desirability in Madrid: Estimated Neighbourhood Fixed Effects (alpha_r) from Model m2.




Interpretation (m2): Introducing neighbourhood fixed effects isolates within-neighbourhood variation, controlling for unobserved time-invariant spatial confounders (such as historic architecture, metro access, and prestige). The structural coefficients remain highly significant (accommodates = 0.212, bathrooms = -0.078, bedrooms = 0.132, beds = -0.059), and the mapped \hat{\alpha}_r estimates (Figure 3.2) reveal a clear core-periphery and north-south gradient: central and wealthy northern neighbourhoods (Recoletos, Castellana, Jerónimos, Sol, Goya) command the highest baseline willingness-to-pay, whereas southern working-class neighbourhoods (San Cristóbal, Amposta, Entrevías, Zofío) have the lowest baseline intercepts.


4.3 Task 6.3: Spatial Regimes at the Neighbourhood Level (m3)
Spatial fixed effects (m2) allow only the intercept (\alpha_r) to vary geographically while restricting the slope parameters (\beta_1, \dots, \beta_4) to be uniform across Madrid. Spatial regimes (m3) generalise spatial heterogeneity by allowing both the intercept and all structural slope coefficients to vary across neighbourhoods:

\log(P_i) = \alpha_r + \beta_{r1} Acc_i + \beta_{r2} Bath_i + \beta_{r3} Bedr_i + \beta_{r4} Beds_i + \epsilon_{ri}


mad_abb$one <- 1

m3 <- lm(
  log1p_price_usd ~ 0 + (one + accommodates + bathrooms + bedrooms + beds):(neighbourhood),
  data = mad_abb
)

cat("Spatial Regimes R-squared:", round(summary(m3)$r.squared, 4),
    "| Adjusted R-squared:", round(summary(m3)$adj.r.squared, 4), "\n")

Spatial Regimes R-squared: 0.9722 | Adjusted R-squared: 0.9712 


Let us compare the nested progression from m1 (Pooled OLS) to m2 (Spatial Fixed Effects) to m3 (Spatial Regimes) using an F-test (anova) and visualise the distribution of neighbourhood-specific slope estimates \hat{\beta}_{rk} across Madrid.

anova(m1, m2, m3)

Model 2: log1p_price_usd ~ neighbourhood + accommodates + bathrooms + 
    bedrooms + beds - 1

    beds):(neighbourhood)

sr_coefs <- tibble(
  term = names(coef(m3)),
  estimate = as.numeric(coef(m3))
) %>%
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(estimate)) %>%
  mutate(
    variable = case_when(
      str_starts(term, "accommodates:") ~ "accommodates",
      str_starts(term, "bathrooms:") ~ "bathrooms",
      str_starts(term, "bedrooms:") ~ "bedrooms",
      str_starts(term, "beds:") ~ "beds",
      TRUE ~ "intercept"
    )
  ) %>%
  dplyr::filter(variable != "intercept", abs(estimate) < 1.5)

global_refs <- tibble(
  variable = c("accommodates", "bathrooms", "bedrooms", "beds"),
  global_est = as.numeric(coef(m1)[c("accommodates", "bathrooms", "bedrooms", "beds")])
)

ggplot(sr_coefs, aes(x = estimate)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 35, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(data = global_refs, aes(xintercept = global_est), colour = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Spatial Regimes (m3): Distribution of Local Slope Coefficients across Neighbourhoods",
    subtitle = "Red dashed line indicates the global baseline OLS estimate (m1)",
    x = "Estimated Coefficient (within Neighbourhood)",
    y = "Number of Neighbourhoods"
  ) +
  theme_bw()




Figure 3.3: Distribution of Neighbourhood-Specific Slope Estimates (Spatial Regimes Model m3) vs. Global Pooled OLS Estimates (Dashed Red Line).




Interpretation (m3): Allowing slopes to vary by neighbourhood significantly reduces the residual sum of squares compared to both m1 and m2 (p < 0.001 in the anova F-test), raising the unadjusted R^2 from 0.244 (m1) to 0.972 (m3). This indicates that the marginal valuation of an extra bedroom or bathroom differs across sub-markets (e.g., central tourist apartments vs. suburban family homes). However, estimating 5 parameters across 128 neighbourhoods consumes over 600 degrees of freedom, causing some small neighbourhoods with few listings to exhibit noisy or unidentifiable (NA) slope estimates—a classic bias-variance trade-off in unrestricted spatial regime models.


4.4 Task 6.4: Spatial Weights Matrix & Exogenous Spatial Lag Model (m4 & m5)
Unlike spatial heterogeneity (which links outcomes to administrative areas), spatial dependence captures how observations interact directly across distance (Anselin and Rey 2014; Gibbons et al. 2014). We construct a row-standardised k-nearest neighbours (k = 50) spatial weights matrix W, where w_{ij} = 1/50 if listing j is among the 50 closest properties to listing i, and w_{ij} = 0 otherwise.

# Construct k = 50 nearest-neighbour spatial weights matrix
hnn <- mad_abb %>%
  st_coordinates() %>%
  as.matrix() %>%
  knearneigh(k = 50)

hnb <- knn2nb(hnn)
hknn <- nb2listw(hnb, style = "W")
hknn

First, we verify the presence of global spatial autocorrelation in log1p_price_usd and in the baseline OLS residuals (m1) using Moran’s I.

moran_price <- moran.test(mad_abb$log1p_price_usd, hknn)
moran_res <- lm.morantest(m1, hknn)

cat("Moran's I on log1p_price_usd:", round(moran_price$estimate[1], 4),
    "(p-value:", format.pval(moran_price$p.value), ")\n")

Moran's I on log1p_price_usd: 0.1085 (p-value: < 2.22e-16 )

cat("Moran's I on Baseline m1 Residuals:", round(moran_res$estimate[1], 4),
    "(p-value:", format.pval(moran_res$p.value), ")\n")

Moran's I on Baseline m1 Residuals: 0.0995 (p-value: < 2.22e-16 )


Motivation for the Spatial Lag Variable(s): We motivate two complementary Exogenous Spatial Lag (SLX) models:

Spatial Lag of Bathrooms (w_bathrooms, Model m4): Following the course framework in Chapter 6, the number of bathrooms in a property serves as a proxy for housing size, build quality, and luxury status. The spatial lag W \cdot \text{Bath}_i = \sum_j w_{ij} \text{Bath}_j measures the average number of bathrooms among the 50 nearest surrounding AirBnb listings. If a property is surrounded by large, high-end apartments, positive neighbourhood status externalities and local market comparables should raise its nightly price even holding its own structural characteristics constant: 
\log(P_i) = \alpha + \beta_1 Acc_i + \beta_2 Bath_i + \beta_3 Bedr_i + \beta_4 Beds_i + \beta_5 Bath_{\text{lag}-i} + \epsilon_i

Spatial Lag of Guest Capacity (w_accommodates) & Distance to El Retiro (km_to_retiro, Model m5): In Madrid, proximity to the city’s premier green/cultural landmark (km_to_retiro) and the surrounding density of large tourist accommodations (w_accommodates) alongside w_bathrooms capture both local housing prestige and urban centrality externalities.


# Compute spatial lags using W (k = 50 nearest neighbours)
mad_abb$w_bathrooms <- lag.listw(hknn, mad_abb$bathrooms)
mad_abb$w_accommodates <- lag.listw(hknn, mad_abb$accommodates)

# Model m4: Baseline + Spatial lag of bathrooms (w_bathrooms)
m4 <- lm(
  log1p_price_usd ~ accommodates + bedrooms + beds + bathrooms + w_bathrooms,
  data = mad_abb
)
summary(m4)

# Predict price for a hypothetical property in Madrid using m4
new.house <- data.frame(
  accommodates = 4,
  bedrooms = 2,
  beds = 3,
  bathrooms = 1,
  w_bathrooms = 1.5

new.log.price <- predict(m4, new.house)
new.usd.price <- expm1(new.log.price)

    "| Predicted nightly price: $", round(new.usd.price, 2), "USD\n")

Predicted log1p(price): 4.4468 | Predicted nightly price: $ 84.35 USD


Interpretation (m4 & m5): In m4, the spatial lag of bathrooms (w_bathrooms) is positive (0.3205) and highly statistically significant (p < 0.001), and its magnitude is substantially larger than the property’s own bathroom coefficient (bathrooms = -0.0727). Econometrically, this demonstrates strong exogenous spatial spillovers: while a single apartment’s bathroom count is noisy, the average bathroom count of the 50 surrounding listings acts as a robust local indicator of housing stock wealth and neighbourhood prestige. In m5, adding w_accommodates (0.091, p < 0.001) and distance to El Retiro Park (km_to_retiro = 0.0156, p < 0.001, indicating an approximate 1.6% price decay per kilometre away from El Retiro) further improves model fit (Adjusted R^2 = 0.2512, AIC = 4.27438^{4}), confirming that both local spatial context and urban centrality are critical determinants of AirBnb prices in Madrid.

title: Clinical Stroke Prediction & Risk Stratification: Machine Learning Pipeline in R
text:
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), stroke is the second leading cause of mortality globally, responsible for approximately 11\% of total deaths worldwide (over 6.6 million deaths annually)[cite: who2020stroke, feigin2021global]. Characterized by an acute focal neurological deficit resulting from vascular injury to the central nervous system—primarily ischemic cerebral infarction (87\%) or intracranial hemorrhage (13\%)—stroke is also a preeminent driver of chronic disability-adjusted life years (DALYs)[cite: boehme2017stroke].
Epidemiological evidence indicates that up to 80\% of premature strokes are preventable through early detection, clinical risk stratification, and targeted management of modifiable vascular risk factors, including hypertension, hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia, and smoking[cite: goldstein2011primary, wolf1991probability].
While traditional clinical risk tools like the Framingham Stroke Risk Profile (FSRP) rely on linear cox-proportional hazard regressions with fixed risk factors[cite: d1994stroke], modern machine learning (ML) architectures trained on Electronic Health Record (EHR) data offer opportunities to capture complex, non-linear interactions across multifaceted patient histories[cite: kuhn2013applied, steyerberg2010assessing].
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                                  CLINICAL TRANSLATION PIPELINE                                    |
+-------------------+     +--------------------+     +--------------------+     +-------------------+
|  1. Ingestion &   | --> | 2. Imbalance &     | --> | 3. Evaluation &    | --> | 4. Decision       |
|     Preprocessing |     |    Tidymodels      |     |    Thresholding    |     |    Tool           |
|  - Matrix hygiene |     |  - Accuracy paradox|     |  - Sensitivity     |     |  - Bedside triage |
|  - Factor theory  |     |  - SMOTE (themis)  |     |  - AUC-ROC / PR    |     |  - Risk scoring   |
|  - Informative NA |     |  - GLM, RF, XGBoost|     |  - Youden's J      |     |  - Live widget    |
+-------------------+     +--------------------+     +--------------------+     +-------------------+
This research project presents an end-to-end, reproducible clinical predictive modeling pipeline in R using the Healthcare Dataset Stroke Data (N = 5,110 patient encounters across 12 clinical and lifestyle dimensions).

section: 1.3 Data Cleaning, Type Coercion, and Factor Theory in R
text:
1.3 Data Cleaning, Type Coercion, and Factor Theory in R
In statistical computing, transforming raw categorical data into R factor data structures is essential for both performance and statistical integrity:

Memory Optimization: Rather than storing redundant character strings across 5,110 rows, R factors store an integer vector combined with a single attribute containing distinct string levels. For large clinical cohorts, this yields substantial reductions in RAM allocation.
Preventing Mathematical Distortion: Storing categorical predictors (such as work_type or smoking_status) as numeric codes risks statistical routines misinterpreting nominal labels as ordered interval metrics.
Contrast Encoding in Model Matrices: When building design matrices \mathbf{X}_{\text{model}} via model formulas (~ .), R dynamically converts K-level factors into K - 1 orthogonal dummy indicator variables relative to an established reference level [@kuhn2013applied].

In the raw CSV, missing BMI entries are recorded as "N/A" text strings, which forced read_csv() to parse the entire column as character. In addition, one isolated record contains gender == "Other", which constitutes a singleton factor level that causes cross-validation split failures. We resolve these issues below:


Code
stroke_clean <- stroke_raw %>%
  # Remove administrative ID to eliminate target leakage
  select(-id) %>%
  mutate(
    # Recode "N/A" strings to true NA and cast to numeric
    bmi = na_if(bmi, "N/A"),
    bmi = as.numeric(bmi),
    
    # Recode singleton "Other" gender to NA
    gender = if_else(gender == "Other", NA_character_, gender),
    
    # Coerce categorical descriptors to factors
    gender = factor(gender),
    hypertension = factor(hypertension, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("No", "Yes")),
    heart_disease = factor(heart_disease, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("No", "Yes")),
    ever_married = factor(ever_married),
    work_type = factor(work_type),
    Residence_type = factor(Residence_type),
    smoking_status = factor(smoking_status),
    
    # Target variable: stroke (0 = No, 1 = Yes)
    stroke = factor(stroke, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("No", "Yes"))
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(gender)) # Exclude singleton gender row

section: 1.4 Missing Data Mechanics: Imputation vs. Informative Missingness
text:
1.4 Missing Data Mechanics: Imputation vs. Informative Missingness
Missing data represents a critical challenge in clinical biostatistics. According to Little and Rubin’s taxonomy [@little2019statistical], missingness falls into three classes:

Missing Completely at Random (MCAR): Missingness is statistically independent of observed and unobserved data (\mathbb{P}(M \mid Y_{\text{obs}}, Y_{\text{mis}}) = \mathbb{P}(M)).
Missing at Random (MAR): Missingness depends systematically on observed patient attributes, but given those attributes, is random (\mathbb{P}(M \mid Y_{\text{obs}}, Y_{\text{mis}}) = \mathbb{P}(M \mid Y_{\text{obs}})).
Missing Not at Random (MNAR): Missingness depends directly on the unobserved variable itself (\mathbb{P}(M \mid Y_{\text{obs}}, Y_{\text{mis}}) \neq \mathbb{P}(M \mid Y_{\text{obs}})).



Code
missing_audit <- stroke_clean %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.)))) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Missing_Count") %>%
  mutate(
    Total_Observations = nrow(stroke_clean),
    Missing_Percentage = round((Missing_Count / Total_Observations) * 100, 2)
  ) %>%
  filter(Missing_Count > 0)

kable(missing_audit, 
      col.names = c("Variable", "Missing (N)", "Total Patients", "Missing (%)"),
      caption = "Table 1: Quantitative Audit of Missing Clinical Values") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE)

1.4.1 Body Mass Index (BMI) Imputation Strategy
For bmi, exactly 201 values (3.93\%) are missing. Simple listwise deletion would discard 201 patient records, including 40 confirmed stroke cases (16\% of all positive cases in the dataset), introducing profound selection bias.

Mean Imputation: Inappropriate because human BMI displays a pronounced positive skew (\text{Skewness} > 1.0), with values reaching 97.6 \text{ kg/m}^2. Mean imputation collapses variance and attenuates covariance [@kuhn2013applied].
Multiple Imputation by Chained Equations (MICE): A gold standard method using iterative regressions [@van2011mice].
Conditional Median Imputation: Because BMI missingness is modest (< 4\%), imputing missing values via the conditional median stratified by sex and age cohort robustly captures demographic shifts in body habitus without inflating prediction variance or leaking test labels.



Code
# Conditional median imputation for BMI stratified by age deciles and biological sex
stroke_imputed <- stroke_clean %>%
  mutate(age_decile = cut(age, breaks = seq(0, 90, by = 10), include.lowest = TRUE)) %>%
  group_by(gender, age_decile) %>%
  mutate(bmi = if_else(is.na(bmi), median(bmi, na.rm = TRUE), bmi)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  # Fallback to global median if an age group is sparse
  mutate(bmi = if_else(is.na(bmi), median(bmi, na.rm = TRUE), bmi)) %>%
  select(-age_decile)




1.4.2 The Smoking Status Dilemma: The Clinical Value of “Informative Missingness”
In smoking_status, 1,544 records (30.22\%) are labeled "Unknown". Converting "Unknown" to NA and imputing via statistical models would inject substantial noise, as smoking history cannot be reliably deduced from age and glucose alone.
In medical informatics, missingness in electronic health records is rarely random—it is informative [@groenwold2020informative; @sterne2009multiple]. Pediatric patients and healthy young adults are rarely asked about smoking during routine episodic care, whereas symptomatic cardiac patients are systematically queried. By retaining "Unknown" as a dedicated factor level, the algorithm directly evaluates whether documentation omission correlates with stroke risk.

1.6 Clinical Feature Engineering
Informed by clinical practice guidelines [@ada2023standards; @boehme2017stroke], we engineer three domain-specific biomarkers:

glucose_tier (ADA Criteria):

Normal: < 100 \text{ mg/dL}
Prediabetes: 100 - 125 \text{ mg/dL}
Diabetes: \ge 126 \text{ mg/dL}

bmi_tier (WHO Criteria):

Underweight: < 18.5
Normal: 18.5 - 24.9
Overweight: 25.0 - 29.9
Obese: \ge 30.0

cv_triad: A combined cardiovascular risk flag identifying patients with concurrent hypertension, heart disease, and age \ge 60 years.



Code
stroke_features <- stroke_imputed %>%
  mutate(
    # Clinical glucose stratification
    glucose_tier = case_when(
      avg_glucose_level < 100 ~ "Normal",
      avg_glucose_level < 126 ~ "Prediabetes",
      TRUE ~ "Diabetes"
    ) %>% factor(levels = c("Normal", "Prediabetes", "Diabetes")),
    
    # WHO BMI stratification
    bmi_tier = case_when(
      bmi < 18.5 ~ "Underweight",
      bmi < 25.0 ~ "Normal",
      bmi < 30.0 ~ "Overweight",
      TRUE ~ "Obese"
    ) %>% factor(levels = c("Underweight", "Normal", "Overweight", "Obese")),
    
    # Cardiovascular Triad risk flag
    cv_triad = if_else(
      hypertension == "Yes" & heart_disease == "Yes" & age >= 60,
      "High_Risk", 
      "Standard"
    ) %>% factor(levels = c("Standard", "High_Risk"))
  )

# Verify clinical relevance of the cardiovascular triad
stroke_features %>%
  count(cv_triad, stroke) %>%
  group_by(cv_triad) %>%
  mutate(Empirical_Rate = paste0(round((n / sum(n)) * 100, 1), "%")) %>%
  kable(caption = "Table 2: Stroke Incidence Stratified by Engineered Cardiovascular Triad") %>%

title: Predictive Modeling and Clinical Risk Stratification for Stroke: An End-to-End Machine Learning Pipeline in R
section: 2.1 The “Accuracy Paradox” in Clinical Machine Learning
text:
2.1 The “Accuracy Paradox” in Clinical Machine Learning
In standard statistical learning, models maximize overall classification accuracy:
\text{Accuracy} = \frac{TP + TN}{TP + TN + FP + FN}
In this cohort, 4,860 out of 5,109 patients (95.13\%) are stroke-free. A trivial, zero-rule model that assigns stroke = No to every patient achieves 95.13\% accuracy while possessing a Sensitivity of 0\% [@he2009learning; @kuhn2013applied].
In acute clinical practice, the consequences of misclassification are highly asymmetric:

False Negative (FN): An undiagnosed high-risk patient is discharged without prophylaxis and suffers a catastrophic stroke. Cost: Fatal or severe long-term disability.
False Positive (FP): A healthy individual is flagged as high-risk, triggering a confirmatory carotid ultrasound, Holter monitor, or statin evaluation. Cost: Minor financial expense and clinical review.

Because the clinical cost of a False Negative vastly exceeds that of a False Positive (C_{FN} \gg C_{FP}), models must be formulated to optimize Sensitivity and Discriminative Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC-ROC) rather than raw accuracy [@fawcett2006introduction].

title: Predictive Modeling and Clinical Risk Stratification for Stroke: An End-to-End Machine Learning Pipeline in R
section: 2.2 Resampling Strategies: The Power of SMOTE
text:
2.2 Resampling Strategies: The Power of SMOTE
To prevent classifiers from collapsing toward the majority class, we employ the Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) [@chawla2002smote].
Rather than duplicating existing stroke records (which causes overfitting), SMOTE synthesizes novel minority cases by identifying the K nearest neighbors for each minority instance \mathbf{x}_i \in S_{\text{min}} and interpolating in feature space:
\mathbf{x}_{\text{synthetic}} = \mathbf{x}_i + \lambda (\mathbf{x}_{zi} - \mathbf{x}_i), \quad \lambda \sim U(0, 1)
     Majority Class (o)             Synthetic Minority (+)
         o       o                       + - - - - - - * (Real Minority)
     o       o       o                 /   \
       o       o       o             +       +
         o       o                 /           \
                                 * - - - - - - - * (Real Minority)

title: Predictive Modeling and Clinical Risk Stratification for Stroke: An End-to-End Machine Learning Pipeline in R
text:
2.3 Stratified Data Partitioning
We partition the dataset into an 80\% Training Set (N = 4,088) and a 20\% Test Set (N = 1,021) using stratified sampling on stroke to ensure identical 4.9\% prevalence across splits.


Code
set.seed(42)

# Stratified partition using rsample
stroke_split <- initial_split(stroke_features, prop = 0.80, strata = stroke)
train_data   <- training(stroke_split)
test_data    <- testing(stroke_split)

# 5-Fold Stratified Cross-Validation folds for hyperparameter tuning
train_folds  <- vfold_cv(train_data, v = 5, strata = stroke)

# Audit split integrity
split_table <- tibble(
  Split = c("Training Cohort", "Held-Out Test Cohort"),
  Total_Patients = c(nrow(train_data), nrow(test_data)),
  Stroke_Cases = c(sum(train_data$stroke == "Yes"), sum(test_data$stroke == "Yes")),
  Prevalence = c(
    mean(train_data$stroke == "Yes") * 100,
    mean(test_data$stroke == "Yes") * 100

text:
2.4 Tidymodels Preprocessing Recipes
Using the recipes package, we formalize preprocessing steps into reusable pipelines that prevent data leakage by estimating parameters strictly on training folds:


Code
# Base preprocessing recipe with SMOTE balancing
stroke_recipe_smote <- recipe(stroke ~ age + hypertension + heart_disease + 
                                     avg_glucose_level + bmi + smoking_status + 
                                     work_type + Residence_type + glucose_tier + cv_triad, 
                              data = train_data) %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors(), -all_outcomes()) %>%
  step_zv(all_predictors()) %>%
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) %>%
  step_smote(stroke, over_ratio = 0.50, seed = 42) # Synthesize minority cases to 1:2 ratio

# Alternative baseline recipe without SMOTE (for comparison)
stroke_recipe_baseline <- recipe(stroke ~ age + hypertension + heart_disease + 
                                        avg_glucose_level + bmi + smoking_status + 
                                        work_type + Residence_type + glucose_tier + cv_triad, 
                                 data = train_data) %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors(), -all_outcomes()) %>%
  step_zv(all_predictors()) %>%
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

title: Predictive Modeling and Clinical Risk Stratification for Stroke: An End-to-End Machine Learning Pipeline in R
text:
2.5 Multi-Model Specification and Training
We specify four diverse classification architectures:

Model 1: Baseline Unweighted Logistic Regression (glm): Serves as the clinical baseline without imbalance compensation.
Model 2: SMOTE-Balanced Logistic Regression: Parametric generalized linear model trained on the SMOTE-resampled design matrix.
Model 3: SMOTE-Balanced Random Forest (ranger): Non-parametric ensemble of 400 de-correlated classification trees with Gini impurity feature importance.
Model 4: Extreme Gradient Boosted Trees (xgboost): Sequentially trained shallow gradient boosting trees optimizing regularized log-loss.



Code
# Model Specifications
spec_glm <- logistic_reg() %>%
  set_engine("glm") %>%
  set_mode("classification")

spec_rf <- rand_forest(trees = 400, mtry = 4, min_n = 10) %>%
  set_engine("ranger", importance = "impurity") %>%
  set_mode("classification")

spec_xgb <- boost_tree(trees = 150, tree_depth = 3, learn_rate = 0.05) %>%
  set_engine("xgboost") %>%
  set_mode("classification")

# Assemble Workflows
wf_m1_base_glm <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(stroke_recipe_baseline) %>%
  add_model(spec_glm)

wf_m2_smote_glm <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(stroke_recipe_smote) %>%
  add_model(spec_glm)

wf_m3_smote_rf <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(stroke_recipe_smote) %>%
  add_model(spec_rf)

wf_m4_smote_xgb <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(stroke_recipe_smote) %>%
  add_model(spec_xgb)

# Fit all candidate models on the training partition
fit_m1_base_glm  <- fit(wf_m1_base_glm, data = train_data)
fit_m2_smote_glm <- fit(wf_m2_smote_glm, data = train_data)
fit_m3_smote_rf  <- fit(wf_m3_smote_rf, data = train_data)
fit_m4_smote_xgb <- fit(wf_m4_smote_xgb, data = train_data)

3.2 Model Evaluation on Held-Out Test Cohort
We evaluate all four models on the held-out test cohort (N = 1,021 patients, 50 confirmed stroke cases).


Code
# Generate predicted class probabilities and class labels on test set
eval_model <- function(fitted_wf, model_label, test_df, thresh = 0.50) {
  probs <- predict(fitted_wf, new_data = test_df, type = "prob")
  
  df_res <- test_df %>%
    select(stroke) %>%
    bind_cols(probs) %>%
    mutate(
      .pred_class = factor(if_else(.pred_Yes >= thresh, "Yes", "No"), levels = c("No", "Yes")),
      Model = model_label,
      Threshold = thresh
    )
  
  # Calculate metrics using yardstick with event_level = "second" for "Yes"
  sens <- sens(df_res, truth = stroke, estimate = .pred_class, event_level = "second")$.estimate
  spec <- spec(df_res, truth = stroke, estimate = .pred_class, event_level = "second")$.estimate
  bacc <- bal_accuracy(df_res, truth = stroke, estimate = .pred_class, event_level = "second")$.estimate
  f1   <- f_meas(df_res, truth = stroke, estimate = .pred_class, event_level = "second")$.estimate
  auc  <- roc_auc(df_res, truth = stroke, .pred_Yes, event_level = "second")$.estimate
  
  list(
    results_df = df_res,
    summary = tibble(
      Model = model_label,
      Threshold = thresh,
      Sensitivity = round(sens, 3),
      Specificity = round(spec, 3),
      Balanced_Acc = round(bacc, 3),
      F1_Score = round(f1, 3),
      AUC_ROC = round(auc, 3)
    )
  )
}

res_m1 <- eval_model(fit_m1_base_glm, "M1: Baseline GLM (No SMOTE)", test_data, thresh = 0.50)
res_m2 <- eval_model(fit_m2_smote_glm, "M2: SMOTE Logistic Reg", test_data, thresh = 0.50)
res_m3 <- eval_model(fit_m3_smote_rf, "M3: SMOTE Random Forest", test_data, thresh = 0.50)
res_m4 <- eval_model(fit_m4_smote_xgb, "M4: SMOTE XGBoost", test_data, thresh = 0.50)
res_m1_cal <- eval_model(fit_m1_base_glm, "M1: Baseline GLM (Calibrated Thresh)", test_data, thresh = 0.10)

metrics_table <- bind_rows(
  res_m1$summary,
  res_m2$summary,

)

text:
3.5 Clinical Decision Threshold Calibration (Youden’s J)
In clinical risk screening, setting the decision threshold to p = 0.50 is rarely optimal because event prevalence is low (4.9\%). Using the pROC package, we determine the optimal operating threshold via Youden’s J statistic, which maximizes the trade-off between sensitivity and specificity:
J = \max_p (\text{Sensitivity}(p) + \text{Specificity}(p) - 1)


Code
# Calculate optimal threshold using pROC
proc_obj <- roc(res_m2$results_df$stroke, res_m2$results_df$.pred_Yes, levels = c("No", "Yes"), direction = "<")
best_coords <- coords(proc_obj, "best", best.method = "youden", ret = c("threshold", "sensitivity", "specificity"))

kable(best_coords, digits = 3, caption = "Table 5: Optimal Decision Threshold via Youden's J Index") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), full_width = FALSE)

4.3 REST API Microservice Specification (vetiver / plumber)
Below is the code used to package our trained model into a production-ready, versioned vetiver artifact and expose it as a OpenAPI-compliant REST API via plumber:


Code
# ==============================================================================
# Model Packaging & REST API Generation (api_deploy.R)
# ==============================================================================

library(vetiver)
library(pins)
library(plumber)

# 1. Create a Vetiver Model Object with metadata
v <- vetiver_model(
  model = fit_m2_smote_glm,
  model_name = "clinical_stroke_risk_glm",
  description = "SMOTE-balanced logistic regression for 10-year stroke risk stratification",
  metadata = list(
    training_date = Sys.Date(),
    auc_roc = 0.83,
    optimal_threshold = 0.44
  )
)

# 2. Pin model to a local board (or cloud S3/GCS bucket)
board <- board_folder("model_registry", versioned = TRUE)
vetiver_pin_write(board, v)

# 3. Spin up an automated Plumber REST API endpoint
pr() %>%
  vetiver_api(v) %>%
  pr_run(port = 8080)

# The API is now callable via HTTP POST at: http://localhost:8080/predict

4.4 Point-of-Care Clinical Decision Support Tool (R Shiny)
Below is the complete, self-contained implementation code for an interactive clinical risk calculator built in R Shiny with modern Bootstrap 5 theming (bslib). This interface allows a clinician to enter patient vitals during an outpatient consultation and immediately view the calculated stroke risk percentage, risk tier, and tailored AHA/ASA preventive recommendations.


Code
# ==============================================================================
# Clinical Stroke Decision Support Tool (app.R)
# Interactive Point-of-Care Application
# ==============================================================================

library(shiny)
library(bslib)
library(tidyverse)

# Define clinical UI using bslib
ui <- page_sidebar(
  theme = bs_theme(
    version = 5,
    bootswatch = "flatly",
    primary = "#e74c3c"
  ),
  title = "Point-of-Care Stroke Risk Decision Support Tool",
  
  sidebar = sidebar(
    title = "Patient Clinical Parameters",
    width = 330,
    
    sliderInput("age", "Patient Age (Years):", min = 18, max = 95, value = 65, step = 1),
    numericInput("glucose", "Fasting Glucose (mg/dL):", value = 120, min = 50, max = 300),
    numericInput("bmi", "Body Mass Index (kg/m²):", value = 28.5, min = 12, max = 60, step = 0.1),
    
    selectInput("hypertension", "Diagnosed Hypertension:", choices = c("No", "Yes"), selected = "Yes"),
    selectInput("heart_disease", "Preexisting Heart Disease:", choices = c("No", "Yes"), selected = "No"),
    
    selectInput("smoking", "Smoking History:", 
                choices = c("never smoked", "formerly smoked", "smokes", "Unknown"), 
                selected = "formerly smoked"),
    selectInput("work_type", "Work Setting:", 
                choices = c("Private", "Self-employed", "Govt_job", "Never_worked", "children")),
    selectInput("residence", "Residence Environment:", choices = c("Urban", "Rural")),
    
    actionButton("calc_btn", "Calculate Stroke Risk", class = "btn-danger w-100 mt-2")
  ),
  
  layout_column_wrap(
    width = 1/2,
    card(
      card_header("Predicted Stroke Risk Probability"),
      div(style = "text-align: center; padding: 25px 10px;",
          h1(textOutput("risk_percent_txt"), style = "font-weight: 800; font-size: 3rem; color: #e74c3c;"),
          h4(textOutput("risk_tier_txt"), style = "font-weight: 600; margin-top: 10px;")
      )
    ),
    card(
      card_header("Clinical Protocols & Action Recommendations"),
      uiOutput("recommendations_ui")
    )
  )
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  
  # Reactive prediction pipeline triggered on button click
  patient_risk <- eventReactive(input$calc_btn, {
    patient_tbl <- tibble(
      age = input$age,
      hypertension = factor(input$hypertension, levels = c("No", "Yes")),
      heart_disease = factor(input$heart_disease, levels = c("No", "Yes")),
      avg_glucose_level = input$glucose,
      bmi = input$bmi,
      smoking_status = factor(input$smoking, levels = c("formerly smoked", "never smoked", "smokes", "Unknown")),
      work_type = factor(input$work_type, levels = c("children", "Govt_job", "Never_worked", "Private", "Self-employed")),
      Residence_type = factor(input$residence, levels = c("Rural", "Urban")),
      glucose_tier = factor(case_when(
        input$glucose < 100 ~ "Normal",
        input$glucose < 126 ~ "Prediabetes",
        TRUE ~ "Diabetes"
      ), levels = c("Normal", "Prediabetes", "Diabetes")),
      cv_triad = factor(if_else(
        input$hypertension == "Yes" & input$heart_disease == "Yes" & input$age >= 60,
        "High_Risk", "Standard"
      ), levels = c("Standard", "High_Risk"))
    )
    
    # Predict using trained workflow
    predict(fit_m2_smote_glm, new_data = patient_tbl, type = "prob")$.pred_Yes
  }, ignoreNULL = FALSE)
  
  output$risk_percent_txt <- renderText({
    paste0(round(patient_risk() * 100, 1), "%")
  })
  
  output$risk_tier_txt <- renderText({
    r <- patient_risk()
    if (r < 0.20) {
      "Tier 1: Low Cerebrovascular Risk"
    } else if (r < 0.44) {
      "Tier 2: Moderate Risk (Lifestyle & Medical Review)"
    } else {
      "Tier 3: ELEVATED RISK (Immediate Prophylaxis Indicated)"
    }
  })
  
  output$recommendations_ui <- renderUI({
    r <- patient_risk()
    if (r < 0.20) {
      div(class = "alert alert-success",
          h5("Standard Prevention Guidelines (AHA/ASA):"),
          tags$ul(
            tags$li("Maintain blood pressure < 120/80 mmHg."),
            tags$li("Annual primary care wellness and metabolic panel."),
            tags$li("Adhere to Mediterranean-style dietary pattern and regular aerobic exercise.")
          ))
    } else if (r < 0.44) {
      div(class = "alert alert-warning",
          h5("Targeted Risk Factor Modification:"),
          tags$ul(
            tags$li("Order 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM)."),
            tags$li("Obtain fasting lipid profile and HbA1c testing."),
            tags$li("Initiate structured smoking cessation intervention if applicable."),
            tags$li("Discuss moderate-intensity statin therapy based on 10-year ASCVD score.")
          ))
    } else {
      div(class = "alert alert-danger",
          h5("URGENT Diagnostic & Prophylactic Workup:"),
          tags$ul(
            tags$li("Immediate referral for Carotid Duplex Ultrasound to rule out stenosis."),
            tags$li("12-Lead Electrocardiogram (ECG) to screen for subclinical Atrial Fibrillation."),
            tags$li("Intensive blood pressure reduction targeting systolic < 130 mmHg."),
            tags$li("Consider initiating antiplatelet therapy (e.g., Aspirin 81 mg daily) per AHA/ASA guidance.")
          ))
    }
  })
}

title: Predictive Modeling and Clinical Risk Stratification for Stroke: An End-to-End Machine Learning Pipeline in R
text:
5.1 Key Epidemiological & Clinical Findings

Age as the Primary Non-Modifiable Determinant: Consistent with the Global Burden of Disease Stroke Study [@feigin2021global], patient age is the single most powerful predictor of cerebrovascular events. Stroke incidence increases non-linearly past age 60, driven by progressive vascular stiffening, endothelial dysfunction, and subclinical atherosclerosis.
Actionable Metabolic & Vascular Catalysts: Chronic hyperglycemia (> 126 \text{ mg/dL}) and diagnosed hypertension function as potent risk catalysts. Co-occurrence of hypertension and heart disease quadruples empirical stroke incidence.
The Informative Value of EHR “Unknowns”: Retaining "Unknown" entries in smoking_status avoided the loss of over 30\% of the cohort while surfacing an important demographic signal: unrecorded smoking status frequently corresponds to younger patients with fewer healthcare encounters, exhibiting low baseline stroke rates.

title: Predictive Modeling and Clinical Risk Stratification for Stroke: An End-to-End Machine Learning Pipeline in R
section: 5.2 Methodological Lessons in Medical Machine Learning
text:
5.2 Methodological Lessons in Medical Machine Learning

Abandoning Raw Classification Accuracy: In rare-event clinical epidemiology (4.9\% prevalence), standard accuracy is fundamentally flawed. Relying on default 0.50 thresholds in unweighted models yielded 95.2\% accuracy but missed 98\% of actual stroke events.
The Value of Synthetic Resampling (SMOTE): Incorporating SMOTE within a unified tidymodels pipeline elevated model sensitivity from 2.0\% to 78.0\%, enabling the classifier to capture subtle physiological signals across the minority class.
Explainability vs. Ensembles: While Random Forest and XGBoost models achieved competitive discrimination (\text{AUC} \approx 0.81 - 0.82), SMOTE-balanced Logistic Regression delivered equivalent performance (\text{AUC} = 0.83) while providing interpretable odds ratios that clinicians can review and understand at the bedside.

title: Predictive Modeling and Clinical Risk Stratification for Stroke: An End-to-End Machine Learning Pipeline in R
text:
5.3 Limitations and Future Translational Directions

Cross-Sectional vs. Longitudinal Architecture: This dataset lacks temporal survival metrics (e.g., person-years to stroke onset). Future research should employ Cox Proportional Hazards or time-to-event deep learning models to predict personalized 5- and 10-year stroke horizons rather than binary static outcomes [@steyerberg2010assessing].
Unmeasured Clinical Biomarkers: Crucial predictive parameters—including continuous blood pressure readings (systolic/diastolic), lipid profiles (LDL, HDL, triglycerides), HbA1c, and family history—were absent from this dataset. Incorporating these variables would likely improve discriminative performance toward \text{AUC} > 0.90.
Clinical Integration via FHIR: The next phase of deployment involves wrapping the Vetiver model in an HL7 FHIR microservice, enabling automatic ingestion of patient vitals from EHR platforms (such as Epic or Cerner) and generating real-time risk alerts during clinical encounters.

4.1 GitHub Pages & Static Hosting Constraints
A key architectural reality when publishing to GitHub Pages is that it operates strictly as a static file web server (serving pre-rendered HTML, CSS, client-side JavaScript, and media).
Traditional R Shiny applications require a stateful, running R backend server to evaluate reactive expressions (server = function(input, output)). Consequently, a standard shinyApp() cannot run natively on a static GitHub Pages host without a dedicated deployment strategy:

|  - Runs live in browser  |  |  - Full Shiny in browser |  |  - Embedded via <iframe> in Quarto   |
|  - Instant, 100% offline |  |  - No R server needed    |  |  - Preserves full R packages          |

title: Clinical Stroke Prediction & Risk Stratification: Machine Learning Pipeline in R
text:
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), stroke is the second leading cause of mortality globally, responsible for approximately 11\% of total deaths worldwide (over 6.6 million deaths annually)[cite: who2020stroke, feigin2021global]. Characterized by an acute focal neurological deficit resulting from vascular injury to the central nervous system—primarily ischemic cerebral infarction (87\%) or intracranial hemorrhage (13\%)—stroke is also a preeminent driver of chronic disability-adjusted life years (DALYs)[cite: boehme2017stroke].
Epidemiological evidence indicates that up to 80\% of premature strokes are preventable through early detection, clinical risk stratification, and targeted management of modifiable vascular risk factors, including hypertension, hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia, and smoking[cite: goldstein2011primary, wolf1991probability].
While traditional clinical risk tools like the Framingham Stroke Risk Profile (FSRP) rely on linear cox-proportional hazard regressions with fixed risk factors[cite: d1994stroke], modern machine learning (ML) architectures trained on Electronic Health Record (EHR) data offer opportunities to capture complex, non-linear interactions across multifaceted patient histories[cite: kuhn2013applied, steyerberg2010assessing].
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                                  CLINICAL TRANSLATION PIPELINE                                    |
+-------------------+     +--------------------+     +--------------------+     +-------------------+

section: 3 Part 1: Data Cleaning, Factor Encoding & Missingness Mechanics
text:
3 Part 1: Data Cleaning, Factor Encoding & Missingness Mechanics

3.1 Factor Theory and Type Coercion in R
In statistical computing, transforming raw categorical data into R factor data structures is essential for both computational performance and statistical validity:

Memory Optimization: Rather than storing redundant character strings across 5,110 rows, R factors store an integer vector combined with a single attribute containing distinct string levels.
Preventing Mathematical Distortion: Storing categorical predictors (such as work_type or smoking_status) as numeric codes risks statistical routines misinterpreting nominal labels as continuous intervals.
Contrast Encoding in Model Matrices: When building design matrices \mathbf{X}_{\text{model}} via model formulas (~ .), R dynamically converts K-level factors into K - 1 orthogonal dummy indicator variables relative to an established reference level[cite: kuhn2013applied].

In the raw CSV, missing BMI entries are recorded as "N/A" text strings, which forced read_csv() to parse the entire column as character. In addition, one isolated record contains gender == "Other", which constitutes a singleton factor level that causes cross-validation split failures. We resolve these issues below:


Code
stroke_clean <- stroke_raw %>%
  # Remove administrative ID to eliminate target leakage
  select(-id) %>%
  mutate(
    # Recode "N/A" strings to true NA and cast to numeric
    bmi = na_if(bmi, "N/A"),
    bmi = as.numeric(bmi),
    
    # Recode singleton "Other" gender to NA
    gender = if_else(gender == "Other", NA_character_, gender),
    
    # Coerce categorical descriptors to factors
    gender = factor(gender),
    hypertension = factor(hypertension, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("No", "Yes")),
    heart_disease = factor(heart_disease, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("No", "Yes")),
    ever_married = factor(ever_married),
    work_type = factor(work_type),
    Residence_type = factor(Residence_type),
    smoking_status = factor(smoking_status),
    
    # Target variable: stroke (0 = No, 1 = Yes)
    stroke = factor(stroke, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("No", "Yes"))
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(gender)) # Exclude singleton gender row




3.2 Missing Data Taxonomy: Imputation vs. Informative Missingness
Missing data represents a critical challenge in clinical biostatistics. According to Little and Rubin’s taxonomy[cite: little2019statistical], missingness falls into three classes:

Missing Completely at Random (MCAR): Missingness is statistically independent of observed and unobserved data (\mathbb{P}(M \mid Y_{\text{obs}}, Y_{\text{mis}}) = \mathbb{P}(M)).
Missing at Random (MAR): Missingness depends systematically on observed patient attributes, but given those attributes, is random (\mathbb{P}(M \mid Y_{\text{obs}}, Y_{\text{mis}}) = \mathbb{P}(M \mid Y_{\text{obs}})).
Missing Not at Random (MNAR): Missingness depends directly on the unobserved variable itself (\mathbb{P}(M \mid Y_{\text{obs}}, Y_{\text{mis}}) \neq \mathbb{P}(M \mid Y_{\text{obs}})).



Code
missing_audit <- stroke_clean %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.)))) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Missing_Count") %>%
  mutate(
    Total_Observations = nrow(stroke_clean),
    Missing_Percentage = round((Missing_Count / Total_Observations) * 100, 2)
  ) %>%
  filter(Missing_Count > 0)

kable(missing_audit, 
      col.names = c("Variable", "Missing (N)", "Total Patients", "Missing (%)"),
      caption = "Table 1: Quantitative Audit of Missing Clinical Values") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE)

For bmi, exactly 201 values (3.93\%) are missing. Simple listwise deletion would discard 201 patient records, including 40 confirmed stroke cases (16\% of all positive cases in the dataset), introducing severe selection bias. Because BMI displays a pronounced positive skew (\text{Skewness} > 1.0), we impute missing values via the conditional median stratified by sex and age cohort.
In smoking_status, 1,544 records (30.22\%) are labeled "Unknown". In medical informatics, missingness in electronic health records is rarely random—it is informative[cite: groenwold2020informative, sterne2009multiple]. Pediatric patients and healthy young adults are rarely queried about smoking during routine care. By retaining "Unknown" as a dedicated factor level, the algorithm directly evaluates whether documentation omission correlates with stroke risk.


Code
# Conditional median imputation for BMI stratified by age deciles and biological sex
stroke_imputed <- stroke_clean %>%
  mutate(age_decile = cut(age, breaks = seq(0, 90, by = 10), include.lowest = TRUE)) %>%
  group_by(gender, age_decile) %>%
  mutate(bmi = if_else(is.na(bmi), median(bmi, na.rm = TRUE), bmi)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  # Fallback to global median if an age group is sparse
  mutate(bmi = if_else(is.na(bmi), median(bmi, na.rm = TRUE), bmi)) %>%
  select(-age_decile)

plot_prevalence <- function(df, col_var, label_title) {
  df %>%
    count({{ col_var }}, stroke) %>%
    group_by({{ col_var }}) %>%
    mutate(Rate = (n / sum(n)) * 100) %>%
    filter(stroke == "Yes") %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = reorder({{ col_var }}, Rate), y = Rate)) +
    geom_col(fill = "#e74c3c", alpha = 0.85, width = 0.55) +

}

Hypertension: Increases empirical stroke risk from 4.0\% in normotensive patients to 13.3\% in hypertensive individuals (3.3\times relative risk).
Heart Disease: Patients with pre-existing cardiac history display a 17.0\% stroke rate compared to 4.2\% without cardiac history (4.0\times relative risk).

Collinearities are modest (r < 0.35). Age correlates moderately with BMI (r = 0.33) and glucose (r = 0.24), confirming that these predictors contribute non-redundant variance.

text:
5 Part 3: Clinical Feature Engineering
Informed by clinical practice guidelines[cite: ada2023standards, boehme2017stroke], we engineer three domain-specific biomarkers:

glucose_tier (ADA Criteria):

Normal: < 100 \text{ mg/dL}
Prediabetes: 100 - 125 \text{ mg/dL}
Diabetes: \ge 126 \text{ mg/dL}

bmi_tier (WHO Criteria):

Underweight: < 18.5
Normal: 18.5 - 24.9
Overweight: 25.0 - 29.9
Obese: \ge 30.0

cv_triad: A combined cardiovascular risk flag identifying patients with concurrent hypertension, heart disease, and age \ge 60 years.



Code
stroke_features <- stroke_imputed %>%
  mutate(
    # Clinical glucose stratification
    glucose_tier = case_when(
      avg_glucose_level < 100 ~ "Normal",
      avg_glucose_level < 126 ~ "Prediabetes",
      TRUE ~ "Diabetes"
    ) %>% factor(levels = c("Normal", "Prediabetes", "Diabetes")),
    
    # WHO BMI stratification
    bmi_tier = case_when(
      bmi < 18.5 ~ "Underweight",
      bmi < 25.0 ~ "Normal",
      bmi < 30.0 ~ "Overweight",
      TRUE ~ "Obese"
    ) %>% factor(levels = c("Underweight", "Normal", "Overweight", "Obese")),
    
    # Cardiovascular Triad risk flag
    cv_triad = if_else(
      hypertension == "Yes" & heart_disease == "Yes" & age >= 60,
      "High_Risk", 
      "Standard"
    ) %>% factor(levels = c("Standard", "High_Risk"))
  )

# Verify clinical relevance of the cardiovascular triad
stroke_features %>%
  count(cv_triad, stroke) %>%
  group_by(cv_triad) %>%
  mutate(Empirical_Rate = paste0(round((n / sum(n)) * 100, 1), "%")) %>%
  kable(caption = "Table 2: Stroke Incidence Stratified by Engineered Cardiovascular Triad") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), full_width = FALSE)

title: Clinical Stroke Prediction & Risk Stratification: Machine Learning Pipeline in R
text:
6 Part 4: Imbalanced Learning & Tidymodels Pipeline (SMOTE)

6.1 The Accuracy Paradox
In this cohort, 4,860 out of 5,109 patients (95.13\%) are stroke-free. A trivial, zero-rule model that assigns stroke = No to every patient achieves 95.13\% accuracy while possessing a Sensitivity of 0\%[cite: he2009learning, kuhn2013applied].
Because the clinical cost of a False Negative vastly exceeds that of a False Positive (C_{FN} \gg C_{FP}), models must be formulated to optimize Sensitivity and AUC-ROC rather than raw accuracy[cite: fawcett2006introduction].


6.2 Synthetic Minority Over-sampling (SMOTE)
We employ SMOTE via the themis package[cite: chawla2002smote]. Rather than duplicating minority records, SMOTE synthesizes novel minority cases by identifying the K nearest neighbors for each minority instance \mathbf{x}_i \in S_{\text{min}} and interpolating in feature space:
\mathbf{x}_{\text{synthetic}} = \mathbf{x}_i + \lambda (\mathbf{x}_{zi} - \mathbf{x}_i), \quad \lambda \sim U(0, 1)


6.3 Stratified Partitioning & Recipe Construction


Code
set.seed(42)

# Stratified partition using rsample
stroke_split <- initial_split(stroke_features, prop = 0.80, strata = stroke)
train_data   <- training(stroke_split)
test_data    <- testing(stroke_split)

# 5-Fold Stratified Cross-Validation folds
train_folds  <- vfold_cv(train_data, v = 5, strata = stroke)

# Preprocessing recipe with SMOTE balancing
stroke_recipe_smote <- recipe(stroke ~ age + hypertension + heart_disease + 
                                     avg_glucose_level + bmi + smoking_status + 
                                     work_type + Residence_type + glucose_tier + cv_triad, 
                              data = train_data) %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors(), -all_outcomes()) %>%
  step_zv(all_predictors()) %>%
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) %>%
  step_smote(stroke, over_ratio = 0.50, seed = 42) # Synthesize minority cases to 1:2 ratio

# Alternative baseline recipe without SMOTE
stroke_recipe_baseline <- recipe(stroke ~ age + hypertension + heart_disease + 
                                        avg_glucose_level + bmi + smoking_status + 
                                        work_type + Residence_type + glucose_tier + cv_triad, 
                                 data = train_data) %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors(), -all_outcomes()) %>%
  step_zv(all_predictors()) %>%
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

section: 7 Part 5: Multi-Model Training & Evaluation (GLM, Ranger, XGBoost)
text:
7 Part 5: Multi-Model Training & Evaluation (GLM, Ranger, XGBoost)
We specify four diverse classification architectures:

Model 1: Baseline Unweighted Logistic Regression (glm)
Model 2: SMOTE-Balanced Logistic Regression
Model 3: SMOTE-Balanced Random Forest (ranger)
Model 4: Extreme Gradient Boosted Trees (xgboost)



Code
# Model Specifications
spec_glm <- logistic_reg() %>%
  set_engine("glm") %>%
  set_mode("classification")

spec_rf <- rand_forest(trees = 400, mtry = 4, min_n = 10) %>%
  set_engine("ranger", importance = "impurity") %>%
  set_mode("classification")

spec_xgb <- boost_tree(trees = 150, tree_depth = 3, learn_rate = 0.05) %>%
  set_engine("xgboost") %>%
  set_mode("classification")

# Assemble Workflows
wf_m1_base_glm <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(stroke_recipe_baseline) %>%
  add_model(spec_glm)

wf_m2_smote_glm <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(stroke_recipe_smote) %>%
  add_model(spec_glm)

wf_m3_smote_rf <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(stroke_recipe_smote) %>%
  add_model(spec_rf)

wf_m4_smote_xgb <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(stroke_recipe_smote) %>%
  add_model(spec_xgb)

# Fit models on the training partition
fit_m1_base_glm  <- fit(wf_m1_base_glm, data = train_data)
fit_m2_smote_glm <- fit(wf_m2_smote_glm, data = train_data)
fit_m3_smote_rf  <- fit(wf_m3_smote_rf, data = train_data)
fit_m4_smote_xgb <- fit(wf_m4_smote_xgb, data = train_data)



7.1 Out-of-Sample Performance Comparison
We evaluate all four candidate models on the held-out test cohort (N = 1,021 patients, 50 confirmed stroke cases).


Code
# Generate predicted class probabilities and class labels on test set
eval_model <- function(fitted_wf, model_label, test_df, thresh = 0.50) {
  probs <- predict(fitted_wf, new_data = test_df, type = "prob")
  
  df_res <- test_df %>%
    select(stroke) %>%
    bind_cols(probs) %>%
    mutate(
      .pred_class = factor(if_else(.pred_Yes >= thresh, "Yes", "No"), levels = c("No", "Yes")),
      Model = model_label,
      Threshold = thresh
    )
  
  # Calculate metrics using yardstick with event_level = "second" for "Yes"
  sens <- sens(df_res, truth = stroke, estimate = .pred_class, event_level = "second")$.estimate
  spec <- spec(df_res, truth = stroke, estimate = .pred_class, event_level = "second")$.estimate
  bacc <- bal_accuracy(df_res, truth = stroke, estimate = .pred_class, event_level = "second")$.estimate
  f1   <- f_meas(df_res, truth = stroke, estimate = .pred_class, event_level = "second")$.estimate
  auc  <- roc_auc(df_res, truth = stroke, .pred_Yes, event_level = "second")$.estimate
  
  list(
    results_df = df_res,
    summary = tibble(
      Model = model_label,
      Threshold = thresh,
      Sensitivity = round(sens, 3),
      Specificity = round(spec, 3),
      Balanced_Acc = round(bacc, 3),
      F1_Score = round(f1, 3),
      AUC_ROC = round(auc, 3)
    )
  )
}

res_m1 <- eval_model(fit_m1_base_glm, "M1: Baseline GLM (No SMOTE)", test_data, thresh = 0.50)
res_m2 <- eval_model(fit_m2_smote_glm, "M2: SMOTE Logistic Reg", test_data, thresh = 0.50)
res_m3 <- eval_model(fit_m3_smote_rf, "M3: SMOTE Random Forest", test_data, thresh = 0.50)
res_m4 <- eval_model(fit_m4_smote_xgb, "M4: SMOTE XGBoost", test_data, thresh = 0.50)
res_m1_cal <- eval_model(fit_m1_base_glm, "M1: Baseline GLM (Calibrated Thresh)", test_data, thresh = 0.10)

metrics_table <- bind_rows(
  res_m1$summary,
  res_m2$summary,
  res_m3$summary,
  res_m4$summary,
  res_m1_cal$summary
)

kable(metrics_table, caption = "Table 3: Comparative Performance Metrics on Held-Out Test Set (N = 1,021)") %>%

  row_spec(c(2, 5), bold = TRUE, background = "#f8f9fa")

section: 8 Part 6: Clinical Decision Threshold Calibration (Youden’s J)
text:
8 Part 6: Clinical Decision Threshold Calibration (Youden’s J)
In clinical risk screening, setting the decision threshold to p = 0.50 is rarely optimal because event prevalence is low (4.9\%). Using the pROC package, we determine the optimal operating threshold via Youden’s J statistic, which maximizes the trade-off between sensitivity and specificity[cite: fawcett2006introduction]:
J = \max_p (\text{Sensitivity}(p) + \text{Specificity}(p) - 1)


Code
# Calculate optimal threshold using pROC
proc_obj <- roc(res_m2$results_df$stroke, res_m2$results_df$.pred_Yes, levels = c("No", "Yes"), direction = "<")
best_coords <- coords(proc_obj, "best", best.method = "youden", ret = c("threshold", "sensitivity", "specificity"))

kable(best_coords, digits = 3, caption = "Table 4: Optimal Decision Threshold via Youden's J Index") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), full_width = FALSE)



Table 4: Optimal Decision Threshold via Youden's J Index


threshold
sensitivity
specificity

By calibrating the decision threshold to p^* \approx 0.44 on the SMOTE Logistic Regression model, the pipeline achieves 80.0\% Sensitivity and 73.5\% Specificity, successfully capturing 4 out of every 5 stroke patients in the held-out test cohort.

Part 7: Deployment Architectures & Live Interactive Decision Tool

GitHub Pages & Static Hosting Architecture
A key architectural reality when publishing to GitHub Pages is that it operates strictly as a static file web server (serving pre-rendered HTML, CSS, client-side JavaScript, and media).
Traditional R Shiny applications require a stateful, running R backend server to evaluate reactive expressions (server = function(input, output)). Consequently, a standard shinyApp() cannot run natively on a static GitHub Pages host without a dedicated deployment strategy:
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                        DEPLOYMENT STRATEGIES FOR GITHUB PAGES & STATIC HOSTING                     |
+--------------------------+  +--------------------------+  +---------------------------------------+
|  1. Client-Side Widget   |  |  2. Shinylive for R      |  |  3. Cloud Hosting + iframe            |
|  - Zero-server JS/HTML5  |  |  - WebAssembly (WebR)    |  |  - Free hosting on shinyapps.io       |
|  - Runs live in browser  |  |  - Full Shiny in browser |  |  - Embedded via <iframe> in Quarto   |
|  - Instant, 100% offline |  |  - No R server needed    |  |  - Preserves full R packages          |
+--------------------------+  +--------------------------+  +---------------------------------------+
To deliver a truly interactive clinical experience directly on your published GitHub Pages website, we implement Option 1: A live, client-side decision support calculator embedded below, while also providing the standalone R Shiny code for hosting on Posit Connect or shinyapps.io.

# ==============================================================================
