library(shiny)
library(bslib)
library(tidyverse)

# Define clinical UI using bslib
ui <- page_sidebar(
  theme = bs_theme(
    version = 5,
    bootswatch = "flatly",
    primary = "#e74c3c"
  ),
  title = "Point-of-Care Stroke Risk Decision Support Tool",
  
  sidebar = sidebar(
    title = "Patient Clinical Parameters",
    width = 330,
    
    sliderInput("age", "Patient Age (Years):", min = 18, max = 95, value = 65, step = 1),
    numericInput("glucose", "Fasting Glucose (mg/dL):", value = 120, min = 50, max = 300),
    numericInput("bmi", "Body Mass Index (kg/m²):", value = 28.5, min = 12, max = 60, step = 0.1),
    
    selectInput("hypertension", "Diagnosed Hypertension:", choices = c("No", "Yes"), selected = "Yes"),
    selectInput("heart_disease", "Preexisting Heart Disease:", choices = c("No", "Yes"), selected = "No"),
    
    selectInput("smoking", "Smoking History:", 
                choices = c("never smoked", "formerly smoked", "smokes", "Unknown"), 
                selected = "formerly smoked"),
    selectInput("work_type", "Work Setting:", 
                choices = c("Private", "Self-employed", "Govt_job", "Never_worked", "children")),
    selectInput("residence", "Residence Environment:", choices = c("Urban", "Rural")),
    
    actionButton("calc_btn", "Calculate Stroke Risk", class = "btn-danger w-100 mt-2")
  ),
  
  layout_column_wrap(
    width = 1/2,
    card(
      card_header("Predicted Stroke Risk Probability"),
      div(style = "text-align: center; padding: 25px 10px;",
          h1(textOutput("risk_percent_txt"), style = "font-weight: 800; font-size: 3rem; color: #e74c3c;"),
          h4(textOutput("risk_tier_txt"), style = "font-weight: 600; margin-top: 10px;")
      )
    ),
    card(
      card_header("Clinical Protocols & Action Recommendations"),
      uiOutput("recommendations_ui")
    )
  )
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  
  patient_risk <- eventReactive(input$calc_btn, {
    patient_tbl <- tibble(
      age = input$age,
      hypertension = factor(input$hypertension, levels = c("No", "Yes")),
      heart_disease = factor(input$heart_disease, levels = c("No", "Yes")),
      avg_glucose_level = input$glucose,
      bmi = input$bmi,
      smoking_status = factor(input$smoking, levels = c("formerly smoked", "never smoked", "smokes", "Unknown")),
      work_type = factor(input$work_type, levels = c("children", "Govt_job", "Never_worked", "Private", "Self-employed")),
      Residence_type = factor(input$residence, levels = c("Rural", "Urban")),
      glucose_tier = factor(case_when(
        input$glucose < 100 ~ "Normal",
        input$glucose < 126 ~ "Prediabetes",
        TRUE ~ "Diabetes"
      ), levels = c("Normal", "Prediabetes", "Diabetes")),
      cv_triad = factor(if_else(
        input$hypertension == "Yes" & input$heart_disease == "Yes" & input$age >= 60,
        "High_Risk", "Standard"
      ), levels = c("Standard", "High_Risk"))
    )
    
    predict(fit_m2_smote_glm, new_data = patient_tbl, type = "prob")$.pred_Yes
  }, ignoreNULL = FALSE)
  
  output$risk_percent_txt <- renderText({
    paste0(round(patient_risk() * 100, 1), "%")
  })
  
  output$risk_tier_txt <- renderText({
    r <- patient_risk()
    if (r < 0.20) {
      "Tier 1: Low Cerebrovascular Risk"
    } else if (r < 0.44) {
      "Tier 2: Moderate Risk (Lifestyle & Medical Review)"
    } else {
      "Tier 3: ELEVATED RISK (Immediate Prophylaxis Indicated)"
    }
  })
  
  output$recommendations_ui <- renderUI({
    r <- patient_risk()
    if (r < 0.20) {
      div(class = "alert alert-success",
          h5("Standard Prevention Guidelines (AHA/ASA):"),
          tags$ul(
            tags$li("Maintain blood pressure < 120/80 mmHg."),
            tags$li("Annual primary care wellness and metabolic panel."),
            tags$li("Adhere to Mediterranean-style dietary pattern and regular aerobic exercise.")
          ))
    } else if (r < 0.44) {
      div(class = "alert alert-warning",
          h5("Targeted Risk Factor Modification:"),
          tags$ul(
            tags$li("Order 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM)."),
            tags$li("Obtain fasting lipid profile and HbA1c testing."),
            tags$li("Initiate structured smoking cessation intervention if applicable."),
            tags$li("Discuss moderate-intensity statin therapy based on 10-year ASCVD score.")
          ))
    } else {
      div(class = "alert alert-danger",
          h5("URGENT Diagnostic & Prophylactic Workup:"),
          tags$ul(
            tags$li("Immediate referral for Carotid Duplex Ultrasound to rule out stenosis."),
            tags$li("12-Lead Electrocardiogram (ECG) to screen for subclinical Atrial Fibrillation."),
            tags$li("Intensive blood pressure reduction targeting systolic < 130 mmHg."),
            tags$li("Consider initiating antiplatelet therapy (e.g., Aspirin 81 mg daily) per AHA/ASA guidance.")
          ))
    }
  })
}

title: Clinical Stroke Prediction & Risk Stratification: Machine Learning Pipeline in R
text:
10 Part 8: Epidemiological Findings & Methodological Takeaways

10.1 Key Clinical Findings

Age as the Primary Non-Modifiable Determinant: Consistent with the Global Burden of Disease Stroke Study[cite: feigin2021global], patient age is the single most powerful predictor of cerebrovascular events. Stroke incidence increases non-linearly past age 60, driven by progressive vascular stiffening, endothelial dysfunction, and subclinical atherosclerosis.
Actionable Metabolic & Vascular Catalysts: Chronic hyperglycemia (> 126 \text{ mg/dL}) and diagnosed hypertension function as potent risk catalysts. Co-occurrence of hypertension and heart disease quadruples empirical stroke incidence.
The Informative Value of EHR “Unknowns”: Retaining "Unknown" entries in smoking_status avoided the loss of over 30\% of the cohort while surfacing an important demographic signal: unrecorded smoking status frequently corresponds to younger patients with fewer healthcare encounters, exhibiting low baseline stroke rates.



10.2 Methodological Lessons in Medical Machine Learning

Abandoning Raw Classification Accuracy: In rare-event clinical epidemiology (4.9\% prevalence), standard accuracy is fundamentally flawed. Relying on default 0.50 thresholds in unweighted models yielded 95.2\% accuracy but missed 98\% of actual stroke events.
The Value of Synthetic Resampling (SMOTE): Incorporating SMOTE within a unified tidymodels pipeline elevated model sensitivity from 2.0\% to 78.0\%, enabling the classifier to capture subtle physiological signals across the minority class.
Explainability vs. Ensembles: While Random Forest and XGBoost models achieved competitive discrimination (\text{AUC} \approx 0.81 - 0.82), SMOTE-balanced Logistic Regression delivered equivalent performance (\text{AUC} = 0.83) while providing interpretable odds ratios that clinicians can review and understand at the bedside.

title: Point Pattern Analysis, Predictive Checks, and Spatial Econometrics of Madrid AirBnb Prices
text:
2 Point Data Analysis (Chapter 4 Tasks)
Chapter 4 focuses on visualising dense spatial point patterns and interpolating continuous attribute surfaces from point samples [3].

2.1 Exploratory Price Distribution & Spatial Binning
Before constructing the spatial Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) and Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) surfaces, we examine the non-spatial distribution of raw (price_usd) versus log-transformed (log1p_price_usd) prices, alongside 2D spatial binning of listing coordinates.


Code
# Histogram + 1D KDE of raw price_usd
p_raw_hist <- ggplot(mad_abb, aes(x = price_usd)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, aes(y = after_stat(density)), fill = "grey35", colour = "white") +
  geom_density(fill = "#FF6666", alpha = 0.45, colour = "#FF6666", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Raw AirBnb Price (USD)",
    x = "Price (USD)",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Histogram + 1D KDE of log1p_price_usd
p_log_hist <- ggplot(mad_abb, aes(x = log1p_price_usd)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, aes(y = after_stat(density)), fill = "grey35", colour = "white") +
  geom_density(fill = "#FF6666", alpha = 0.45, colour = "#FF6666", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Log-Transformed AirBnb Price",
    x = "log(1 + Price USD)",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

grid.arrange(p_raw_hist, p_log_hist, ncol = 2)





Figure 1.1: Distribution and 1D KDE of Raw USD Prices (left) vs. Log-Transformed Prices (right) in Madrid.




Raw AirBnb prices are heavily right-skewed (mean = $118.98, median = $60, maximum = $9999), with most properties clustered below $150 per night and a thin tail of luxury listings. Taking the natural logarithm (log1p_price_usd) compresses extreme values and yields a near-symmetric, bell-shaped distribution centered around 4.19.
To address point overplotting across the 18399 locations, we first compare raw point plotting with two-dimensional square binning (geom_bin2d) and hexagonal binning (geom_hex).


Code
mad_coords <- as.data.frame(st_coordinates(mad_abb))

# Square 2D binning
sqbin <- ggplot() +
  geom_bin2d(data = mad_coords, aes(x = X, y = Y), bins = 40) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "viridis", name = "Count") +
  labs(title = "2D Square Binning", x = "Longitude (X)", y = "Latitude (Y)") +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_minimal()

# Hexagonal 2D binning
hexbin_plot <- ggplot() +
  geom_hex(data = mad_coords, aes(x = X, y = Y), bins = 40) +
  scale_fill_continuous(type = "viridis", name = "Count") +
  labs(title = "2D Hexagonal Binning", x = "Longitude (X)", y = "Latitude (Y)") +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_minimal()

grid.arrange(sqbin, hexbin_plot, ncol = 2)





Figure 1.2: Spatial Distribution of Madrid AirBnb Listings using Square Binning (left) and Hexagonal Binning (right).






2.2 Task 4.1: Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) of AirBnb Locations in Madrid
To obtain a smooth, continuous surface representing the spatial intensity (probability density) of AirBnb property locations across Madrid, we apply two-dimensional Kernel Density Estimation (stat_density2d_filled).


Code
kde_surface <- ggplot(data = mad_abb) +
  stat_density2d_filled(
    data = mad_coords,
    aes(x = X, y = Y),
    alpha = 0.85,
    n = 100
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "viridis", name = "Density Level") +
  geom_sf(alpha = 0) +
  labs(
    title = "Spatial Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) of AirBnb Locations in Madrid",
    subtitle = "Continuous probability surface of listing concentration (WGS 84)",
    x = "Longitude",
    y = "Latitude"
  ) +
  theme_bw()

kde_surface





Figure 1.3: Two-Dimensional Spatial Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) of AirBnb Property Locations in Madrid.




Interpretation of the KDE Surface: The spatial KDE reveals an intense, monocentric concentration of AirBnb properties in the historic and tourist core of Madrid (Centro district, around longitudes -3.71^\circ to -3.69^\circ and latitudes 40.41^\circ to 40.43^\circ, covering neighbourhoods such as Sol, Embajadores, Palacio, Cortes, Justicia, and Universidad). Density decays radially outward into surrounding residential districts (Chamberí, Salamanca, Arganzuela, Retiro, and Tetuán), with peripheral suburban districts exhibiting very sparse listing density.


2.3 Task 4.2: Spatial Interpolation of AirBnb Prices via Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW)
While KDE estimates the density of point occurrences, it does not show how property values vary across space. To construct a continuous surface of AirBnb prices (\hat{z}(x) = \sum_i w_i z_i / \sum_i w_i), we apply Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) interpolation [3], [4]:

Create a regular target grid (mad.grid): A 100 \times 100 grid (10,000 evenly spaced prediction centres) spanning the bounding box of mad_abb.
Compute IDW predictions: Use gstat::idw() with nmax = 150 nearest neighbours for both raw USD prices (price_usd ~ 1) and log-transformed prices (log1p_price_usd ~ 1).
Render the interpolated raster surfaces: Map the predicted values (var1.pred) across the grid.



Code
# 1. Create a 100 x 100 regular grid of cell centres over Madrid
mad.grid <- mad_abb %>%
  st_bbox() %>%
  st_as_sfc() %>%
  st_make_grid(
    n = 100,
    what = "centers"
  ) %>%
  st_as_sf() %>%
  cbind(., st_coordinates(.))

# Ensure identical CRS between source locations and target grid
st_crs(mad.grid) <- st_crs(mad_abb)

# 2. Fit IDW for raw price_usd (nmax = 150 nearest neighbours)
idw.raw <- idw(
  price_usd ~ 1,
  locations = mad_abb,
  newdata = mad.grid,
  nmax = 150
) %>%
  cbind(st_coordinates(.))

# 3. Fit IDW for log1p_price_usd (nmax = 150 nearest neighbours)
idw.log <- idw(
  log1p_price_usd ~ 1,
  locations = mad_abb,
  newdata = mad.grid,
  nmax = 150
) %>%
  cbind(st_coordinates(.))


Let us inspect the first rows of the interpolated IDW spatial object and plot both the raw price surface and the log-price surface.


Code
head(st_drop_geometry(idw.raw), 5)



  





Code
p_idw_raw <- ggplot(idw.raw, aes(x = X, y = Y, fill = var1.pred)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_viridis_b(option = "viridis", name = "Pred. USD ($)") +
  theme_void() +
  geom_sf(alpha = 0) +
  labs(
    title = "IDW Surface: Raw Price (USD)",
    subtitle = "Binned Viridis scale (nmax = 150)"
  ) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

p_idw_log <- ggplot(idw.log, aes(x = X, y = Y, fill = var1.pred)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", name = "Pred. log(Price)") +
  theme_void() +
  geom_sf(alpha = 0) +
  labs(
    title = "IDW Surface: Log Price",
    subtitle = "Continuous Magma scale (nmax = 150)"
  ) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

grid.arrange(p_idw_raw, p_idw_log, ncol = 2)





Figure 1.4: Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) Interpolated Surfaces of Madrid AirBnb Prices: Raw USD Price (left) and Log Price (right), using nmax = 150.




We can also use the IDW model to predict the nightly price of a single hypothetical property located near El Retiro Park (X = -3.6830, Y = 40.4153):


Code
pt_retiro <- c(X = -3.6830, Y = 40.4153) %>%
  st_point() %>%
  st_sfc(crs = st_crs(mad_abb)) %>%
  st_sf()

idw.one <- idw(price_usd ~ 1, locations = mad_abb, newdata = pt_retiro, nmax = 150)




Code
cat("Predicted nightly price near El Retiro Park: $", round(idw.one$var1.pred[1], 2), "USD\n")


Predicted nightly price near El Retiro Park: $ 166.67 USD


Interpretation of the IDW Price Surface: Unlike the KDE map—where intensity peaks strictly in the historic center—the IDW price surface highlights distinct high-price corridors extending into affluent districts such as Salamanca, Chamberí, Chamartín (north-central Madrid), and the eastern perimeter near San Blas-Canillejas (around the Wanda Metropolitano stadium and IFEMA exhibition centre), while southern districts (Usera, Villaverde, Puente de Vallecas, Carabanchel) form a persistent low-price belt.

3 Regression Modelling & Predictive Checks (Chapter 5 Tasks)
Chapter 5 focuses on building regression models of property prices and evaluating their adequacy through Predictive Performance Checks (PPC) that account for both point predictions and inferential/predictive simulation uncertainty [5].

3.1 Task 5.1: Baseline Linear Regression Model for Raw Price (P_i)
We first estimate the baseline Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) model explaining raw price in USD (price_usd) as a linear function of four core structural property characteristics:

P_i = \alpha + \beta_1 Acc_i + \beta_2 Bath_i + \beta_3 Bedr_i + \beta_4 Beds_i + \epsilon_i

3.3 Task 5.3: Predictive Check Analysis & Model Comparison
To evaluate how well each model captures the true data-generating process, we perform two levels of Predictive Performance Checks (PPC) following [5]:

Point-Estimate Predictive Check: Comparing the empirical kernel density of the deterministic fitted values (\hat{y}_i = X_i\hat{\beta}) against the observed outcome distribution (y_i).
Simulated Predictive Check (Inferential + Predictive Uncertainty): Using arm::sim() to draw posterior parameter realisations (\tilde{\beta}, \tilde{\sigma}) and simulating 250 synthetic outcome vectors \tilde{y} \sim \mathcal{N}(X\tilde{\beta}, \tilde{\sigma}^2).



Code
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 3, 1))

# 1. Point-estimate check for Raw Price model

  density(ba.price$fitted.values),

  col = "black",

  xlab = "Price (USD)",
  ylab = "Density",
  main = "Point Check: Raw Price Model"
)

legend("topright", legend = c("Predicted (Fitted)", "Actual"), col = c("black", "red"), lwd = 2, bty = "n")

# 2. Point-estimate check for Log Price model

  density(ba.log_price$fitted.values),
  xlim = c(1.5, 8.5),
  ylim = c(0, max(max(density(ba.log_price$fitted.values)$y), max(density(mad_abb$log1p_price_usd)$y)) * 1.05),

Figure 2.1: Point-Estimate Predictive Checks: Fitted vs. Actual Density for the Raw Price Model (left) and Log-Price Model (right).




Code
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))


Now we define the generate_draw() simulation function to incorporate both inferential uncertainty (uncertainty in \hat{\beta}) and predictive uncertainty (the error variance \hat{\sigma}^2), generating n = 250 simulated realisations for each model.


Code
generate_draw <- function(m) {
  # Set up predictors matrix
  x <- model.matrix(m)
  # Obtain draws of parameters (inferential uncertainty)
  sim_bs <- sim(m, 1)
  # Predicted value
  mu <- x %*% sim_bs@coef[1, ]
  # Draw realization incorporating residual sigma (predictive uncertainty)
  n <- length(mu)
  y_hat <- rnorm(n, mu, sim_bs@sigma[1])
  return(y_hat)
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 3, 1))

  ylab = "Density",

)

  lines(density(tmp_y), col = "grey75", lwd = 0.2)
}

  col = "white",

  ylab = "Density",
  main = "Predictive Check (n=250): Log Price"
)

  tmp_y <- generate_draw(ba.log_price)

}

Figure 2.2: Full Predictive Check with 250 Simulated Realisations (Grey) for the Raw Price Model (left) and Log-Price Model (right).




Code
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))


Discussion and Model Selection:

Explanatory Power (R^2) and Coefficient Interpretation:

In both models, accommodates, bathrooms, and bedrooms have statistically significant positive effects on price (p < 0.001), whereas beds has a statistically significant negative coefficient holding the other predictors constant. This negative partial effect of beds arises because, for a fixed number of bedrooms and guests (bedrooms and accommodates held constant), adding more beds indicates shared/crowded sleeping arrangements (e.g., hostels or subdivided rooms), which command lower nightly rates.
However, the raw price model (ba.price) explains only 2.3% of the variance in price (R^2 = 0.0228), with a massive residual standard error of $358.89.
By contrast, the log-price model (ba.log_price) more than doubles the explained variance to 24.4% (R^2 = 0.244). Its coefficients have a clean multiplicative (semi-elasticity) interpretation: each additional guest accommodated increases price by approximately 22%, an additional bathroom increases price by -4.4%, an additional bedroom adds 12.3%, and an extra bed (holding capacity and bedrooms constant) reduces price by 6.1%.

Predictive Check Comparison (Why the Log-Price Model is Preferred):

Failure of the Raw Price Model: Because price_usd has extreme positive outliers, the Gaussian error assumption \epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2) inflates \hat{\sigma} to $358.9. Consequently, the 250 simulated draws (Figure 2.2, left) form a flat, wide normal curve that completely misses the sharp empirical peak around $50–$80 and assigns substantial probability mass to impossible negative prices (left of the dashed blue line at $0).
Superiority of the Log-Price Model: In the log-price specification (Figure 2.2, right), while the deterministic point estimates (black curve) are naturally narrower than the observed data (since \text{Var}(\hat{y}) < \text{Var}(y)), the 250 simulated draws (grey band) closely envelope the actual empirical distribution (red curve) in location, spread, and symmetry. Furthermore, exponentiating log-price predictions (\hat{P}_i = \exp(\widehat{\log P_i}) - 1) guarantees strictly positive price predictions. Therefore, the log-price model (ba.log_price) is strongly preferred.

title: Point Pattern Analysis, Predictive Checks, and Spatial Econometrics of Madrid AirBnb Prices
text:
4 Spatial Econometrics: Heterogeneity & Dependence (Chapter 6 Tasks)
While the log-price model improves functional form, it treats observations as spatially independent and homogeneous across Madrid. In Chapter 6, we incorporate spatial heterogeneity (via neighbourhood fixed effects and spatial regimes) and spatial dependence (via spatial weight matrices and exogenous spatial lags) [6], [7], [8].


Code
p_map_price <- mad_abb %>%
  ggplot(aes(color = log1p_price_usd)) +
  geom_sf(size = 0.4, alpha = 0.75) +

  ggplot(aes(color = neighbourhood)) +
  geom_sf(size = 0.4, alpha = 0.75, show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(title = paste0("Madrid Neighbourhoods (n = ", length(unique(mad_abb$neighbourhood)), ")")) +

Multiple R-squared:  0.244, Adjusted R-squared:  0.2438 
F-statistic:  1484 on 4 and 18394 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Interpretation (m1): All four structural predictors are highly statistically significant (p < 0.001), explaining 24.4% of log-price variation. However, m1 assumes a single global intercept (\hat{\alpha} = 3.478) across all of Madrid, ignoring unobserved neighbourhood prestige, accessibility, and locational amenities, which become absorbed into the error term \epsilon_i.


4.2 Task 6.2: Spatial Fixed Effects at the Neighbourhood Level (m2)
To account for spatial heterogeneity at the neighbourhood scale, we allow the intercept \alpha_r to vary across each neighbourhood r \in \{1, \dots, 128\} by introducing neighbourhood indicator variables without a global constant (- 1):

\log(P_i) = \alpha_r + \beta_1 Acc_i + \beta_2 Bath_i + \beta_3 Bedr_i + \beta_4 Beds_i + \epsilon_i



Code
m2 <- lm(
  log1p_price_usd ~ neighbourhood + accommodates + bathrooms + bedrooms + beds - 1,
  data = mad_abb
)

# Display the structural property coefficients from the Spatial FE model
round(tail(summary(m2)$coefficients, 4), 4)


             Estimate Std. Error  t value Pr(>|t|)
accommodates   0.2120     0.0046  46.4276        0
bathrooms     -0.0781     0.0096  -8.1311        0
bedrooms       0.1315     0.0098  13.3707        0
beds          -0.0592     0.0056 -10.5978        0


Code
cat("Spatial FE R-squared:", round(summary(m2)$r.squared, 4),
    "| Adjusted R-squared:", round(summary(m2)$adj.r.squared, 4), "\n")


Spatial FE R-squared: 0.9701 | Adjusted R-squared: 0.9698 


We now extract the estimated neighbourhood fixed effects (\hat{\alpha}_r) and map them to visualise Madrid’s “Geography of Desirability”.


Code
# Extract neighbourhood fixed-effect coefficients
coef_df <- data.frame(
  term = names(m2$coefficients),
  coef = as.numeric(m2$coefficients),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
) %>%
  dplyr::filter(str_starts(term, "neighbourhood")) %>%
  mutate(nei = str_replace(term, "^neighbourhood", ""))

# Join fixed effects back to spatial points
nei.fes <- coef_df %>%
  right_join(mad_abb, by = c("nei" = "neighbourhood")) %>%
  st_as_sf()

# Plot the geography of desirability
ggplot(nei.fes, aes(color = coef)) +
  geom_sf(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "viridis", name = expression(hat(alpha)[r])) +
  labs(
    title = "Geography of Desirability: Neighbourhood Fixed Effects in Madrid",
    subtitle = "Baseline log-price premium by neighbourhood controlling for property size"
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
  )





Figure 3.2: Geography of Desirability in Madrid: Estimated Neighbourhood Fixed Effects (alpha_r) from Model m2.




Interpretation (m2): Introducing neighbourhood fixed effects isolates within-neighbourhood variation, controlling for unobserved time-invariant spatial confounders (such as historic architecture, metro access, and prestige). The structural coefficients remain highly significant (accommodates = 0.212, bathrooms = -0.078, bedrooms = 0.132, beds = -0.059), and the mapped \hat{\alpha}_r estimates (Figure 3.2) reveal a clear core-periphery and north-south gradient: central and wealthy northern neighbourhoods (Recoletos, Castellana, Jerónimos, Sol, Goya) command the highest baseline willingness-to-pay, whereas southern working-class neighbourhoods (San Cristóbal, Amposta, Entrevías, Zofío) have the lowest baseline intercepts.


4.3 Task 6.3: Spatial Regimes at the Neighbourhood Level (m3)
Spatial fixed effects (m2) allow only the intercept (\alpha_r) to vary geographically while restricting the slope parameters (\beta_1, \dots, \beta_4) to be uniform across Madrid. Spatial regimes (m3) generalise spatial heterogeneity by allowing both the intercept and all structural slope coefficients to vary across neighbourhoods:

\log(P_i) = \alpha_r + \beta_{r1} Acc_i + \beta_{r2} Bath_i + \beta_{r3} Bedr_i + \beta_{r4} Beds_i + \epsilon_{ri}



Code
mad_abb$one <- 1

m3 <- lm(
  log1p_price_usd ~ 0 + (one + accommodates + bathrooms + bedrooms + beds):(neighbourhood),
  data = mad_abb
)

cat("Spatial Regimes R-squared:", round(summary(m3)$r.squared, 4),
    "| Adjusted R-squared:", round(summary(m3)$adj.r.squared, 4), "\n")


Spatial Regimes R-squared: 0.9722 | Adjusted R-squared: 0.9712 


Let us compare the nested progression from m1 (Pooled OLS) to m2 (Spatial Fixed Effects) to m3 (Spatial Regimes) using an F-test (anova) and visualise the distribution of neighbourhood-specific slope estimates \hat{\beta}_{rk} across Madrid.


Code
anova(m1, m2, m3)



  





Code
sr_coefs <- tibble(
  term = names(coef(m3)),
  estimate = as.numeric(coef(m3))
) %>%
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(estimate)) %>%
  mutate(
    variable = case_when(
      str_starts(term, "accommodates:") ~ "accommodates",
      str_starts(term, "bathrooms:") ~ "bathrooms",
      str_starts(term, "bedrooms:") ~ "bedrooms",
      str_starts(term, "beds:") ~ "beds",
      TRUE ~ "intercept"
    )
  ) %>%
  dplyr::filter(variable != "intercept", abs(estimate) < 1.5)

global_refs <- tibble(
  variable = c("accommodates", "bathrooms", "bedrooms", "beds"),
  global_est = as.numeric(coef(m1)[c("accommodates", "bathrooms", "bedrooms", "beds")])
)

ggplot(sr_coefs, aes(x = estimate)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 35, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(data = global_refs, aes(xintercept = global_est), colour = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Spatial Regimes (m3): Distribution of Local Slope Coefficients across Neighbourhoods",
    subtitle = "Red dashed line indicates the global baseline OLS estimate (m1)",
    x = "Estimated Coefficient (within Neighbourhood)",
    y = "Number of Neighbourhoods"
  ) +
  theme_bw()





Figure 3.3: Distribution of Neighbourhood-Specific Slope Estimates (Spatial Regimes Model m3) vs. Global Pooled OLS Estimates (Dashed Red Line).




Interpretation (m3): Allowing slopes to vary by neighbourhood significantly reduces the residual sum of squares compared to both m1 and m2 (p < 0.001 in the anova F-test), raising the unadjusted R^2 from 0.244 (m1) to 0.972 (m3). This indicates that the marginal valuation of an extra bedroom or bathroom differs across sub-markets (e.g., central tourist apartments vs. suburban family homes). However, estimating 5 parameters across 128 neighbourhoods consumes over 600 degrees of freedom, causing some small neighbourhoods with few listings to exhibit noisy or unidentifiable (NA) slope estimates—a classic bias-variance trade-off in unrestricted spatial regime models.


4.4 Task 6.4: Spatial Weights Matrix & Exogenous Spatial Lag Model (m4 & m5)
Unlike spatial heterogeneity (which links outcomes to administrative areas), spatial dependence captures how observations interact directly across distance [9], [10]. We construct a row-standardised k-nearest neighbours (k = 50) spatial weights matrix W, where w_{ij} = 1/50 if listing j is among the 50 closest properties to listing i, and w_{ij} = 0 otherwise.


Code
# Construct k = 50 nearest-neighbour spatial weights matrix
hnn <- mad_abb %>%
  st_coordinates() %>%
  as.matrix() %>%
  knearneigh(k = 50)

hnb <- knn2nb(hnn)
hknn <- nb2listw(hnb, style = "W")
hknn

Moran's I on Baseline m1 Residuals: 0.0995 (p-value: < 2.22e-16 )


Motivation for the Spatial Lag Variable(s): We motivate two complementary Exogenous Spatial Lag (SLX) models:

Spatial Lag of Bathrooms (w_bathrooms, Model m4): Following the course framework in Chapter 6, the number of bathrooms in a property serves as a proxy for housing size, build quality, and luxury status. The spatial lag W \cdot \text{Bath}_i = \sum_j w_{ij} \text{Bath}_j measures the average number of bathrooms among the 50 nearest surrounding AirBnb listings. If a property is surrounded by large, high-end apartments, positive neighbourhood status externalities and local market comparables should raise its nightly price even holding its own structural characteristics constant: 
\log(P_i) = \alpha + \beta_1 Acc_i + \beta_2 Bath_i + \beta_3 Bedr_i + \beta_4 Beds_i + \beta_5 Bath_{\text{lag}-i} + \epsilon_i

Spatial Lag of Guest Capacity (w_accommodates) & Distance to El Retiro (km_to_retiro, Model m5): In Madrid, proximity to the city’s premier green/cultural landmark (km_to_retiro) and the surrounding density of large tourist accommodations (w_accommodates) alongside w_bathrooms capture both local housing prestige and urban centrality externalities.

mad_abb$w_accommodates <- lag.listw(hknn, mad_abb$accommodates)

title: Multilevel, Geographically Weighted and Spatio-Temporal Modelling of COVID-19 in England
text:
This report examines the spatial, hierarchical, and spatio-temporal determinants of COVID-19 infection risk across England. It addresses the research tasks at the end of Chapter 7 (Multilevel Modelling – Part 1), Chapter 8 (Multilevel Modelling – Part 2), Chapter 9 (Geographically Weighted Regression), and Chapter 10 (Spatio-Temporal Analysis) of my coursework.


We load the required packages for spatial data handling, multilevel mixed-effects modelling, geographically weighted regression (GWR), spatio-temporal basis-function modelling (FRK), and thematic mapping.


Code
# Data manipulation and date parsing
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)

# Spatial and spatio-temporal objects
library(sf)
library(sp)
library(spacetime)

# Multilevel modelling and diagnostics
library(lme4)
library(merTools)
library(car)
library(lmtest)

# Geographically Weighted Regression
library(spgwr)

# Spatio-Temporal Fixed Rank Kriging & Count GLMs
library(FRK)
library(MASS)

# Visualisation, mapping, correlation, and reporting tables
library(tmap)
library(ggplot2)
library(gridExtra)
library(gghighlight)
library(viridis)
library(RColorBrewer)
library(corrplot)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(jtools)

sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE)
tmap_mode("plot")
set.seed(453)

# Compatibility alias for tmap v4
if (!exists("tm_scale_bar", mode = "function") && exists("tm_scalebar", mode = "function")) {
  tm_scale_bar <- tm_scalebar
}





We load the England COVID-19 GeoPackage (covid19_eng.gpkg) from data/data_r/stm_covid/assignment_2_covid/ and the English Region boundary shapefile (Regions_December_2019_Boundaries_EN_BGC.shp) from data/data_r/stm_covid/gwr/.


Code
# Robust path resolution across project-level, site-level, and interactive environments
covid_candidates <- c(
  file.path("..", "..", "..", "data", "data_r", "stm_covid", "assignment_2_covid", "covid19_eng.gpkg"),
  file.path("data", "data_r", "stm_covid", "assignment_2_covid", "covid19_eng.gpkg"),
  "/Users/jay/Desktop/websiteV02/data/data_r/stm_covid/assignment_2_covid/covid19_eng.gpkg"
)
covid_path <- covid_candidates[file.exists(covid_candidates)][1]

reg_candidates <- c(
  file.path("..", "..", "..", "data", "data_r", "stm_covid", "gwr", "Regions_December_2019_Boundaries_EN_BGC.shp"),
  file.path("data", "data_r", "stm_covid", "gwr", "Regions_December_2019_Boundaries_EN_BGC.shp"),
  "/Users/jay/Desktop/websiteV02/data/data_r/stm_covid/gwr/Regions_December_2019_Boundaries_EN_BGC.shp"
)
reg_path <- reg_candidates[file.exists(reg_candidates)][1]

sdf <- st_read(covid_path, quiet = TRUE)
reg_shp <- st_read(reg_path, quiet = TRUE)

sdf <- sf::st_make_valid(sdf)
reg_shp <- sf::st_make_valid(reg_shp)


Let us inspect a selection of key administrative, demographic, deprivation, and daily COVID-19 columns across the first five Upper Tier Local Authority Districts (UTLADs).


Code
head(st_drop_geometry(sdf[1:5, c(3, 4, 9, 10, 381, 385, 386, 387, 403, 406)]))



  



Hierarchical Geographical Scales of Analysis: The dataset exhibits a strict two-level nested geographical hierarchy:

Level-1 Units (Individual/Micro Scale): N = 149 Upper Tier Local Authority Districts (UTLADs) (comprising Counties, Metropolitan Districts, Unitary Authorities, and London Boroughs, identified by ctyua19cd and ctyua19nm), projected in British National Grid (EPSG:27700).
Level-2 Units (Group/Macro Scale): J = 9 Government Office Regions (Region: North East, North West, Yorkshire and The Humber, East Midlands, West Midlands, East of England, London, South East, and South West).

Let us examine the distribution of Level-1 UTLADs nested within each Level-2 Region.


Code
reg_counts <- sdf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(Region, name = "UTLAD_Count") %>%
  arrange(UTLAD_Count)

cat("Mean number of UTLADs per Region:", round(mean(reg_counts$UTLAD_Count), 2), "\n")


Mean number of UTLADs per Region: 16.56 


Code
ggplot(reg_counts, aes(x = reorder(Region, UTLAD_Count), y = UTLAD_Count)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = UTLAD_Count), hjust = -0.3, size = 3.5) +
  coord_flip() +
  ylim(0, 38) +
  labs(
    title = "Hierarchical Nesting: UTLADs per Region in England",
    x = "Region (Level-2 Unit)",
    y = "Number of UTLADs (Level-1 Units)"
  ) +
  theme_classic()





Figure 1.1: Number of Level-1 UTLADs Nested within Each Level-2 English Region.







Following the guidance in Chapter 7, we construct a consistent set of variables used across the cross-sectional models in Chapters 7, 8, and 9:

Dependent Variable (covid19_r): We focus on the UK’s Third Wave (01 December 2020 to 29 January 2021, columns X2020.12.01 through X2021.01.29), driven by the Alpha (B.1.1.7) variant. We sum daily confirmed cases over this 60-day window (cum_covid) and compute the cumulative COVID-19 infection risk per 1,000 residents: 
\text{covid19\_r}_i = \text{round}\left(\frac{\text{cum\_covid}_i}{\text{Residents}_i} \times 1000\right)

Explanatory Variables (Compositional Proportions): We select four theoretically grounded socio-demographic and housing proportions capturing local vulnerability and transmission exposure:

crowded_hou (\text{Crowded\_housing} / \text{Households}): Share of households living in overcrowded accommodation (\ge 1 person per room), which facilitates indoor household transmission.
elderly ((\text{Age\_65\_to\_84} + \text{Age\_85plus}) / \text{Residents}): Share of residents aged 65 and over, capturing demographic age structure and shielding behaviour.
ethnic ((\text{Mixed} + \text{Indian} + \text{Pakistani} + \text{Bangladeshi} + \text{Chinese} + \text{Other\_Asian} + \text{Black} + \text{Other\_ethnicity}) / \text{Residents}): Share of non-white ethnic minority population, reflecting structural, urban, and front-line occupational exposure disparities.
lt_illness (\text{Long\_term\_ill} / \text{Residents}): Share of residents whose day-to-day activities are limited by long-term illness or disability, capturing underlying health vulnerability and socioeconomic deprivation [1].


We also compute mean-centered versions of each predictor (z_x = x - \bar{x}) to aid interpretation of random-slope correlations in Chapter 8 [2].


Code
# 1. Compute cumulative COVID-19 cases for 01/12/2020 - 29/01/2021 (Wave 3)
cum_cases_vec <- sdf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  dplyr::select("X2020.12.01":"X2021.01.29") %>%

title: Multilevel, Geographically Weighted and Spatio-Temporal Modelling of COVID-19 in England
text:
This report examines the spatial, hierarchical, and spatio-temporal determinants of COVID-19 infection risk across England. It addresses the research tasks at the end of Chapter 7 (Multilevel Modelling – Part 1), Chapter 8 (Multilevel Modelling – Part 2), Chapter 9 (Geographically Weighted Regression), and Chapter 10 (Spatio-Temporal Analysis) of my coursework.


We load the required packages for spatial data handling, multilevel mixed-effects modelling, geographically weighted regression (GWR), spatio-temporal basis-function modelling (FRK), and thematic mapping.


Code
# Data manipulation and date parsing
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)

# Spatial and spatio-temporal objects
library(sf)
library(sp)
library(spacetime)

# Multilevel modelling and diagnostics
library(lme4)
library(merTools)
library(car)
library(lmtest)

# Geographically Weighted Regression
library(spgwr)

# Spatio-Temporal Fixed Rank Kriging & Count GLMs
library(FRK)
library(MASS)

# Visualisation, mapping, correlation, and reporting tables
library(tmap)
library(ggplot2)
library(gridExtra)
library(gghighlight)
library(viridis)
library(RColorBrewer)
library(corrplot)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(jtools)

sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE)
tmap_mode("plot")
set.seed(453)

# Compatibility alias for tmap v4
if (!exists("tm_scale_bar", mode = "function") && exists("tm_scalebar", mode = "function")) {
  tm_scale_bar <- tm_scalebar
}





We load the England COVID-19 GeoPackage (covid19_eng.gpkg) from data/data_r/stm_covid/assignment_2_covid/ and the English Region boundary shapefile (Regions_December_2019_Boundaries_EN_BGC.shp) from data/data_r/stm_covid/gwr/.


Code
# Robust path resolution across project-level, site-level, and interactive environments
covid_candidates <- c(
  file.path("..", "..", "..", "data", "data_r", "stm_covid", "assignment_2_covid", "covid19_eng.gpkg"),
  file.path("data", "data_r", "stm_covid", "assignment_2_covid", "covid19_eng.gpkg"),
  "/Users/jay/Desktop/websiteV02/data/data_r/stm_covid/assignment_2_covid/covid19_eng.gpkg"
)
covid_path <- covid_candidates[file.exists(covid_candidates)][1]

reg_candidates <- c(
  file.path("..", "..", "..", "data", "data_r", "stm_covid", "gwr", "Regions_December_2019_Boundaries_EN_BGC.shp"),
  file.path("data", "data_r", "stm_covid", "gwr", "Regions_December_2019_Boundaries_EN_BGC.shp"),
  "/Users/jay/Desktop/websiteV02/data/data_r/stm_covid/gwr/Regions_December_2019_Boundaries_EN_BGC.shp"
)
reg_path <- reg_candidates[file.exists(reg_candidates)][1]

sdf <- st_read(covid_path, quiet = TRUE)
reg_shp <- st_read(reg_path, quiet = TRUE)

sdf <- sf::st_make_valid(sdf)
reg_shp <- sf::st_make_valid(reg_shp)


Let us inspect a selection of key administrative, demographic, deprivation, and daily COVID-19 columns across the first five Upper Tier Local Authority Districts (UTLADs).


Code
head(st_drop_geometry(sdf[1:5, c(3, 4, 9, 10, 381, 385, 386, 387, 403, 406)]))



  



Hierarchical Geographical Scales of Analysis: The dataset exhibits a strict two-level nested geographical hierarchy:

Level-1 Units (Individual/Micro Scale): N = 149 Upper Tier Local Authority Districts (UTLADs) (comprising Counties, Metropolitan Districts, Unitary Authorities, and London Boroughs, identified by ctyua19cd and ctyua19nm), projected in British National Grid (EPSG:27700).
Level-2 Units (Group/Macro Scale): J = 9 Government Office Regions (Region: North East, North West, Yorkshire and The Humber, East Midlands, West Midlands, East of England, London, South East, and South West).

Let us examine the distribution of Level-1 UTLADs nested within each Level-2 Region.


Code
reg_counts <- sdf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(Region, name = "UTLAD_Count") %>%
  arrange(UTLAD_Count)

cat("Mean number of UTLADs per Region:", round(mean(reg_counts$UTLAD_Count), 2), "\n")


Mean number of UTLADs per Region: 16.56 


Code

  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = UTLAD_Count), hjust = -0.3, size = 3.5) +
  coord_flip() +
  ylim(0, 38) +
  labs(
    title = "Hierarchical Nesting: UTLADs per Region in England",
    x = "Region (Level-2 Unit)",
    y = "Number of UTLADs (Level-1 Units)"
  ) +
  theme_classic()





Figure 1.1: Number of Level-1 UTLADs Nested within Each Level-2 English Region.







Following the guidance in Chapter 7, we construct a consistent set of variables used across the cross-sectional models in Chapters 7, 8, and 9:

Dependent Variable (covid19_r): We focus on the UK’s Third Wave (01 December 2020 to 29 January 2021, columns X2020.12.01 through X2021.01.29), driven by the Alpha (B.1.1.7) variant. We sum daily confirmed cases over this 60-day window (cum_covid) and compute the cumulative COVID-19 infection risk per 1,000 residents: 
\text{covid19\_r}_i = \text{round}\left(\frac{\text{cum\_covid}_i}{\text{Residents}_i} \times 1000\right)

Explanatory Variables (Compositional Proportions): We select four theoretically grounded socio-demographic and housing proportions capturing local vulnerability and transmission exposure:

crowded_hou (\text{Crowded\_housing} / \text{Households}): Share of households living in overcrowded accommodation (\ge 1 person per room), which facilitates indoor household transmission.
elderly ((\text{Age\_65\_to\_84} + \text{Age\_85plus}) / \text{Residents}): Share of residents aged 65 and over, capturing demographic age structure and shielding behaviour.
ethnic ((\text{Mixed} + \text{Indian} + \text{Pakistani} + \text{Bangladeshi} + \text{Chinese} + \text{Other\_Asian} + \text{Black} + \text{Other\_ethnicity}) / \text{Residents}): Share of non-white ethnic minority population, reflecting structural, urban, and front-line occupational exposure disparities.
lt_illness (\text{Long\_term\_ill} / \text{Residents}): Share of residents whose day-to-day activities are limited by long-term illness or disability, capturing underlying health vulnerability and socioeconomic deprivation [1].


We also compute mean-centered versions of each predictor (z_x = x - \bar{x}) to aid interpretation of random-slope correlations in Chapter 8 [2].


Code
# 1. Compute cumulative COVID-19 cases for 01/12/2020 - 29/01/2021 (Wave 3)
cum_cases_vec <- sdf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  dplyr::select("X2020.12.01":"X2021.01.29") %>%
  rowSums(na.rm = TRUE)

sdf$cum_covid <- cum_cases_vec

# 2. Compute COVID-19 infection rate per 1,000 residents and compositional predictors

    covid19_r = round((cum_covid / Residents) * 1000),

  mutate(
    z_crowded_hou = crowded_hou - mean(crowded_hou, na.rm = TRUE),
    z_elderly = elderly - mean(elderly, na.rm = TRUE),
    z_ethnic = ethnic - mean(ethnic, na.rm = TRUE),
    z_lt_illness = lt_illness - mean(lt_illness, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# Create focused spatial dataframe for Chapters 7, 8, and 9
nsdf <- sdf %>%
  dplyr::select(
    objectid, ctyua19cd, ctyua19nm, Region, long, lat,
    Residents, Households, cum_covid, covid19_r,
    crowded_hou, elderly, ethnic, lt_illness, imd_score,
    z_crowded_hou, z_elderly, z_ethnic, z_lt_illness

title: Multilevel, Geographically Weighted and Spatio-Temporal Modelling of COVID-19 in England
section: 2 Multilevel Modelling — Part 1: Varying Intercepts (Chapter 7 Tasks)
text:
2 Multilevel Modelling — Part 1: Varying Intercepts (Chapter 7 Tasks)
Standard OLS regression assumes observations are independent, ignoring the clustering of UTLADs within Regions and consequently underestimating standard errors [3]. We address this using two-level random-intercept models estimated via Restricted Maximum Likelihood (REML) in lme4.

2.1 Task 7.1: Varying-Intercept Null Model (m1_mlm)
We specify a two-level varying-intercept model with no explanatory variables, partitioning total variance in y_{ij} (covid19_r for UTLAD i in Region j) into a national fixed intercept (\beta_0), a Region-level random intercept deviation (u_{0j} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_{u0})), and a UTLAD-level residual (e_{ij} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_e)):

y_{ij} = \beta_0 + u_{0j} + e_{ij}



Code
# Baseline intercept-only OLS for reference
m0_ols <- lm(covid19_r ~ 1, data = nsdf)

# Model 1: Varying-intercept null model by Region
m1_mlm <- lmer(covid19_r ~ 1 + (1 | Region), data = nsdf)
summary(m1_mlm)

2.2 Task 7.2: Varying-Intercept Model with Explanatory Variables (m2_mlm)
Next, we include our four UTLAD-level compositional predictors (crowded_hou, elderly, ethnic, lt_illness) while allowing the intercept to vary by Region:

y_{ij} = (\beta_0 + u_{0j}) + \beta_1 \text{Crowded}_{ij} + \beta_2 \text{Elderly}_{ij} + \beta_3 \text{Ethnic}_{ij} + \beta_4 \text{LTIll}_{ij} + e_{ij}

2.3 Task 7.3: Variance Partition Coefficient (VPC)
The Variance Partition Coefficient (VPC) measures the proportion of total unexplained variance in covid19_r attributable to differences between Regions (Level 2):

\text{VPC} = \frac{\sigma^2_{u0}}{\sigma^2_{u0} + \sigma^2_e}

We extract the variance components from both m1_mlm and m2_mlm to compute their exact VPCs.


Code
vc_m1 <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(m1_mlm))
vpc_m1 <- vc_m1$vcov[1] / sum(vc_m1$vcov)

vc_m2 <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(m2_mlm))
vpc_m2 <- vc_m2$vcov[1] / sum(vc_m2$vcov)

vpc_table <- tibble(
  Model = c("Model 1: Null Varying-Intercept", "Model 2: Varying-Intercept + 4 Predictors"),

  `Region SD` = round(c(vc_m1$sdcor[1], vc_m2$sdcor[1]), 3),
  `UTLAD Residual Variance (Level 1)` = round(c(vc_m1$vcov[2], vc_m2$vcov[2]), 3),
  `UTLAD Residual SD` = round(c(vc_m1$sdcor[2], vc_m2$sdcor[2]), 3),
  `VPC (%)` = round(c(vpc_m1 * 100, vpc_m2 * 100), 2)
)

2.4 Task 7.4: Caterpillar Plots & Spatial Mapping of Varying Intercepts
We use merTools::REsim() and plotREsim() to generate Empirical Bayes caterpillar plots of the regional random intercepts (u_{0j}) for both m1_mlm and m2_mlm, and map the regional residuals across England.


Code
re_m1 <- REsim(m1_mlm, n.sims = 500)
re_m2 <- REsim(m2_mlm, n.sims = 500)

p_cat_m1 <- plotREsim(re_m1) +
  labs(title = "Model 1: Null Varying Intercepts", subtitle = "Unconditional regional deviations")

p_cat_m2 <- plotREsim(re_m2) +
  labs(title = "Model 2: Adjusted Varying Intercepts", subtitle = "Conditioned on demographic/housing composition")

grid.arrange(p_cat_m1, p_cat_m2, ncol = 2)

  left_join(re_m2 %>% dplyr::select(groupID, mean_m2 = mean), by = c("Region" = "groupID"))

  tm_fill(col = "mean_m1", title = "u_0j (Model 1)", palette = "RdBu", midpoint = 0, style = "cont") +
  tm_borders(col = "white", lwd = 0.05) +

  tm_borders(col = "black", lwd = 0.8) +
  tm_layout(main.title = "Null Model Regional Residuals", main.title.size = 0.95, bg.color = "white")

map_re2 <- tm_shape(nsdf_re) +
  tm_fill(col = "mean_m2", title = "u_0j (Model 2)", palette = "RdBu", midpoint = 0, style = "cont") +
  tm_borders(col = "white", lwd = 0.05) +
  tm_shape(reg_shp) +
  tm_borders(col = "black", lwd = 0.8) +
  tm_layout(main.title = "Adjusted Model Regional Residuals", main.title.size = 0.95, bg.color = "white")

tmap_arrange(map_re1, map_re2, ncol = 2)





Figure 2.2: Spatial Distribution of Region-Level Random Intercepts (u_0j): Unconditional Null Model 1 (left) vs. Covariate-Adjusted Model 2 (right).




Analysis and Discussion (Chapter 7):

Extent of Variation Across Geographical Scales:

In the unconditional null model (m1_mlm), the between-region variance is 157.65 (\text{SD} = 12.56) and the within-region (between-UTLAD) variance is 115.8 (\text{SD} = 10.76), yielding a VPC of 57.7%. Thus, over 58% of the total variance in Wave-3 COVID-19 infection rates across England is explained by macro-scale differences between the 9 Regions—reflecting the regionalised emergence and spread of the Alpha variant in London, the South East, and the East of England during December 2020–January 2021.
Once the four UTLAD-level compositional predictors (crowded_hou, elderly, ethnic, lt_illness) are added in m2_mlm, both Level-2 regional variance (dropping to 128.8) and Level-1 UTLAD variance (dropping to 93.04) decrease substantially, reducing the conditional VPC to 58.1%. This shows that roughly 18.3% of the initial between-region variance was driven by regional differences in overcrowding, ethnic composition, age structure, and long-term illness. After accounting for composition, most remaining unexplained variance (41.9%) lies at the local UTLAD scale (Level 1).

Interpretation of Fixed Effects and Varying Intercepts:

In m2_mlm, crowded_hou (\hat{\beta}_1 = 94.04), ethnic (\hat{\beta}_3 = 22), and lt_illness (\hat{\beta}_4 = 126.99) are positively associated with COVID-19 infection risk, whereas elderly (\hat{\beta}_2 = -55.8) is negatively associated after controlling for long-term illness (reflecting stricter shielding and lower workplace mobility among older cohorts).
The caterpillar plots (Figure 2.1) show statistically significant regional differences (bold confidence intervals not overlapping zero): in m1_mlm, London exhibits a large positive residual above the national average (\hat{u}_{0,\text{London}} = +23.91), while South West (\hat{u}_{0,\text{SW}} = -12.27) and Yorkshire and The Humber (\hat{u}_{0,\text{YH}} = -13.92) lie significantly below average. Crucially, in m2_mlm, once London’s high household overcrowding and ethnic diversity are controlled for, London’s regional intercept residual shrinks dramatically toward zero (\hat{u}_{0,\text{London}} = 17.15), whereas the North West, East of England, and South East remain significantly above average and the South West and Yorkshire and The Humber remain significantly below average.

title: Multilevel, Geographically Weighted and Spatio-Temporal Modelling of COVID-19 in England
section: 3 Multilevel Modelling — Part 2: Varying Slopes (Chapter 8 Tasks)
text:
3 Multilevel Modelling — Part 2: Varying Slopes (Chapter 8 Tasks)
Varying-intercept models assume that the effect (slope) of each explanatory variable is constant across all Regions. In Chapter 8, we relax this assumption to test whether the relationship between local socio-demographic vulnerability and COVID-19 risk varies across Regions [2], [3].

3.1 Exploratory Analysis of Varying Slopes by Region
We first inspect faceted scatterplots of covid19_r against lt_illness and ethnic across the 9 English Regions.


Code
ggplot(nsdf, aes(x = lt_illness * 100, y = covid19_r)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey30", size = 1.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, colour = "firebrick", fill = "pink", alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ Region, nrow = 3, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(
    title = "Varying Regional Slopes: COVID-19 Infection Risk vs. Long-Term Illness (%)",
    x = "Long-Term Illness (% of Residents)",
    y = "COVID-19 Cases per 1,000 Residents"
  ) +
  theme_classic()





Figure 3.1: Regional Variation in the Linear Relationship between COVID-19 Infection Rate and Long-Term Illness Share across the 9 English Regions.




Figure 3.1 reveals pronounced regional heterogeneity in slopes: the association between long-term illness (lt_illness) and COVID-19 infection rate is strongly positive in the North West, North East, West Midlands, and Yorkshire and The Humber, but flat or slightly negative in London and the South West. This motivates allowing the slope of z_lt_illness (mean-centered long-term illness share) to vary by Region.


3.2 Task 8.1: Varying-Slope Model (m3_mlm)
First, we estimate a varying-slope model (m3_mlm) using our mean-centered predictors (z_crowded_hou, z_elderly, z_ethnic, z_lt_illness), where the slope of z_lt_illness varies across Regions ((0 + z_lt_illness | Region)) while the intercept is fixed:

y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 z_{\text{Crowded},ij} + \beta_2 z_{\text{Elderly},ij} + \beta_3 z_{\text{Ethnic},ij} + (\beta_4 + u_{4j}) z_{\text{LTIll},ij} + e_{ij}



Code
m3_mlm <- lmer(
  covid19_r ~ z_crowded_hou + z_elderly + z_ethnic + z_lt_illness + (0 + z_lt_illness | Region),
  data = nsdf
)
summary(m3_mlm)

Next, we fit the full varying-intercept and varying-slope model (m4_mlm), allowing both the baseline intercept (\beta_0 + u_{0j}) and the slope of long-term illness (\beta_4 + u_{4j}) to vary by Region:

3.4 Task 8.3: Model Comparison & Discussion
We formally compare our multilevel specifications (m1_mlm Null Varying-Intercept, m2_mlm_c Varying-Intercept with Predictors, m3_mlm Varying-Slope Only, and m4_mlm Varying-Intercept + Varying-Slope) using Likelihood Ratio Tests (anova refitted with Maximum Likelihood).


Code
anova_res <- anova(m1_mlm, m2_mlm_c, m3_mlm, m4_mlm)
anova_res$deviance <- anova_res[["-2*log(L)"]]
anova_res



  



Analysis and Discussion (Chapter 8):

Comparison of Varying-Slope (m3_mlm) vs. Varying-Intercept + Varying-Slope (m4_mlm):

Which is better and why? The varying-intercept and varying-slope model (m4_mlm, or the parsimonious varying-intercept model m2_mlm_c) vastly outperforms the varying-slope-only model (m3_mlm). Specifically, m3_mlm yields an AIC of 1180.8 (deviance = 1166.8), whereas adding varying regional intercepts in m4_mlm lowers AIC dramatically to 1130.8 (deviance = 1112.8, p < 0.001). As emphasised by [3], forcing all regions to share a single baseline intercept (m3_mlm) while allowing only the slope to tilt severely misspecifies the large baseline differences in regional infection waves across England.
Comparing m2_mlm_c (varying-intercept) against m4_mlm (varying-intercept and varying-slope), adding the random slope and covariance parameters lowers deviance marginally, showing that while the relationship between long-term illness and COVID-19 exhibits regional heterogeneity (stronger positive slopes in northern industrial regions such as the North West and Yorkshire and The Humber), the dominant source of regional hierarchy is baseline intercept variation (u_{0j}).

Varying Slope Estimates and Intercept-Slope Correlation:

Across all UTLADs, the fixed average slope for z_lt_illness in m4_mlm is strongly positive (\hat{\beta}_4 = 137.12), indicating that a 1 percentage point increase in long-term illness share is associated with roughly 1.37 additional COVID-19 cases per 1,000 residents on average.
The correlation between regional intercept residuals (u_{0j}) and regional slope residuals (u_{4j}) in m4_mlm captures how baseline regional wave intensity interacts with health deprivation sensitivity: northern regions (North West, North East) exhibit steeper positive slopes (where chronic health deprivation strongly amplifies local infection risk), whereas southern regions with lower prevalence (South West) exhibit flatter slopes.

title: Multilevel, Geographically Weighted and Spatio-Temporal Modelling of COVID-19 in England
text:
4 Geographically Weighted Regression (Chapter 9 Tasks)
Multilevel models capture spatial non-stationarity across discrete administrative containers (Region). However, epidemiological processes and socio-economic relationships often vary continuously across space and cut across regional boundaries [4], [5]. In Chapter 9, we apply Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR) to estimate local regression parameters for every individual UTLAD.

4.1 Global OLS Baseline, Multicollinearity (VIF) & Residual Diagnostics
We first examine the pairwise Pearson correlations among our explanatory variables and fit a global OLS regression (ols_gwr) as a benchmark.


Code
df_corr <- nsdf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  dplyr::select(covid19_r, crowded_hou, elderly, ethnic, lt_illness, imd_score)

cormat <- cor(df_corr, use = "complete.obs", method = "pearson")
sig_test <- corrplot::cor.mtest(df_corr, conf.level = 0.95)

corrplot::corrplot(
  cormat,
  type = "lower",
  method = "circle",
  order = "original",
  tl.cex = 0.85,
  p.mat = sig_test$p,
  sig.level = 0.05,
  col = viridis::viridis(100, option = "plasma"),
  diag = FALSE
)





Figure 4.1: Correlogram of Wave-3 COVID-19 Infection Rate and Compositional Explanatory Variables (Crosses Indicate p > 0.05).

4.2 Task 9.1: GWR with Fixed vs. Adaptive Bandwidths

  data = nsdf_sp,
  coords = coords_mat,
  longlat = TRUE,
  adapt = FALSE,
  gweight = gwr.Gauss,
  verbose = FALSE
)

4.3 Task 9.2: Multiple-Map Figures of Spatial Coefficient Variation & Statistical Significance
Using the Adaptive-Bandwidth GWR (ab_gwr), we extract the local parameter estimates (\hat{\beta}_{ik}) and their local standard errors, compute the local t-statistics (t_{ik} = \hat{\beta}_{ik} / \text{SE}(\hat{\beta}_{ik})), and classify coefficients with |t_{ik}| > 2 as statistically significant [7].


Code
# Attach local coefficients from Adaptive GWR
nsdf$amb_crowded <- ab_out$crowded_hou
nsdf$amb_elderly <- ab_out$elderly
nsdf$amb_ethnic <- ab_out$ethnic
nsdf$amb_lt_ill <- ab_out$lt_illness

# Compute local t-statistics
nsdf$t_crowded <- ab_out$crowded_hou / ab_out$crowded_hou_se
nsdf$t_elderly <- ab_out$elderly / ab_out$elderly_se
nsdf$t_ethnic <- ab_out$ethnic / ab_out$ethnic_se
nsdf$t_lt_ill <- ab_out$lt_illness / ab_out$lt_illness_se

# Classify statistical significance (|t| > 2)
classify_t <- function(t_vec) {
  factor(
    ifelse(t_vec < -2, "Sig. Negative (t < -2)",
           ifelse(t_vec > 2, "Sig. Positive (t > 2)", "Non-significant (|t| <= 2)")),
    levels = c("Sig. Negative (t < -2)", "Non-significant (|t| <= 2)", "Sig. Positive (t > 2)")
  )
}

nsdf$sig_crowded <- classify_t(nsdf$t_crowded)
nsdf$sig_elderly <- classify_t(nsdf$t_elderly)
nsdf$sig_ethnic <- classify_t(nsdf$t_ethnic)

Analysis and Discussion (Chapter 9):

Spatial Non-Stationarity (Variation in Size, Direction, and Significance):

Both GWR models raise the explained variance from 49.7% (global OLS) to over 92.5% (Quasi-global R^2), demonstrating pronounced spatial non-stationarity across England.
Long-Term Illness (lt_illness): Exhibits a stark North–South and urban–periphery divide (Figure 4.4d and Figure 4.5d), ranging from -125.6 to 888.4, with 67 UTLADs showing statistically significant positive effects (t > 2, concentrated across the North West, North East, Midlands, and Thames Estuary) and 3 UTLADs showing significant negative effects.
Elderly Population (elderly): Ranges from -529 to 153.1, with 18 UTLADs displaying statistically significant negative associations (t < -2), indicating that areas with older demographic profiles experienced significantly lower Wave-3 transmission rates once chronic illness and overcrowding are controlled for.
Overcrowded Housing (crowded_hou) & Non-White Ethnic Share (ethnic): Both display strong positive local effects in specific regional clusters (11 and 56 UTLADs with t > 2, respectively), particularly across outer London, the South East, the Midlands, and Lancashire/Greater Manchester, while becoming statistically insignificant in rural shire counties where ethnic minority and overcrowded household shares are uniformly low.

Appropriate Bandwidth Selection (Fixed vs. Adaptive Kernel):

The Adaptive Bandwidth (abw = 0.03) is theoretically and empirically superior to the Fixed Bandwidth (fbw = 46.4 km) for England’s UTLAD geography.
Why? English UTLADs vary drastically in physical area and centroid spacing: London comprises 32 compact boroughs within a ~25 km radius, and metropolitan regions (Greater Manchester, Merseyside, West Midlands, Tyne and Wear) also consist of tightly packed districts, whereas rural shire counties (Cumbria, Northumberland, Cornwall, Devon, North Yorkshire) span vast territories. A fixed distance kernel (46.4 km) encompasses dozens of dissimilar authorities in London (over-smoothing urban heterogeneity and Increasing bias) while capturing very few neighbours in rural Cornwall or Cumbria (inflating variance and standard errors). The adaptive kernel dynamically expands in sparse rural areas and contracts in dense metropolitan cores, achieving a lower AIC (940.2 vs. 1027.5) and higher Quasi-global R^2 (0.925 vs. 0.846).

title: Multilevel, Geographically Weighted and Spatio-Temporal Modelling of COVID-19 in England
text:
5 Spatio-Temporal Data Analysis & Modelling (Chapter 10 Tasks)
Cross-sectional multilevel and GWR models analyse a single temporal aggregation (“snapshot”) and cannot capture how the pandemic’s trajectory evolved over time or how spatial and temporal dependencies interact [8], [9]. In Chapter 10, we reshape covid19_eng.gpkg into a long space-time format, construct a formal STIDF object, visualise space-time patterns, and fit Fixed Rank Kriging (FRK) basis-function regression models.

5.1 Spatio-Temporal Data Wrangling & STIDF Construction
We reshape the daily COVID-19 columns (X2020.12.01 to X2021.01.29, covering the 60 days of Wave 3 across all 149 UTLADs = 8,940 space-time observations) from time-wide to space-time long format (covid19_spt), parse dates via lubridate::ymd(), compute daily new cases per 100,000 residents (n_covid19_r) and running cumulative cases per 100,000 (c_covid19_r), and construct a spacetime::STIDF object [10].


Code
# Reshape Wave-3 daily cases (2020-12-01 to 2021-01-29) from wide to long format
covid_long <- sdf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  dplyr::select(
    objectid, ctyua19cd, ctyua19nm, Region, long, lat,
    Residents, crowded_hou, elderly, ethnic, lt_illness, imd_score,
    "X2020.12.01":"X2021.01.29"
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("X20"),
    names_to = "raw_date",
    values_to = "daily_cases"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    # Clean date string ("X2020.12.01" -> "2020-12-01") and parse with lubridate
    date = ymd(str_replace_all(str_remove(raw_date, "^X"), "\\.", "-")),
    daily_cases = pmax(0, daily_cases),
    day = day(date),
    week = isoweek(date),
    month = month(date),
    year = year(date),
    # Continuous study day index (1 to 60)
    time_index = as.numeric(date - min(date)) + 1
  ) %>%
  group_by(ctyua19cd) %>%
  arrange(date, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(
    cum_cases_wave3 = cumsum(daily_cases),
    # Daily rate of new COVID-19 cases per 100,000 residents (non-negative integer count rate)
    n_covid19_r = pmax(0, round((daily_cases / Residents) * 100000)),
    # Cumulative Wave-3 cases per 100,000 residents
    c_covid19_r = round((cum_cases_wave3 / Residents) * 100000)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# Join spatial polygon geometry for spatial-temporal mapping
covid19_spt <- nsdf %>%
  dplyr::select(ctyua19cd, geom) %>%
  right_join(covid_long, by = "ctyua19cd") %>%
  st_as_sf()

# Construct formal STIDF object using the spacetime package
spat_pts <- sp::SpatialPoints(coords = as.matrix(covid_long[, c("long", "lat")]))
covid19_stobj <- STIDF(
  sp = spat_pts,
  time = covid_long$date,
  data = as.data.frame(covid_long[, c("ctyua19nm", "Region", "daily_cases", "n_covid19_r", "c_covid19_r", "time_index")])
)
class(covid19_stobj)


[1] "STIDF"
attr(,"package")
[1] "spacetime"




5.2 Task 10.1: Spatio-Temporal Visualisations & Exploratory Dependence Analysis
We produce four complementary spatio-temporal visualisations to interrogate the space-time dynamics of the outbreak:

Faceted Weekly Spatial Choropleth Maps (tmap): Tracking the geographic spread of weekly new COVID-19 cases per 100,000 residents across UTLADs.
Highlighted Time-Series Trajectories (gghighlight): Comparing daily and cumulative trajectories in the highest-incidence UTLADs against the national ensemble.
Hovmöller Space-Time Heatmap: Collapsing populous UTLADs (Residents > 260,000) onto the vertical axis against daily time (date) on the horizontal axis.
Empirical Spatial/Temporal Means, Time-Series Decomposition & Temporal Autocorrelation: Decomposing the daily aggregate series (frequency = 7) into trend, weekly seasonal reporting cycles, and random noise.



Code
# Create ordered study week label (Week 1 to Week 9 of Wave 3)
covid19_spt <- covid19_spt %>%
  mutate(study_week = paste0("W", ceiling(time_index / 7)))

daycases_week <- covid19_spt %>%
  group_by(study_week, ctyua19nm, ctyua19cd, Residents) %>%
  summarise(n_daycases = sum(daily_cases, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(wn_covid19_r = (n_daycases / Residents) * 100000)

  tm_fill(
    "wn_covid19_r",
    title = "Weekly Cases / 100k",
    palette = magma(256),
    style = "cont",

    legend.is.portrait = FALSE
  ) +
  tm_facets(by = "study_week", ncol = 3) +
  tm_borders(col = "white", lwd = 0.1) +
  tm_layout(
    bg.color = "white",
    legend.outside = TRUE,
    legend.outside.position = "bottom",
    panel.label.size = 1.2,
    main.title = "Weekly New COVID-19 Cases per 100,000 across England (Dec 2020 - Jan 2021)",
    main.title.size = 1.1
  )

Next, we compute the empirical temporal mean across UTLADs, measure first-order temporal autocorrelation (r_{t, t-1}), and decompose the aggregate weekly time-series (frequency = 7).


Code
# Empirical temporal mean and aggregate daily count series
tm_av <- covid_long %>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  summarise(
    tm_mu_emp = mean(n_covid19_r, na.rm = TRUE),
    new_cases = sum(n_covid19_r, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Temporal autocorrelation at lag t - 1
lag_cor <- cor(tm_av$new_cases[-nrow(tm_av)], tm_av$new_cases[-1])
cat("First-order temporal autocorrelation (t vs t-1):", round(lag_cor, 4), "\n")


First-order temporal autocorrelation (t vs t-1): 0.7809 


Code
# Additive weekly time-series decomposition (frequency = 7 days)
total_cases_ts <- ts(tm_av$new_cases, start = 1, frequency = 7)
dec_ts <- decompose(total_cases_ts)
plot(dec_ts)





Figure 5.4: Additive Time-Series Decomposition (Observed, Trend, Weekly Seasonal, and Random Components) of Aggregate Daily COVID-19 Rates.






5.3 Task 10.2: Fitting Spatio-Temporal Models (FRK Basis Functions & Count GLMs)
To model n_covid19_r across space and time while accounting for spatio-temporal autocorrelation and overdispersion [9], [11], we construct Gaussian spatial radial basis functions (FRK::auto_basis with nres = 1) evaluated at all UTLA coordinates (FRK::eval_basis).


Code
# 1. Construct Gaussian radial basis functions over UTLA coordinates
G <- auto_basis(
  data = sp::SpatialPoints(as.matrix(covid_long[, c("long", "lat")])),
  nres = 1,
  type = "Gaussian"
)

# 2. Evaluate basis functions at each space-time observation
S <- eval_basis(
  basis = G,
  s = as.matrix(covid_long[, c("long", "lat")])
) %>%
  as.matrix()

colnames(S) <- paste0("B", 1:ncol(S))
cat("Number of generated Gaussian spatial basis functions:", ncol(S), "\n")


Number of generated Gaussian spatial basis functions: 9 


Code
# 3. Combine covariates and basis functions into the regression dataframe
reg_df <- cbind(covid_long, S) %>%
  dplyr::select(
    ctyua19nm, n_covid19_r, long, lat, time_index,
    crowded_hou, elderly, ethnic, lt_illness,
    starts_with("B")
  )


We now estimate five progressive spatio-temporal regression specifications:

lm_m (OLS Linear Trend-Surface + Basis Functions): Assumes Gaussian errors.
poisson_m1 (Poisson GLM with Log Link): Models count rates via y_{it} \sim \text{Poisson}(\exp(X_{it}\beta)) and tests for overdispersion (\text{Deviance} / \text{df}_{\text{residual}}).
qpoisson_m1 (Quasi-Poisson GLM): Adjusts standard errors for overdispersion (\text{Var}(Y) = \phi \mu).
nb_m1 (Negative Binomial GLM): Relaxes the mean-variance equality via MASS::glm.nb.
nb_m2 (Negative Binomial GLM with Space-Time Interactions): Incorporates two-way interactions between longitude, latitude, and time ((long + lat + time_index)^2) alongside all contextual predictors and spatial basis functions.



Code
# Base equation: spatial trend + temporal trend + 4 contextual covariates + basis functions
eq_st1 <- n_covid19_r ~ long + lat + time_index + crowded_hou + elderly + ethnic + lt_illness + .
reg_data_clean <- dplyr::select(reg_df, -ctyua19nm)

# 1. Linear Regression (OLS)
lm_m <- lm(formula = eq_st1, data = reg_data_clean)
summary(lm_m)

5.4 Analysis and Discussion (Chapter 10)

Comparison of GWR and Spatio-Temporal (ST) Model Results Across Space:

Consistency of Contextual Effects: Once space-time trends and FRK Gaussian basis functions (B1–B9) are controlled for in the Negative Binomial models (nb_m1 and nb_m2), the global contextual predictors align closely with the dominant local patterns identified by GWR in Chapter 9: crowded_hou, ethnic, and lt_illness exhibit positive and statistically significant associations with COVID-19 infection risk (p < 0.001), whereas elderly displays a statistically significant negative coefficient (p < 0.001).
How GWR and ST Capture Spatial Variation Differently: GWR (Chapter 9) models spatial non-stationarity by allowing the slopes of crowded_hou, elderly, ethnic, and lt_illness to vary locally across the 149 UTLADs within a single cross-sectional time window. By contrast, the FRK Spatio-Temporal model (Chapter 10) estimates global partial effects for the demographic covariates while decomposing continuous spatial variation and spatial dependence into a linear combination of radial basis functions (B1–B9, nearly all of which are highly statistically significant at p < 0.001 in nb_m1 and nb_m2) alongside explicit coordinate trends (long, lat) and space-time interactions.
Furthermore, the Poisson model exhibits severe overdispersion (\text{Deviance}/\text{df} = 19.2 \gg 1), which causes standard Poisson standard errors to be artificially small. Moving to the Negative Binomial (nb_m1 and nb_m2) reduces residual deviance from 1.71098^{5} to 9261, providing much more reliable statistical inference.

Significant Variations Over Time and Space-Time Interactions:

Temporal Autocorrelation and Trend: The exploratory analysis demonstrates strong positive first-order temporal autocorrelation (r_{t, t-1} = 0.781) and a clear 7-day seasonal reporting cycle (Figure 5.4), alongside an inverted-U wave trajectory that surged through December 2020 and peaked in early January 2021 before declining under national lockdown.
Space-Time Interaction Terms (nb_m2): In nb_m1, the main effect of time_index is positive and highly statistically significant (\hat{\beta}_{\text{time}} = 0.0139, p < 0.001), confirming a significant upward temporal trend across the Wave-3 window. Even more revealingly, in nb_m2, the space-time interaction terms long:time_index and lat:time_index (as well as long:lat) are highly statistically significant:

The significant lat:time_index interaction captures the south-to-north diffusion of the Alpha variant during Wave 3: whereas early December 2020 cases were heavily concentrated in Kent, London, and the South East (lower latitude, higher longitude), infection rates accelerated northward and westward (long:time_index and lat:time_index) into the Midlands, North West, and Cumbria as time progressed through January 2021 (as visually confirmed by the weekly maps in Figure 5.1 and the Hovmöller diagram in Figure 5.3).

title: Ordinary Least Squares Regression for modelling Green Central Heating in Census 2021
text:
The focal point of this report centres around the research question: “What are the key determinants impacting the implementation of green central heating in the districts of the UK?” This question is highly relevant in the context of rising environmental awareness, residential decarbonisation targets, and the transition toward a sustainable energy future. Domestic heating accounts for a substantial share of national greenhouse gas emissions, meaning that the adoption of green central heating systems—such as heat pumps, biomass boilers, solar thermal, and district or communal heat networks—stands as a crucial pillar in reducing residential carbon footprints and promoting energy-efficient practices.
Understanding the socio-economic, demographic, and housing-stock factors that shape the uptake of green central heating technologies provides actionable insight for both public policymakers and private-sector energy markets. Effective decarbonisation policy requires more than technological availability; it requires identifying how lifestyle patterns, housing tenure, dwelling structure, and local heating infrastructure interact across different local authorities.
This report is systematically organised to follow the end-to-end statistical modelling workflow required by ENVS450 Assignment 2:

Literature Review and Variables Selection Rationale summarises existing empirical research on sustainable household technology adoption and motivates our candidate predictors.
Methodology & Setup introduces the 2021 Census district-level dataset (\(N = 331\) local authority districts across \(55\) variables) and outlines the quantitative modelling strategy.
Univariate Description of Outcome Variable examines the distribution, skewness, central tendency, and dispersion of Green_Central_Heating.
Correlation Analysis of Outcome Variable screens bivariate associations between Green_Central_Heating and all other continuous and categorical variables in the dataset (excluding the identifier District) using rank-based correlation (Table 1).
Selection of Predictor Variables justifies the five chosen candidate predictors (four continuous and one newly constructed binary categorical variable, Age_Profile).
Regression Model Fitting Strategy & Initial ‘Best’ Model Identification applies the Narrative approach across three sequential Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) models (model1, model2, model3) to assess confounding (“explained away” effects) and identify the initial ‘best’ main-effects specification (Tables 2 & 3).
Interaction Effect Evaluation tests all two-way multiplicative interactions among the main predictors (model2i_first, Table 4) and uses backwards elimination to retain statistically significant interactions (model2i, Table 5 and Figures 1–3).
Enhancing the ‘Best’ Model (Polynomials) evaluates non-linear quadratic terms across the continuous predictors (Table 6) to arrive at the final preferred model (M2, Table 7).
Assessment of the Final Model conducts regression diagnostics—residual normality (Figure 4), homoscedasticity (Figure 5), multicollinearity (\(\text{VIF}\)), and error independence (Durbin-Watson)—evaluates the relative importance of predictors via Adequacy (Figure 6), and synthesises what the model reveals about the UK housing landscape.

title: Ordinary Least Squares Regression for modelling Green Central Heating in Census 2021
section: 2 Literature Review and Variables Selection Rationale
text:
2 Literature Review and Variables Selection Rationale
Recent studies in environmental sciences and energy socio-economics have investigated the drivers behind household adoption of sustainable technologies such as green central heating. Empirical research demonstrates that residential technology adoption is not merely a function of technological availability, but is strongly conditioned by socio-economic and demographic characteristics (Hooks et al., 2022). Educational attainment, economic activity, housing type, tenure, and environmental awareness play central roles in the uptake of green energy technologies, as highlighted by Bruckmann, Willibald and Blanco (2021) in their regional study of sustainable technology diffusion without strong policy mandates.
Drawing on this literature, potential district-level determinants include economic activity and employment structure (Full_Time_Employee), dwelling morphology (Detached), household tenure (Owned), demographic age structure (Age_Profile), and existing heating infrastructure (No_Central_Heating). In particular, examining the proportion of households with no central heating (No_Central_Heating) allows us to test whether off-grid districts lacking conventional mains-gas central heating are more inclined to adopt alternative green central heating options, or whether a lack of central heating instead reflects urban deprivation and lower capacity for capital-intensive energy retrofits.

title: Ordinary Least Squares Regression for modelling Green Central Heating in Census 2021
text:
3 Methodology & Setup

3.1 Dataset Description
The data analysed in this report come from the 2021 Census collected by the Office for National Statistics (ONS) in March 2021 (Office for National Statistics, 2023). The course dataset (Census_2021.Rdata) is aggregated to the local authority district level across England and Wales and contains \(N = 331\) districts (rows) and \(55\) variables (columns):

\(49\) continuous numeric variables, mostly expressed as percentages of households, residents, or workers in each district (plus district-level summary measures such as Mean_Age and population Density).
\(6\) categorical factor variables capturing administrative geography (District, County, Region, Super_Region, South_East, and Country).



3.2 Environment Setup and Package Loading
The R chunk below checks that all required packages are installed in the active R environment, loads them in the appropriate order (loading ENVS450 after tidyverse so course helper functions like skew(), cor.results(), coeffs(), and regress.compare() are available while preserving dplyr::select() over MASS::select()), loads Census_2021.Rdata, and sources the course helper script Session_10_functions.R (which provides adequacy_lm()).


Check/install required packages, load libraries, and load Census 2021 data
