3.3 Analytical Workflow
Our modelling workflow proceeds in five stages:

Univariate exploration of the continuous outcome variable Green_Central_Heating to assess its distributional shape and select appropriate summary statistics.
Bivariate correlation screening across all candidate variables in the dataset (excluding the identifier District), alongside the creation of a recoded binary demographic factor Age_Profile (dichotomising Age_65_plus at its median into "Youthful" vs. "Ageing" districts).
Narrative regression modelling starting from a single focal predictor (Full_Time_Employee in model1), adding housing and heating controls (Detached, No_Central_Heating, Owned in model2), and testing the demographic factor (Age_Profile in model3) to identify our initial ‘best’ model.
Refinement via interactions and polynomials, first testing all \(\binom{4}{2} = 6\) two-way interactions (model2i_first) and eliminating non-significant terms to obtain model2i (Model 2 IS), then testing quadratic polynomial terms (M1–M4) to arrive at the final model M2.
Model diagnostics and predictor adequacy, evaluating residual normality, constant error variance, multicollinearity, autocorrelation, and single-predictor \(R^2\) adequacy (adequacy_lm()).

title: Ordinary Least Squares Regression for modelling Green Central Heating in Census 2021
text:
4 Univariate Description of Outcome Variable
Our outcome variable of interest is Green_Central_Heating, a continuous variable measuring the percentage of households in a local authority district that use one or more ‘green’ forms of central heating (defined in the Census 2021 data dictionary as renewable energy systems such as heat pumps or biomass, district/communal heat networks, or tank/bottled gas).

4.1 Skewness, Central Tendency, and Dispersion
Before summarising a continuous variable, we examine its skewness, which measures the asymmetry of its distribution around its mean \(\bar{Y}\):
\[\text{Skewness} = \frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_i - \bar{Y})^3}{\left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_i - \bar{Y})^2\right]^{3/2}}\]
A symmetric normal distribution has \(\text{Skewness} \approx 0\), whereas distributions with \(|\text{Skewness}| > 1\) are substantially skewed. When a continuous variable has \(\text{Skewness} > 1\), the arithmetic mean and standard deviation are distorted by extreme values in the right tail. We therefore use the Median (\(50\text{th}\) percentile, \(Q_2\)) to measure central tendency and the Inter-Quartile Range (\(\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1\)) to measure dispersion across the middle \(50\%\) of districts.


Compute skewness, median, and IQR for Green_Central_Heating

5 Correlation Analysis of Outcome Variable
To satisfy Instruction #5 (“Examine how strongly correlated your outcome variable is with ALL of the other variables in the dataset”) and prepare a categorical demographic predictor for Instruction #6, we create a working copy of the dataset (census_copy) and construct a binary categorical variable, Age_Profile, by splitting districts at the median percentage of residents aged 65 and over (Age_65_plus):

Districts with Age_65_plus < median(Age_65_plus) are classified as "Youthful".
Districts with Age_65_plus >= median(Age_65_plus) are classified as "Ageing".


5.1 Choice of Correlation Measure and Treatment of Variable Types
Following the course correlation guidelines (Assignment-2--correlations.html):

Exclusion of Identifier Variables: District is a unique nominal identifier for each local authority (1 to 331 in alphabetical order) rather than a substantive characteristic, so it is excluded from the correlation analysis (ID_variables <- "District").
Continuous Predictors (\(48\) variables): Because the continuous outcome Green_Central_Heating is positively skewed (\(\text{skew} = 1.73\)) and several continuous predictors also exhibit skewness, Spearman’s rank correlation (\(\rho\), method = "spearman") is the primary non-parametric measure of monotonic association, supplemented alongside Pearson’s linear correlation (\(r\), method = "pearson"): \[r_{xy} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i - \bar{x})^2 \sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \bar{y})^2}}\]
Categorical / Nominal Predictors (\(6\) variables: County, Region, Super_Region, South_East, Country, and Age_Profile): Because the outcome variable is continuous, Cramér’s \(V\) cannot be computed. Converting factor variables to numeric codes (as.numeric) allows Spearman’s \(\rho\) (and Pearson’s \(r\)) to be calculated via cor.results(). For binary variables (South_East and Age_Profile), the magnitude of the correlation is invariant to category order; for multi-category nominal variables (County, Region, Super_Region, Country), the coefficient depends on factor category ordering and serves only as a rough guide.



Create Age_Profile and compute Table 1 (Spearman and Pearson correlations with all continuous and categorical predictors, excluding District)
# Create census_copy and recode Age_65_plus into binary factor Age_Profile
census_copy <- census %>%
  mutate(
    Age_Profile = ifelse(
      census$Age_65_plus < median(census$Age_65_plus),
      "Youthful",
      "Ageing"
    ),
    Age_Profile = factor(Age_Profile)
  )

# Exclude the ID variable District
ID_variables <- "District"

# Part A: Continuous variables (48 predictors)
cont_vars <- census_copy %>%
  select(-all_of(ID_variables)) %>%
  select_if(is.numeric)

cor_mat_spearman <- cor(cont_vars, method = "spearman", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
cor_mat_pearson  <- cor(cont_vars, method = "pearson", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

res_cont_spearman <- cor.results(
  cor_mat_spearman,
  data = cont_vars,
  var.name = "Green_Central_Heating",
  sort.by = "abs.r"
)

res_cont_pearson <- cor.results(
  cor_mat_pearson,
  data = cont_vars,
  var.name = "Green_Central_Heating",
  sort.by = "abs.r"
)

table1_cont <- res_cont_spearman %>%
  transmute(
    Variable = y,
    Type = "Continuous",
    `Spearman rho` = round(r, 4),
    `Spearman p` = round(p.value, 2),
    `Spearman sig.` = sig.,
    `95% CI lb` = round(`95pct.ci.lb`, 3),
    `95% CI ub` = round(`95pct.ci.ub`, 3)
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    res_cont_pearson %>%
      transmute(
        Variable = y,
        `Pearson r` = round(r, 4),
        `Pearson sig.` = sig.
      ),
    by = "Variable"
  )

# Part B: Categorical variables (excluding District)
cat_var_names <- census_copy %>%
  select(-all_of(ID_variables)) %>%
  select_if(~ is.factor(.) & !is.ordered(.)) %>%
  names()

census_nominal <- census_copy %>%
  select(all_of(c("Green_Central_Heating", cat_var_names))) %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), as.numeric))

cor_nom_spearman <- cor(census_nominal, method = "spearman", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
cor_nom_pearson  <- cor(census_nominal, method = "pearson", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

res_nom_spearman <- cor.results(
  cor_nom_spearman,
  data = census_nominal,
  var.name = "Green_Central_Heating",
  sort.by = "abs.r"
)

res_nom_pearson <- cor.results(
  cor_nom_pearson,
  data = census_nominal,
  var.name = "Green_Central_Heating",
  sort.by = "abs.r"
)

table1_cat <- res_nom_spearman %>%
  transmute(
    Variable = y,
    Type = ifelse(y %in% c("Age_Profile", "South_East"), "Categorical (Binary)", "Categorical (Nominal)"),
    `Spearman rho` = round(r, 4),
    `Spearman p` = round(p.value, 2),
    `Spearman sig.` = sig.,
    `95% CI lb` = round(`95pct.ci.lb`, 3),
    `95% CI ub` = round(`95pct.ci.ub`, 3)
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    res_nom_pearson %>%
      transmute(
        Variable = y,
        `Pearson r` = round(r, 4),
        `Pearson sig.` = sig.
      ),
    by = "Variable"
  )

table1_combined <- bind_rows(table1_cont, table1_cat)

kable(
  table1_combined,
  align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "c", "r", "r", "r", "c"),

)

Strongest positive associations: Under both Spearman’s \(\rho\) and Pearson’s \(r\), Extractive_Job (\(\rho = 0.733^{**}, r = 0.868^{**}\)), Age_65_plus (\(\rho = 0.566^{**}, r = 0.577^{**}\)), Mean_Age (\(\rho = 0.556^{**}, r = 0.567^{**}\)), and Detached (\(\rho = 0.525^{**}, r = 0.519^{**}\)) show strong positive associations with Green_Central_Heating. Districts characterised by agricultural/extractive activity, older age profiles, and detached housing stock have higher shares of green central heating.
Strongest negative associations: Full_Time_Employee (\(\rho = -0.371^{**}, r = -0.475^{**}\)) and Age_0_to_19 (\(\rho = -0.506^{**}, r = -0.467^{**}\)) are strongly negatively correlated with Green_Central_Heating, alongside urban high-density indicators such as Flats (\(\rho = -0.527^{**}, r = -0.303^{**}\)) and Density (\(\rho = -0.489^{**}, r = -0.322^{**}\)).
Other selected predictors: No_Central_Heating (\(\rho = 0.140^{*}, r = 0.261^{**}\)) and Owned (\(\rho = 0.200^{**}, r = 0.191^{**}\)) are positively associated with Green_Central_Heating, while the binary categorical factor Age_Profile ("Youthful" vs. "Ageing") exhibits a strong negative correlation (\(\rho = -0.526^{**}, r = -0.493^{**}\)), confirming that youthful districts have significantly lower green central heating uptake than ageing districts.

6.1 Rationale for Predictor Selection

Full_Time_Employee (Continuous): Measures the percentage of working residents in full-time employment (\(>30\) hours/week), capturing district-level economic activity and urban labour-market concentration. (Note: while higher education attainment, Degree_plus, was initially considered based on the technology-adoption literature, it showed a weak bivariate correlation with Green_Central_Heating in Table 1 [\(r = -0.077, p = 0.16\)], whereas Full_Time_Employee showed a strong significant relationship [\(r = -0.475, p < 0.01\)].)
No_Central_Heating (Continuous): Captures the percentage of households without central heating, testing whether off-gas-grid districts lacking conventional heating infrastructure are more likely to adopt alternative green central heating systems.
Detached (Continuous): Represents housing morphology (% detached houses/bungalows), which directly governs the physical space and structural suitability for installing heat pumps, biomass boilers, or tank/bottled gas systems.
Owned (Continuous): Represents household tenure (% owner-occupied), reflecting the financial autonomy and long-term incentive of homeowners to invest in heating upgrades compared with renters.
Age_Profile (Categorical — "Ageing" vs. "Youthful"): Serves as a binary demographic proxy for population age structure and rural-urban demographic sorting.

title: Ordinary Least Squares Regression for modelling Green Central Heating in Census 2021
section: 7 Regression Model Fitting Strategy & Initial ‘Best’ Model Identification
text:
7 Regression Model Fitting Strategy & Initial ‘Best’ Model Identification

7.1 OLS Multiple Regression and Model-Fitting Strategy
For our continuous outcome variable \(Y_i\) (Green_Central_Heating), an Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) multiple linear regression model with \(k\) predictors takes the form:
\[Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{1i} + \beta_2 X_{2i} + \dots + \beta_k X_{ki} + \varepsilon_i, \quad \varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\]
where \(\beta_0\) is the intercept, each partial regression coefficient \(\beta_j\) measures the expected change in \(Y\) for a one-unit increase in \(X_j\) holding all other predictors constant, and \(\varepsilon_i = Y_i - \hat{Y}_i\) is the residual error. We evaluate model fit using the Coefficient of Determination (\(R^2 = 1 - \text{SSR}/\text{SST}\)), Adjusted \(R^2\), and the Akaike Information Criterion (\(\text{AIC} = 2p - 2\ln\hat{L}\)), where lower \(\text{AIC}\) values indicate a superior balance between goodness of fit and model parsimony.
Among the four regression model-fitting strategies covered in ENVS450 (Narrative, Backwards elimination, Backward stepwise, and All subsets), we explicitly adopt the Narrative approach. Starting with a baseline model containing our focal socio-economic predictor Full_Time_Employee (Model 1), we sequentially introduce housing and heating infrastructure controls—Detached, No_Central_Heating, and Owned (Model 2)—followed by the demographic factor Age_Profile (Model 3). This allows us to test how much of the initial bivariate effect of Full_Time_Employee is “explained away” by confounding housing and demographic differences across districts, stopping when adding further predictors yields negligible substantive gain in explanatory power (\(R^2\)) relative to added model complexity.


7.2 Fitting Models 1, 2, and 3 (Tables 2 & 3)


Fit Model 1, Model 2, and Model 3 following the Narrative approach
# Model 1: Focal socio-economic predictor of interest
model1 <- lm(Green_Central_Heating ~ Full_Time_Employee, data = census_copy)

# Model 2: Add housing structure, heating infrastructure, and tenure controls
model2 <- lm(
  Green_Central_Heating ~ Full_Time_Employee + Detached + No_Central_Heating + Owned,
  data = census_copy
)

# Model 3: Add demographic age structure (binary categorical variable Age_Profile)
# Reference category (0) = "Ageing"; Comparison category (1) = "Youthful"
model3 <- lm(
  Green_Central_Heating ~ Full_Time_Employee + Detached + No_Central_Heating + Owned + Age_Profile,
  data = census_copy
)

stars_fn <- function(p) {
  case_when(
    is.na(p) ~ "",
    p < 0.01 ~ " **",
    p < 0.05 ~ " *",
    TRUE     ~ ""
  )
}

fmt_coef <- function(model) {
  tidy(model) %>%
    transmute(
      Term = term,
      val = paste0(sprintf("%.2f", estimate), stars_fn(p.value))
    )
}

t2_terms <- fmt_coef(model1) %>% rename(`Model 1` = val) %>%
  full_join(fmt_coef(model2) %>% rename(`Model 2` = val), by = "Term") %>%
  full_join(fmt_coef(model3) %>% rename(`Model 3` = val), by = "Term") %>%
  mutate(across(c(`Model 1`, `Model 2`, `Model 3`), ~ replace_na(.x, "")))

t2_fit <- tibble(
  Term = c("R-squared (%)", "Adjusted R-squared (%)", "AIC"),
  `Model 1` = c(
    sprintf("%.2f", glance(model1)$r.squared * 100),
    sprintf("%.2f", glance(model1)$adj.r.squared * 100),
    sprintf("%.2f", glance(model1)$AIC)
  ),
  `Model 2` = c(
    sprintf("%.2f", glance(model2)$r.squared * 100),
    sprintf("%.2f", glance(model2)$adj.r.squared * 100),
    sprintf("%.2f", glance(model2)$AIC)
  ),
  `Model 3` = c(
    sprintf("%.2f", glance(model3)$r.squared * 100),
    sprintf("%.2f", glance(model3)$adj.r.squared * 100),
    sprintf("%.2f", glance(model3)$AIC)
  )
)

table2_clean <- bind_rows(t2_terms, t2_fit)

kable(

  align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"),
  caption = "Table 2 – Narrative Approach for Initial 'Best' Model (** Significant at 0.01 level. Source: Calculations based on Census 2021 Dataset)"

7.3 Interpretation of Narrative Models (Tables 2 & 3)

Model 1 (Green_Central_Heating ~ Full_Time_Employee): Shows a statistically significant negative slope of \(-0.21^{**}\) (exact: \(-0.2097, p < 0.001\)), explaining \(R^2 = 22.54\%\) of the variance in green central heating with \(\text{AIC} = 1255.30\).
Model 2 (+ Detached + No_Central_Heating + Owned): Adding housing morphology, lack of central heating, and homeownership reduces the magnitude of the Full_Time_Employee slope from \(-0.2097\) to \(-0.1283\) (\(-0.13^{**}\))—a reduction of \(38.8\%\). Thus, nearly two-fifths of the initial apparent effect of Full_Time_Employee in Model 1 is “explained away” once we account for the fact that urban districts with high full-time employment also have fewer detached homes (Detached \(\beta = +0.11^{**}\)) and fewer off-grid properties (No_Central_Heating \(\beta = +0.44^{**}\)). Controlling for these housing factors more than doubles model fit from \(R^2 = 22.54\%\) to \(53.08\%\) (Adjusted \(R^2 = 52.51\%\)) and reduces \(\text{AIC}\) by \(159.93\) points to \(1095.37\).
Model 3 (+ Age_Profile): In Model 3, Age_Profile is entered as a dummy variable where "Ageing" is the reference category (0) and "Youthful" is coded 1. The coefficient Age_ProfileYouthful = -0.54 ** (exact: \(-0.5419, p = 0.00444\)) indicates that holding the other four predictors constant, youthful districts have on average \(0.54\) percentage points lower green central heating than ageing districts, and the Full_Time_Employee slope shrinks further to \(-0.11^{**}\) (exact: \(-0.1066\), a \(49.2\%\) reduction relative to Model 1). However, although Age_ProfileYouthful is statistically significant (\(F = 8.21, p = 0.0044, \Delta\text{AIC} = -6.26\)), its substantive contribution to overall model fit is very modest, increasing \(R^2\) by only \(1.16\) percentage points (from \(53.08\%\) to \(54.24\%\)) and altering the Full_Time_Employee slope by just \(0.02\). Therefore, on grounds of model parsimony and practical interpretability, Model 2 is selected as the Initial ‘Best’ Model (Table 3):

\[\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\text{Green\_Central\_Heating}} &= 13.73 - 0.13(\text{Full\_Time\_Employee}) + 0.11(\text{Detached}) \\
&\quad + 0.44(\text{No\_Central\_Heating}) - 0.06(\text{Owned})
\end{aligned}\]

title: Ordinary Least Squares Regression for modelling Green Central Heating in Census 2021
text:
8 Interaction Effect Evaluation

8.1 Multiplicative Interaction Effects
In an additive linear model (Model 2), the partial slope of each predictor \(X_1\) is assumed to be constant across all levels of the other predictors. Adding a two-way multiplicative interaction term \(\beta_{12}(X_1 \cdot X_2)\) allows the marginal effect of \(X_1\) on \(\hat{Y}\) to depend linearly on the moderator \(X_2\):
\[\frac{\partial \hat{Y}}{\partial X_1} = \beta_1 + \beta_{12} X_2\]
Here, the main-effect coefficient \(\beta_1\) represents the conditional slope of \(X_1\) specifically when \(X_2 = 0\), while \(\beta_{12}\) measures how much the slope of \(X_1\) changes for each one-unit increase in \(X_2\).


8.2 Step 1: Full Two-Way Interactions Model (Model 2 I / model2i_first, Table 4)
Starting from the four continuous predictors in model2, we first fit model2i_first (Model 2 I) containing all four main effects plus all \(\binom{4}{2} = 6\) possible two-way interaction terms:


Fit full 6-interaction model (model2i_first) and reduced 3-interaction model (model2i)
# Model 2 I (model2i_first): All 4 main effects + all 6 two-way interactions
model2i_first <- lm(
  Green_Central_Heating ~ Full_Time_Employee + Detached + No_Central_Heating + Owned +
    Full_Time_Employee:Detached +
    Detached:No_Central_Heating +
    No_Central_Heating:Owned +
    Owned:Full_Time_Employee +
    Detached:Owned +
    Full_Time_Employee:No_Central_Heating,
  data = census_copy
)

# Model 2 IS (model2i): Backwards elimination retaining the 3 significant interactions
model2i <- lm(
  Green_Central_Heating ~ Full_Time_Employee + Detached + No_Central_Heating + Owned +
    Detached:No_Central_Heating +
    No_Central_Heating:Owned +
    Detached:Owned,
  data = census_copy
)

# Produce Table 4 (Full Two-Way Interactions Model: Model 2 I)
t4_tidy <- tidy(model2i_first)

table4_clean <- t4_tidy %>%
  transmute(
    Term = term,
    `Model 2 I Estimate` = paste0(sprintf("%.4f", estimate), stars_fn(p.value)),
    `Std. Error` = sprintf("%.4f", std.error),
    `t-statistic` = sprintf("%.2f", statistic),
    `p-value` = sprintf("%.4f", p.value)
  ) %>%
  bind_rows(
    tibble(
      Term = c("R-squared (%)", "Adjusted R-squared (%)", "AIC"),

8.4 Interpretation of Model 2 IS (model2i)
In Model 2 IS (Table 5), all four main effects and all three retained interaction terms are statistically significant at the \(1\%\) level (\(p < 0.01\)), with \(R^2 = 57.9982\%\) (Adjusted \(R^2 = 57.0879\%\)) and \(\text{AIC} = 1064.7252\) (improving upon Model 2 by \(+4.92\) percentage points in \(R^2\) and \(-30.64\) points in \(\text{AIC}\)):
\[\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\text{Green\_Central\_Heating}} &= 21.8933 - 0.0798(\text{Full\_Time\_Employee}) - 0.2024(\text{Detached}) \\
&\quad - 2.7318(\text{No\_Central\_Heating}) - 0.1879(\text{Owned}) \\
&\quad + 0.0458(\text{Detached} \times \text{No\_Central\_Heating}) \\
&\quad + 0.0353(\text{No\_Central\_Heating} \times \text{Owned}) \\
&\quad + 0.0037(\text{Detached} \times \text{Owned})
\end{aligned}\]

Intercept (21.8933 **): The predicted usage of green central heating is \(21.89\%\) when all predictors equal zero.
Conditional Main Effects vs. Positive Interactions: When Detached = 0 and Owned = 0, a \(1\) percentage point increase in No_Central_Heating changes predicted Green_Central_Heating by \(-2.7318\) percentage points. However, because both Detached:No_Central_Heating (\(+0.0458^{**}\)) and No_Central_Heating:Owned (\(+0.0353^{**}\)) are positive, the marginal effect of No_Central_Heating: \[\frac{\partial \widehat{\text{GCH}}}{\partial \text{No\_Central\_Heating}} = -2.7318 + 0.0458(\text{Detached}) + 0.0353(\text{Owned})\] becomes strongly positive in districts with typical or high shares of detached and owner-occupied housing. We visualise these marginal effects across the observed ranges of the predictors in Figures 1–3.



8.5 Visualising Interaction Effects (Figures 1, 2, and 3)


Plot Figure 1: Marginal effect of Detached across levels of Owned (mean +/- SD)

  ggtitle("") +
  ylab("Green Central Heating ") +
  theme_classic() +
  annotate("text", x = 36, y = 11, label = "(36.5, 10.2)", hjust = 1, vjust = 1, color = "black") +
  annotate("point", x = 36.5, y = 10.2, color = "yellow", size = 4)








Figure 2: Figure 1 – Green Central Heating vs Detached (Owned Constant), showing the crossover point at (36.5, 10.2).





Interpretation of Figure 1 (Detached \(\times\) Owned): Because the interaction Detached:Owned is positive (\(\beta = +0.0037^{**}\)), the positive slope of Green_Central_Heating with respect to Detached is steeper in districts with a high proportion of owner-occupied homes (Owned = 74.82%, green line) than in districts with lower homeownership (Owned = 54.64%, red line). Above the crossover threshold of 36.5% detached households (where predicted green central heating is 10.2%), high-ownership districts exhibit the highest predicted adoption of green central heating.


Plot Figure 2: Marginal effect of No_Central_Heating across levels of Detached
plot_model(model2i, type = "pred", terms = c("No_Central_Heating", "Detached")) +
  ggtitle("") +
  xlab("No Central Heating") +
  ylab("Green Central Heating") +
  theme_classic()








Figure 3: Figure 2 – Green Central Heating vs No Central Heating (Detached Constant).





Interpretation of Figure 2 (No_Central_Heating \(\times\) Detached): In districts with a low percentage of detached houses (Detached = 13.43%, red line), predicted green central heating remains almost flat (\(\sim 8\%–10\%\)) as No_Central_Heating increases. Conversely, in districts with a high percentage of detached houses (Detached = 38.76%, green line), an increase in No_Central_Heating is associated with a steep rise in Green_Central_Heating (reaching over \(35\%\)). This demonstrates that off-grid heating deprivation in dense urban areas does not translate into green central heating, whereas off-gas-grid rural districts with detached properties rely heavily on green/alternative central heating.


Plot Figure 3: Marginal effect of Full_Time_Employee across levels of Owned
plot_model(model2i, type = "pred", terms = c("Full_Time_Employee", "Owned")) +
  ggtitle("") +
  ylab("Green Central Heating") +
  xlab("Full Time Employee") +
  theme_classic()








Figure 4: Figure 3 – Green Central Heating vs Full Time Employee (Owned Constant).





Interpretation of Figure 3 (Full_Time_Employee across Owned): Because Full_Time_Employee does not interact significantly with Owned, the three lines are parallel with a negative slope (\(\beta = -0.0798^{**}\)). Usage of green central heating decreases as the percentage of full-time employees in a district increases, regardless of the level of homeownership.

title: Ordinary Least Squares Regression for modelling Green Central Heating in Census 2021
text:
9 Enhancing the ‘Best’ Model (Polynomials)

9.1 Rationale for Choosing Polynomial Predictors
To evaluate whether non-linear effects can further enhance Model 2 IS (Instruction #10), we consider the three techniques taught in the module: data transformation, polynomial regression, and piecewise regression. We choose polynomial regression—adding a quadratic term \(\beta_2 X^2\) via I(X^2)—because it captures smooth non-linear curvature within an OLS framework while keeping the outcome variable Green_Central_Heating in its natural, directly interpretable percentage units.


9.2 Exploratory Bivariate Linear vs. Quadratic Fit
Before adding quadratic terms to the full interaction model, we can visually compare a bivariate linear fit (~ Owned) against a quadratic term (~ I(Owned^2)):


Compare linear vs quadratic bivariate fits using grid.arrange
m1_exp <- lm(Green_Central_Heating ~ Owned, data = census_copy)
census_copy$predicted_gch_linear <- predict(m1_exp)

g1 <- ggplot(data = census_copy) +
  geom_point(aes(y = Green_Central_Heating, x = Owned), colour = "red", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_line(aes(y = predicted_gch_linear, x = Owned), colour = "blue", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.9) +
  ggtitle("Linear: ~ Owned") +
  xlab("Owned (%)") +
  ylab("Green Central Heating (%)") +
  theme_classic()

m2_exp <- lm(Green_Central_Heating ~ I(Owned^2), data = census_copy)
census_copy$predicted_gch_quad <- predict(m2_exp)

g2 <- ggplot(data = census_copy) +
  geom_point(aes(y = Green_Central_Heating, x = Owned), colour = "red", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_line(aes(y = predicted_gch_quad, x = Owned), colour = "blue", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.9) +
  ggtitle("Quadratic: ~ I(Owned^2)") +
  xlab("Owned (%)") +
  ylab("Green Central Heating (%)") +
  theme_classic()

grid.arrange(g1, g2, ncol = 2)








Figure 5: Exploratory comparison of a linear fit (left) vs. quadratic term I(Owned^2) (right) for Green Central Heating against Owned.







9.3 Evaluating Candidate Polynomial Models (M1–M4, Table 6 & Table 7)
We test adding a quadratic term + I(X^2) to Model 2 IS (model2i) for each of the four continuous predictors in turn:

M1: model2i + I(Owned^2)
M2: model2i + I(Detached^2)
M3: model2i + I(Full_Time_Employee^2)
M4: model2i + I(No_Central_Heating^2)

  data = census_copy
)

M4 <- update(model2i, . ~ . + I(No_Central_Heating^2))

text:
10 Assessment of the Final Model
In accordance with Instruction #12(a)–(d), we assess our final preferred model (M2) across four diagnostic and interpretive dimensions:

Normality of Residuals (skew and density plot)
Homoscedasticity (spreadLevelPlot and Breusch-Pagan ncvTest)
Multicollinearity (\(\text{VIF}\)) and Independence of Errors (durbinWatsonTest)
Relative Importance of Predictors (adequacy_lm) and Real-World Interpretation


10.1 10.1 Model Errors Distribution (Normality of Residuals — Figure 4)


Compute residual skewness and plot residual density (Figure 4) for M2
skew_M2_resid <- skew(M2$residuals)
cat("skew(M2$residuals):", skew_M2_resid, "\n")


skew(M2$residuals): 0.9542924 


Compute residual skewness and plot residual density (Figure 4) for M2
ggplot(data = M2) +
  geom_density(aes(x = .resid), fill = "black") +
  xlab("Model Errors (.resid)") +
  ylab("Density") +
  theme_classic()








Figure 6: Figure 4 – Model Errors (.resid) vs Density for Final Model M2.





Interpretation of Figure 4: Model residuals (\(e_i = Y_i - \hat{Y}_i\)) are centred near zero with a skewness of 0.9542924. Because \(|\text{skew}(e_i)| < 1\), the residual distribution satisfies the course threshold for approximate normality, substantially reducing the raw outcome skewness of \(1.73\). A mild positive tail remains on the right, indicating that a few extreme rural districts have higher green central heating than predicted by the model.


10.2 10.2 Homoscedasticity (Constant Error Variance — Figure 5 & ncvTest)
We test the assumption of constant error variance (\(\text{Var}(\varepsilon_i) = \sigma^2\)) visually via car::spreadLevelPlot(M2) (Figure 5) and formally via the Breusch-Pagan / Cook-Weisberg Non-Constant Variance Score Test (car::ncvTest(M2)), where the null hypothesis (\(H_0\)) is constant error variance (homoscedasticity) and the alternative hypothesis (\(H_1\)) is that error variance changes systematically with the fitted values (heteroscedasticity):


Plot Figure 5: spreadLevelPlot(M2) and run ncvTest(M2)
spreadLevelPlot(M2)



Suggested power transformation:  -1.066471 








Figure 7: Figure 5 – Constant Error Variance vs Fitted values (Spread-Level Plot for Final Model M2).







Run Non-Constant Variance Score Test ncvTest(M2)
ncvTest(M2)


Non-constant Variance Score Test 
Variance formula: ~ fitted.values 
Chisquare = 38.16122, Df = 1, p = 6.5134e-10


Interpretation of Figure 5 and ncvTest(M2): In Figure 5, the dashed reference line slopes upward from left to right and the solid magenta smoother curves across the left and middle of the plot, indicating that the spread of the studentized residuals increases as the predicted values of Green_Central_Heating increase. Formally, ncvTest(M2) yields \(\chi^2 = 38.16122\) (\(\text{df} = 1\)) with \(p = 6.5134 \times 10^{-10} \ll 0.05\). Because \(p < 0.05\), we reject the null hypothesis of constant error variance and conclude that the model exhibits statistically significant heteroscedasticity (error variance is larger in high-adoption rural districts than in low-adoption urban districts).
How this breach of homoscedasticity can be addressed (Instruction #12b):

Power / Box-Cox Transformation of the Outcome Variable: spreadLevelPlot(M2) suggests a stabilising power transformation of \(\lambda = -1.066471\) (approximately an inverse transformation \(Y^{-1}\), or a logarithmic transformation \(\log(Y)\)) to compress the right tail and stabilise error variance.
Heteroscedasticity-Consistent (HC3) Robust Standard Errors: Computing White’s heteroscedasticity-robust standard errors (car::hccm(M2)) provides valid \(t\)-tests and confidence intervals without altering the original percentage scale of Green_Central_Heating.
Weighted Least Squares (WLS): Weighting districts inversely to their estimated error variance.



10.3 10.3 Multicollinearity (\(\text{VIF}\)) & Independence of Errors (Durbin-Watson)
We evaluate multicollinearity among the four core continuous predictors using the Variance Inflation Factor (\(\text{VIF}_j = \frac{1}{1 - R_j^2}\)) on model2, and test for residual autocorrelation using durbinWatsonTest(M2):


Check Variance Inflation Factors (vif) on model2 and Durbin-Watson autocorrelation on M2

vif_mean   <- mean(vif(model2)) %>% round(1)

cat("VIF for each main predictor in model2:\n")


VIF for each main predictor in model2:


Check Variance Inflation Factors (vif) on model2 and Durbin-Watson autocorrelation on M2
print(vif_values)


Full_Time_Employee           Detached No_Central_Heating              Owned 
              1.13               2.61               1.31               2.90 


Check Variance Inflation Factors (vif) on model2 and Durbin-Watson autocorrelation on M2
cat("\nMean VIF:", vif_mean, "\n\n")



Mean VIF: 2 


Check Variance Inflation Factors (vif) on model2 and Durbin-Watson autocorrelation on M2
set.seed(123)
durbinWatsonTest(M2)

   1       0.2997139      1.399649       0
 Alternative hypothesis: rho != 0


Interpretation of Multicollinearity and Independence Diagnostics:

Multicollinearity (vif(model2)): All individual Variance Inflation Factors are well below the warning threshold of \(5\) (Full_Time_Employee = 1.13, No_Central_Heating = 1.31, Detached = 2.61, Owned = 2.90), with a mean \(\text{VIF}\) of 2.0, confirming no problematic multicollinearity among the four main predictors.
Independence of Errors (durbinWatsonTest(M2)): The Durbin-Watson statistic is 1.444645 with a lag-1 residual autocorrelation of 0.2771037 (\(p = 0.000 < 0.05\)). Rejecting \(H_0: \rho = 0\) indicates positive autocorrelation among adjacent districts in the dataset, reflecting geographic clustering across regions. This breach could be remedied by incorporating regional fixed effects (e.g., Region or Super_Region) or estimating a spatial / multilevel regression model.



10.4 10.4 Relative Importance of Predictors (Adequacy — Figure 6)
To evaluate the relative importance of the predictors in our final model (Instruction #12c), we use adequacy_lm(M2) from Session_10_functions.R. In OLS regression, Adequacy is defined as the \(R^2\) of a single-predictor model divided by the \(R^2\) of the full model (\(58.52\%\)), measuring the percentage of the full model’s explanatory power captured by each main or polynomial predictor on its own (noting that adequacy_lm() evaluates main and polynomial terms individually and excludes multiplicative interaction terms):
\[\text{Adequacy}_j (\%) = \left( \frac{R^2_{\text{single predictor } j}}{R^2_{\text{full model}}} \right) \times 100\]

Interpretation of Figure 6:

I(Detached^2) (\(54.03\%\) adequacy, single-predictor \(R^2 = 31.62\%\)) and Detached (\(46.03\%\) adequacy, single-predictor \(R^2 = 26.94\%\)) are by far the most powerful individual predictors of green central heating adoption—the quadratic detached-housing term alone accounts for more than half (\(54\%\)) of the explanatory power of the full model.
Full_Time_Employee (\(38.52\%\) adequacy, single-predictor \(R^2 = 22.54\%\)) is the next most important standalone predictor.
No_Central_Heating (\(11.67\%\) adequacy, \(R^2 = 6.83\%\)) and Owned (\(6.24\%\) adequacy, \(R^2 = 3.65\%\)) have smaller standalone adequacy values because their primary explanatory contribution operates conditionally through their strong multiplicative interactions with Detached and with each other.



10.5 10.5 Real-World Interpretation: What the Model Reveals About the UK (Instruction #12d)
Our final model (M2, explaining \(58.52\%\) of the district-level variation across England and Wales) reveals four key insights into the real-world geography of residential green central heating in 2021:

The Rural & Off-Gas-Grid Housing Effect (Detached, I(Detached^2), and No_Central_Heating): Dwelling morphology (Detached and I(Detached^2)) is the single strongest determinant of green central heating adoption (\(54.03\%\) adequacy). Moreover, the positive interaction between Detached and No_Central_Heating (Figure 2) shows that green central heating uptake is concentrated in rural, low-density districts where detached homes are off the UK’s mains natural-gas grid. In urban districts dominated by flats and terraced housing, a lack of central heating does not lead to green central heating adoption; in rural detached-housing districts off the gas grid, households rely heavily on renewable heat pumps, biomass boilers, communal heat networks, or tank/bottled gas.
The Enabling Role of Homeownership (Owned Interactions): While Owned has a modest standalone correlation (\(r = 0.191\), adequacy \(= 6.24\%\)), its positive interactions with Detached (Figure 1, crossover at \(36.5\%\) detached) and No_Central_Heating highlight a critical tenure divide: in districts with detached, off-grid housing stock, owner-occupation substantially accelerates green heating adoption. Homeowners have the property rights and long-term financial horizon required to invest in alternative heating systems, whereas private and social rented sectors face split-incentive barriers.
Urban Labour Markets vs. Rural Demographics (Full_Time_Employee and Age_Profile): Full_Time_Employee is negatively associated with Green_Central_Heating (\(\beta = -0.0806^{**}\), Figure 3). However, our Narrative modelling (Table 2) demonstrated that nearly half of the initial bivariate effect of Full_Time_Employee is explained away once we control for housing morphology (Detached), heating infrastructure (No_Central_Heating), tenure (Owned), and demographic ageing (Age_Profile). Urban commuter districts with younger, full-time working populations are overwhelmingly connected to the mains gas grid, whereas older, rural districts lead in non-mains/green central heating adoption.
Policy Implications: To achieve broad residential decarbonisation across the UK, climate and energy policy cannot rely solely on off-grid rural homeowners installing heat pumps or biomass in detached houses. Policymakers must address the urban mains-gas and rented housing sectors—expanding district heat networks for high-density flats, providing targeted grants for lower-income urban authorities, and introducing regulatory incentives to overcome landlord-tenant split incentives.

title: Ordinary Least Squares Regression for modelling Green Central Heating in Census 2021
text:
The focal point of this report centres around the research question: “What are the key determinants impacting the implementation of green central heating in the districts of the UK?” This question is highly relevant in the context of rising environmental awareness, residential decarbonisation targets, and the transition toward a sustainable energy future. Domestic heating accounts for a substantial share of national greenhouse gas emissions, meaning that the adoption of green central heating systems—such as heat pumps, biomass boilers, solar thermal, and district or communal heat networks—stands as a crucial pillar in reducing residential carbon footprints and promoting energy-efficient practices.
Understanding the socio-economic, demographic, and housing-stock factors that shape the uptake of green central heating technologies provides actionable insight for both public policymakers and private-sector energy markets. Effective decarbonisation policy requires more than technological availability; it requires identifying how lifestyle patterns, housing tenure, dwelling structure, and local heating infrastructure interact across different local authorities.
This report is systematically organised to follow the end-to-end statistical modelling workflow required by my coursework:

Literature Review and Variables Selection Rationale summarises existing empirical research on sustainable household technology adoption and motivates our candidate predictors.
Methodology & Setup introduces the 2021 Census district-level dataset (N = 331 local authority districts across 55 variables) and outlines the quantitative modelling strategy.
Univariate Description of Outcome Variable examines the distribution, skewness, central tendency, and dispersion of Green_Central_Heating.
Correlation Analysis of Outcome Variable screens bivariate associations between Green_Central_Heating and all other continuous and categorical variables in the dataset (excluding the identifier District) using rank-based correlation (Table 1).
Selection of Predictor Variables justifies the five chosen candidate predictors (four continuous and one newly constructed binary categorical variable, Age_Profile).
Regression Model Fitting Strategy & Initial ‘Best’ Model Identification applies the Narrative approach across three sequential Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) models (model1, model2, model3) to assess confounding (“explained away” effects) and identify the initial ‘best’ main-effects specification (Tables 2 & 3).
Interaction Effect Evaluation tests all two-way multiplicative interactions among the main predictors (model2i_first, Table 4) and uses backwards elimination to retain statistically significant interactions (model2i, Table 5 and Figures 1–3).
Enhancing the ‘Best’ Model (Polynomials) evaluates non-linear quadratic terms across the continuous predictors (Table 6) to arrive at the final preferred model (M2, Table 7).
Assessment of the Final Model conducts regression diagnostics—residual normality (Figure 4), homoscedasticity (Figure 5), multicollinearity (\text{VIF}), and error independence (Durbin-Watson)—evaluates the relative importance of predictors via Adequacy (Figure 6), and synthesises what the model reveals about the UK housing landscape.

section: 2 Literature Review and Variables Selection Rationale
text:
2 Literature Review and Variables Selection Rationale
Recent studies in environmental sciences and energy socio-economics have investigated the drivers behind household adoption of sustainable technologies such as green central heating. Empirical research demonstrates that residential technology adoption is not merely a function of technological availability, but is strongly conditioned by socio-economic and demographic characteristics (Hooks et al., 2022). Educational attainment, economic activity, housing type, tenure, and environmental awareness play central roles in the uptake of green energy technologies, as highlighted by Bruckmann, Willibald and Blanco (2021) in their regional study of sustainable technology diffusion without strong policy mandates.
Drawing on this literature, potential district-level determinants include economic activity and employment structure (Full_Time_Employee), dwelling morphology (Detached), household tenure (Owned), demographic age structure (Age_Profile), and existing heating infrastructure (No_Central_Heating). In particular, examining the proportion of households with no central heating (No_Central_Heating) allows us to test whether off-grid districts lacking conventional mains-gas central heating are more inclined to adopt alternative green central heating options, or whether a lack of central heating instead reflects urban deprivation and lower capacity for capital-intensive energy retrofits.

3 Methodology & Setup

3.1 Dataset Description
The data analysed in this report come from the 2021 Census collected by the Office for National Statistics (ONS) in March 2021 (Office for National Statistics, 2023). The course dataset (Census_2021.Rdata) is aggregated to the local authority district level across England and Wales and contains N = 331 districts (rows) and 55 variables (columns):

49 continuous numeric variables, mostly expressed as percentages of households, residents, or workers in each district (plus district-level summary measures such as Mean_Age and population Density).
6 categorical factor variables capturing administrative geography (District, County, Region, Super_Region, South_East, and Country).



3.2 Environment Setup and Package Loading
The R chunk below checks that all required packages are installed in the active R environment, loads them in the appropriate order (loading ENVS450 after tidyverse so course helper functions like skew(), cor.results(), coeffs(), and regress.compare() are available while preserving dplyr::select() over MASS::select()), loads Census_2021.Rdata from data/data_r/gch_dataNfunc/, and sources the course helper script Session_10_functions.R (which provides adequacy_lm()).


Check/install required packages, load libraries, and load Census 2021 data

  "MASS",       # Supports backwards elimination and regression utilities
  "car",        # Regression diagnostics: vif(), spreadLevelPlot(), ncvTest(), durbinWatsonTest()
  "tidyverse",  # Data wrangling (dplyr, tidyr, forcats) and plotting (ggplot2)
  "broom",      # Tidy model summaries: tidy(), glance(), augment()
  "leaps",      # All-subsets regression support

  "sjPlot",     # Marginal effect interaction plots: plot_model()
  "gridExtra",  # Side-by-side plot arrangement: grid.arrange()
  "knitr"       # Formatted markdown/HTML tables: kable()
)

3.3 Analytical Workflow
Our modelling workflow proceeds in five stages:

Univariate exploration of the continuous outcome variable Green_Central_Heating to assess its distributional shape and select appropriate summary statistics.
Bivariate correlation screening across all candidate variables in the dataset (excluding the identifier District), alongside the creation of a recoded binary demographic factor Age_Profile (dichotomising Age_65_plus at its median into "Youthful" vs. "Ageing" districts).
Narrative regression modelling starting from a single focal predictor (Full_Time_Employee in model1), adding housing and heating controls (Detached, No_Central_Heating, Owned in model2), and testing the demographic factor (Age_Profile in model3) to identify our initial ‘best’ model.
Refinement via interactions and polynomials, first testing all \binom{4}{2} = 6 two-way interactions (model2i_first) and eliminating non-significant terms to obtain model2i (Model 2 IS), then testing quadratic polynomial terms (M1–M4) to arrive at the final model M2.
Model diagnostics and predictor adequacy, evaluating residual normality, constant error variance, multicollinearity, autocorrelation, and single-predictor R^2 adequacy (adequacy_lm()).

title: Ordinary Least Squares Regression for modelling Green Central Heating in Census 2021
text:
4 Univariate Description of Outcome Variable
Our outcome variable of interest is Green_Central_Heating, a continuous variable measuring the percentage of households in a local authority district that use one or more ‘green’ forms of central heating (defined in the Census 2021 data dictionary as renewable energy systems such as heat pumps or biomass, district/communal heat networks, or tank/bottled gas).

4.1 Skewness, Central Tendency, and Dispersion
Before summarising a continuous variable, we examine its skewness, which measures the asymmetry of its distribution around its mean \bar{Y}:
\text{Skewness} = \frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_i - \bar{Y})^3}{\left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_i - \bar{Y})^2\right]^{3/2}}
A symmetric normal distribution has \text{Skewness} \approx 0, whereas distributions with |\text{Skewness}| > 1 are substantially skewed. When a continuous variable has \text{Skewness} > 1, the arithmetic mean and standard deviation are distorted by extreme values in the right tail. We therefore use the Median (50\text{th} percentile, Q_2) to measure central tendency and the Inter-Quartile Range (\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1) to measure dispersion across the middle 50\% of districts.


Compute skewness, median, and IQR for Green_Central_Heating
gch_skew   <- skew(census$Green_Central_Heating)
gch_median <- median(census$Green_Central_Heating, na.rm = TRUE)
gch_iqr    <- IQR(census$Green_Central_Heating, na.rm = TRUE)

cat("skew(census$Green_Central_Heating):  ", gch_skew, " (rounded:", round(gch_skew, 2), ")\n")

title: Ordinary Least Squares Regression for modelling Green Central Heating in Census 2021
text:
5 Correlation Analysis of Outcome Variable
To satisfy Instruction #5 (“Examine how strongly correlated your outcome variable is with ALL of the other variables in the dataset”) and prepare a categorical demographic predictor for Instruction #6, we create a working copy of the dataset (census_copy) and construct a binary categorical variable, Age_Profile, by splitting districts at the median percentage of residents aged 65 and over (Age_65_plus):

Districts with Age_65_plus < median(Age_65_plus) are classified as "Youthful".
Districts with Age_65_plus >= median(Age_65_plus) are classified as "Ageing".


5.1 Choice of Correlation Measure and Treatment of Variable Types
Following the course correlation guidelines (Assignment-2--correlations.html):

Exclusion of Identifier Variables: District is a unique nominal identifier for each local authority (1 to 331 in alphabetical order) rather than a substantive characteristic, so it is excluded from the correlation analysis (ID_variables <- "District").
Continuous Predictors (48 variables): Because the continuous outcome Green_Central_Heating is positively skewed (\text{skew} = 1.73) and several continuous predictors also exhibit skewness, Spearman’s rank correlation (\rho, method = "spearman") is the primary non-parametric measure of monotonic association, supplemented alongside Pearson’s linear correlation (r, method = "pearson"): r_{xy} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i - \bar{x})^2 \sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \bar{y})^2}}
Categorical / Nominal Predictors (6 variables: County, Region, Super_Region, South_East, Country, and Age_Profile): Because the outcome variable is continuous, Cramér’s V cannot be computed. Converting factor variables to numeric codes (as.numeric) allows Spearman’s \rho (and Pearson’s r) to be calculated via cor.results(). For binary variables (South_East and Age_Profile), the magnitude of the correlation is invariant to category order; for multi-category nominal variables (County, Region, Super_Region, Country), the coefficient depends on factor category ordering and serves only as a rough guide.



Create Age_Profile and compute Table 1 (Spearman and Pearson correlations with all continuous and categorical predictors, excluding District)
# Create census_copy and recode Age_65_plus into binary factor Age_Profile
census_copy <- census %>%
  mutate(
    Age_Profile = ifelse(
      census$Age_65_plus < median(census$Age_65_plus),
      "Youthful",
      "Ageing"
    ),
    Age_Profile = factor(Age_Profile)
  )

# Exclude the ID variable District
ID_variables <- "District"

# Part A: Continuous variables (48 predictors)
cont_vars <- census_copy %>%
  select(-all_of(ID_variables)) %>%
  select_if(is.numeric)

5.2 Interpretation of Table 1

Strongest positive associations: Under both Spearman’s \rho and Pearson’s r, Extractive_Job (\rho = 0.733^{**}, r = 0.868^{**}), Age_65_plus (\rho = 0.566^{**}, r = 0.577^{**}), Mean_Age (\rho = 0.556^{**}, r = 0.567^{**}), and Detached (\rho = 0.525^{**}, r = 0.519^{**}) show strong positive associations with Green_Central_Heating. Districts characterised by agricultural/extractive activity, older age profiles, and detached housing stock have higher shares of green central heating.
Strongest negative associations: Full_Time_Employee (\rho = -0.371^{**}, r = -0.475^{**}) and Age_0_to_19 (\rho = -0.506^{**}, r = -0.467^{**}) are strongly negatively correlated with Green_Central_Heating, alongside urban high-density indicators such as Flats (\rho = -0.527^{**}, r = -0.303^{**}) and Density (\rho = -0.489^{**}, r = -0.322^{**}).
Other selected predictors: No_Central_Heating (\rho = 0.140^{*}, r = 0.261^{**}) and Owned (\rho = 0.200^{**}, r = 0.191^{**}) are positively associated with Green_Central_Heating, while the binary categorical factor Age_Profile ("Youthful" vs. "Ageing") exhibits a strong negative correlation (\rho = -0.526^{**}, r = -0.493^{**}), confirming that youthful districts have significantly lower green central heating uptake than ageing districts.

6.1 Rationale for Predictor Selection

Full_Time_Employee (Continuous): Measures the percentage of working residents in full-time employment (>30 hours/week), capturing district-level economic activity and urban labour-market concentration. (Note: while higher education attainment, Degree_plus, was initially considered based on the technology-adoption literature, it showed a weak bivariate correlation with Green_Central_Heating in Table 1 [r = -0.077, p = 0.16], whereas Full_Time_Employee showed a strong significant relationship [r = -0.475, p < 0.01].)
No_Central_Heating (Continuous): Captures the percentage of households without central heating, testing whether off-gas-grid districts lacking conventional heating infrastructure are more likely to adopt alternative green central heating systems.
Detached (Continuous): Represents housing morphology (% detached houses/bungalows), which directly governs the physical space and structural suitability for installing heat pumps, biomass boilers, or tank/bottled gas systems.
Owned (Continuous): Represents household tenure (% owner-occupied), reflecting the financial autonomy and long-term incentive of homeowners to invest in heating upgrades compared with renters.
Age_Profile (Categorical — "Ageing" vs. "Youthful"): Serves as a binary demographic proxy for population age structure and rural-urban demographic sorting.

section: 7 Regression Model Fitting Strategy & Initial ‘Best’ Model Identification
text:
7 Regression Model Fitting Strategy & Initial ‘Best’ Model Identification

7.1 OLS Multiple Regression and Model-Fitting Strategy
For our continuous outcome variable Y_i (Green_Central_Heating), an Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) multiple linear regression model with k predictors takes the form:
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{1i} + \beta_2 X_{2i} + \dots + \beta_k X_{ki} + \varepsilon_i, \quad \varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)
where \beta_0 is the intercept, each partial regression coefficient \beta_j measures the expected change in Y for a one-unit increase in X_j holding all other predictors constant, and \varepsilon_i = Y_i - \hat{Y}_i is the residual error. We evaluate model fit using the Coefficient of Determination (R^2 = 1 - \text{SSR}/\text{SST}), Adjusted R^2, and the Akaike Information Criterion (\text{AIC} = 2p - 2\ln\hat{L}), where lower \text{AIC} values indicate a superior balance between goodness of fit and model parsimony.
Among the four regression model-fitting strategies covered in ENVS450 (Narrative, Backwards elimination, Backward stepwise, and All subsets), we explicitly adopt the Narrative approach. Starting with a baseline model containing our focal socio-economic predictor Full_Time_Employee (Model 1), we sequentially introduce housing and heating infrastructure controls—Detached, No_Central_Heating, and Owned (Model 2)—followed by the demographic factor Age_Profile (Model 3). This allows us to test how much of the initial bivariate effect of Full_Time_Employee is “explained away” by confounding housing and demographic differences across districts, stopping when adding further predictors yields negligible substantive gain in explanatory power (R^2) relative to added model complexity.


7.2 Fitting Models 1, 2, and 3 (Tables 2 & 3)


Fit Model 1, Model 2, and Model 3 following the Narrative approach
# Model 1: Focal socio-economic predictor of interest
model1 <- lm(Green_Central_Heating ~ Full_Time_Employee, data = census_copy)

# Model 2: Add housing structure, heating infrastructure, and tenure controls
model2 <- lm(
  Green_Central_Heating ~ Full_Time_Employee + Detached + No_Central_Heating + Owned,
  data = census_copy
)

# Model 3: Add demographic age structure (binary categorical variable Age_Profile)
# Reference category (0) = "Ageing"; Comparison category (1) = "Youthful"
model3 <- lm(
  Green_Central_Heating ~ Full_Time_Employee + Detached + No_Central_Heating + Owned + Age_Profile,
  data = census_copy
)

stars_fn <- function(p) {
  case_when(
    is.na(p) ~ "",
    p < 0.01 ~ " **",
    p < 0.05 ~ " *",
    TRUE     ~ ""
  )
}

fmt_coef <- function(model) {
  tidy(model) %>%
    transmute(
      Term = term,
      val = paste0(sprintf("%.2f", estimate), stars_fn(p.value))
    )
}

t2_terms <- fmt_coef(model1) %>% rename(`Model 1` = val) %>%
  full_join(fmt_coef(model2) %>% rename(`Model 2` = val), by = "Term") %>%
  full_join(fmt_coef(model3) %>% rename(`Model 3` = val), by = "Term") %>%
  mutate(across(c(`Model 1`, `Model 2`, `Model 3`), ~ replace_na(.x, "")))

t2_fit <- tibble(
  Term = c("R-squared (%)", "Adjusted R-squared (%)", "AIC"),
  `Model 1` = c(
    sprintf("%.2f", glance(model1)$r.squared * 100),
    sprintf("%.2f", glance(model1)$adj.r.squared * 100),
    sprintf("%.2f", glance(model1)$AIC)
  ),
  `Model 2` = c(
    sprintf("%.2f", glance(model2)$r.squared * 100),
    sprintf("%.2f", glance(model2)$adj.r.squared * 100),
    sprintf("%.2f", glance(model2)$AIC)
  ),
  `Model 3` = c(
    sprintf("%.2f", glance(model3)$r.squared * 100),
    sprintf("%.2f", glance(model3)$adj.r.squared * 100),
    sprintf("%.2f", glance(model3)$AIC)
  )
)

table2_clean <- bind_rows(t2_terms, t2_fit)

kable(

7.3 Interpretation of Narrative Models (Tables 2 & 3)

Model 1 (Green_Central_Heating ~ Full_Time_Employee): Shows a statistically significant negative slope of -0.21^{**} (exact: -0.2097, p < 0.001), explaining R^2 = 22.54\% of the variance in green central heating with \text{AIC} = 1255.30.
Model 2 (+ Detached + No_Central_Heating + Owned): Adding housing morphology, lack of central heating, and homeownership reduces the magnitude of the Full_Time_Employee slope from -0.2097 to -0.1283 (-0.13^{**})—a reduction of 38.8\%. Thus, nearly two-fifths of the initial apparent effect of Full_Time_Employee in Model 1 is “explained away” once we account for the fact that urban districts with high full-time employment also have fewer detached homes (Detached \beta = +0.11^{**}) and fewer off-grid properties (No_Central_Heating \beta = +0.44^{**}). Controlling for these housing factors more than doubles model fit from R^2 = 22.54\% to 53.08\% (Adjusted R^2 = 52.51\%) and reduces \text{AIC} by 159.93 points to 1095.37.
Model 3 (+ Age_Profile): In Model 3, Age_Profile is entered as a dummy variable where "Ageing" is the reference category (0) and "Youthful" is coded 1. The coefficient Age_ProfileYouthful = -0.54 ** (exact: -0.5419, p = 0.00444) indicates that holding the other four predictors constant, youthful districts have on average 0.54 percentage points lower green central heating than ageing districts, and the Full_Time_Employee slope shrinks further to -0.11^{**} (exact: -0.1066, a 49.2\% reduction relative to Model 1). However, although Age_ProfileYouthful is statistically significant (F = 8.21, p = 0.0044, \Delta\text{AIC} = -6.26), its substantive contribution to overall model fit is very modest, increasing R^2 by only 1.16 percentage points (from 53.08\% to 54.24\%) and altering the Full_Time_Employee slope by just 0.02. Therefore, on grounds of model parsimony and practical interpretability, Model 2 is selected as the Initial ‘Best’ Model (Table 3):

\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\text{Green\_Central\_Heating}} &= 13.73 - 0.13(\text{Full\_Time\_Employee}) + 0.11(\text{Detached}) \\
&\quad + 0.44(\text{No\_Central\_Heating}) - 0.06(\text{Owned})
\end{aligned}

text:
8 Interaction Effect Evaluation

8.1 Multiplicative Interaction Effects
In an additive linear model (Model 2), the partial slope of each predictor X_1 is assumed to be constant across all levels of the other predictors. Adding a two-way multiplicative interaction term \beta_{12}(X_1 \cdot X_2) allows the marginal effect of X_1 on \hat{Y} to depend linearly on the moderator X_2:
\frac{\partial \hat{Y}}{\partial X_1} = \beta_1 + \beta_{12} X_2
Here, the main-effect coefficient \beta_1 represents the conditional slope of X_1 specifically when X_2 = 0, while \beta_{12} measures how much the slope of X_1 changes for each one-unit increase in X_2.


8.2 Step 1: Full Two-Way Interactions Model (Model 2 I / model2i_first, Table 4)
Starting from the four continuous predictors in model2, we first fit model2i_first (Model 2 I) containing all four main effects plus all \binom{4}{2} = 6 possible two-way interaction terms:


Fit full 6-interaction model (model2i_first) and reduced 3-interaction model (model2i)
# Model 2 I (model2i_first): All 4 main effects + all 6 two-way interactions
model2i_first <- lm(
  Green_Central_Heating ~ Full_Time_Employee + Detached + No_Central_Heating + Owned +
    Full_Time_Employee:Detached +
    Detached:No_Central_Heating +
    No_Central_Heating:Owned +
    Owned:Full_Time_Employee +
    Detached:Owned +
    Full_Time_Employee:No_Central_Heating,
  data = census_copy
)

# Model 2 IS (model2i): Backwards elimination retaining the 3 significant interactions
model2i <- lm(
  Green_Central_Heating ~ Full_Time_Employee + Detached + No_Central_Heating + Owned +
    Detached:No_Central_Heating +
    No_Central_Heating:Owned +
    Detached:Owned,
  data = census_copy
)

# Produce Table 4 (Full Two-Way Interactions Model: Model 2 I)
t4_tidy <- tidy(model2i_first)

table4_clean <- t4_tidy %>%
  transmute(
    Term = term,
    `Model 2 I Estimate` = paste0(sprintf("%.4f", estimate), stars_fn(p.value)),
    `Std. Error` = sprintf("%.4f", std.error),
    `t-statistic` = sprintf("%.2f", statistic),
    `p-value` = sprintf("%.4f", p.value)
  ) %>%
  bind_rows(
    tibble(
      Term = c("R-squared (%)", "Adjusted R-squared (%)", "AIC"),
      `Model 2 I Estimate` = c(
        sprintf("%.2f", glance(model2i_first)$r.squared * 100),
        sprintf("%.2f", glance(model2i_first)$adj.r.squared * 100),

8.4 Interpretation of Model 2 IS (model2i)
In Model 2 IS (Table 5), all four main effects and all three retained interaction terms are statistically significant at the 1\% level (p < 0.01), with R^2 = 57.9982\% (Adjusted R^2 = 57.0879\%) and \text{AIC} = 1064.7252 (improving upon Model 2 by +4.92 percentage points in R^2 and -30.64 points in \text{AIC}):
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\text{Green\_Central\_Heating}} &= 21.8933 - 0.0798(\text{Full\_Time\_Employee}) - 0.2024(\text{Detached}) \\
&\quad - 2.7318(\text{No\_Central\_Heating}) - 0.1879(\text{Owned}) \\
&\quad + 0.0458(\text{Detached} \times \text{No\_Central\_Heating}) \\
&\quad + 0.0353(\text{No\_Central\_Heating} \times \text{Owned}) \\
&\quad + 0.0037(\text{Detached} \times \text{Owned})
\end{aligned}

Intercept (21.8933 **): The predicted usage of green central heating is 21.89\% when all predictors equal zero.
Conditional Main Effects vs. Positive Interactions: When Detached = 0 and Owned = 0, a 1 percentage point increase in No_Central_Heating changes predicted Green_Central_Heating by -2.7318 percentage points. However, because both Detached:No_Central_Heating (+0.0458^{**}) and No_Central_Heating:Owned (+0.0353^{**}) are positive, the marginal effect of No_Central_Heating: \frac{\partial \widehat{\text{GCH}}}{\partial \text{No\_Central\_Heating}} = -2.7318 + 0.0458(\text{Detached}) + 0.0353(\text{Owned}) becomes strongly positive in districts with typical or high shares of detached and owner-occupied housing. We visualise these marginal effects across the observed ranges of the predictors in Figures 1–3.

Figure 2: Figure 1 – Green Central Heating vs Detached (Owned Constant), showing the crossover point at (36.5, 10.2).





Interpretation of Figure 1 (Detached \times Owned): Because the interaction Detached:Owned is positive (\beta = +0.0037^{**}), the positive slope of Green_Central_Heating with respect to Detached is steeper in districts with a high proportion of owner-occupied homes (Owned = 74.82%, green line) than in districts with lower homeownership (Owned = 54.64%, red line). Above the crossover threshold of 36.5% detached households (where predicted green central heating is 10.2%), high-ownership districts exhibit the highest predicted adoption of green central heating.


Plot Figure 2: Marginal effect of No_Central_Heating across levels of Detached

Interpretation of Figure 2 (No_Central_Heating \times Detached): In districts with a low percentage of detached houses (Detached = 13.43%, red line), predicted green central heating remains almost flat (\sim 8\%–10\%) as No_Central_Heating increases. Conversely, in districts with a high percentage of detached houses (Detached = 38.76%, green line), an increase in No_Central_Heating is associated with a steep rise in Green_Central_Heating (reaching over 35\%). This demonstrates that off-grid heating deprivation in dense urban areas does not translate into green central heating, whereas off-gas-grid rural districts with detached properties rely heavily on green/alternative central heating.

title: Ordinary Least Squares Regression for modelling Green Central Heating in Census 2021
text:
9 Enhancing the ‘Best’ Model (Polynomials)

9.1 Rationale for Choosing Polynomial Predictors
To evaluate whether non-linear effects can further enhance Model 2 IS (Instruction #10), we consider the three techniques taught in the module: data transformation, polynomial regression, and piecewise regression. We choose polynomial regression—adding a quadratic term \beta_2 X^2 via I(X^2)—because it captures smooth non-linear curvature within an OLS framework while keeping the outcome variable Green_Central_Heating in its natural, directly interpretable percentage units.


9.2 Exploratory Bivariate Linear vs. Quadratic Fit
Before adding quadratic terms to the full interaction model, we can visually compare a bivariate linear fit (~ Owned) against a quadratic term (~ I(Owned^2)):


Compare linear vs quadratic bivariate fits using grid.arrange
m1_exp <- lm(Green_Central_Heating ~ Owned, data = census_copy)
census_copy$predicted_gch_linear <- predict(m1_exp)

g1 <- ggplot(data = census_copy) +
  geom_point(aes(y = Green_Central_Heating, x = Owned), colour = "red", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_line(aes(y = predicted_gch_linear, x = Owned), colour = "blue", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.9) +
  ggtitle("Linear: ~ Owned") +
  xlab("Owned (%)") +
  ylab("Green Central Heating (%)") +
  theme_classic()

m2_exp <- lm(Green_Central_Heating ~ I(Owned^2), data = census_copy)
census_copy$predicted_gch_quad <- predict(m2_exp)

g2 <- ggplot(data = census_copy) +
  geom_point(aes(y = Green_Central_Heating, x = Owned), colour = "red", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_line(aes(y = predicted_gch_quad, x = Owned), colour = "blue", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.9) +
  ggtitle("Quadratic: ~ I(Owned^2)") +
  xlab("Owned (%)") +
  ylab("Green Central Heating (%)") +
  theme_classic()

grid.arrange(g1, g2, ncol = 2)








Figure 5: Exploratory comparison of a linear fit (left) vs. quadratic term I(Owned^2) (right) for Green Central Heating against Owned.







9.3 Evaluating Candidate Polynomial Models (M1–M4, Table 6 & Table 7)

M1: model2i + I(Owned^2)
M2: model2i + I(Detached^2)
M3: model2i + I(Full_Time_Employee^2)
M4: model2i + I(No_Central_Heating^2)

)

title: Ordinary Least Squares Regression for modelling Green Central Heating in Census 2021
text:
10 Assessment of the Final Model
In accordance with Instruction #12(a)–(d), we assess our final preferred model (M2) across four diagnostic and interpretive dimensions:

Normality of Residuals (skew and density plot)
Homoscedasticity (spreadLevelPlot and Breusch-Pagan ncvTest)
Multicollinearity (\text{VIF}) and Independence of Errors (durbinWatsonTest)
Relative Importance of Predictors (adequacy_lm) and Real-World Interpretation


10.1 10.1 Model Errors Distribution (Normality of Residuals — Figure 4)


Compute residual skewness and plot residual density (Figure 4) for M2
skew_M2_resid <- skew(M2$residuals)
cat("skew(M2$residuals):", skew_M2_resid, "\n")


skew(M2$residuals): 0.9542924 


Compute residual skewness and plot residual density (Figure 4) for M2
ggplot(data = M2) +
  geom_density(aes(x = .resid), fill = "black") +
  xlab("Model Errors (.resid)") +
  ylab("Density") +
  theme_classic()








Figure 6: Figure 4 – Model Errors (.resid) vs Density for Final Model M2.





Interpretation of Figure 4: Model residuals (e_i = Y_i - \hat{Y}_i) are centred near zero with a skewness of 0.9542924. Because |\text{skew}(e_i)| < 1, the residual distribution satisfies the course threshold for approximate normality, substantially reducing the raw outcome skewness of 1.73. A mild positive tail remains on the right, indicating that a few extreme rural districts have higher green central heating than predicted by the model.


10.2 10.2 Homoscedasticity (Constant Error Variance — Figure 5 & ncvTest)
We test the assumption of constant error variance (\text{Var}(\varepsilon_i) = \sigma^2) visually via car::spreadLevelPlot(M2) (Figure 5) and formally via the Breusch-Pagan / Cook-Weisberg Non-Constant Variance Score Test (car::ncvTest(M2)), where the null hypothesis (H_0) is constant error variance (homoscedasticity) and the alternative hypothesis (H_1) is that error variance changes systematically with the fitted values (heteroscedasticity):


Plot Figure 5: spreadLevelPlot(M2) and run ncvTest(M2)
spreadLevelPlot(M2)



Suggested power transformation:  -1.066471 








Figure 7: Figure 5 – Constant Error Variance vs Fitted values (Spread-Level Plot for Final Model M2).







Run Non-Constant Variance Score Test ncvTest(M2)
ncvTest(M2)


Non-constant Variance Score Test 
Variance formula: ~ fitted.values 
Chisquare = 38.16122, Df = 1, p = 6.5134e-10


Interpretation of Figure 5 and ncvTest(M2): In Figure 5, the dashed reference line slopes upward from left to right and the solid magenta smoother curves across the left and middle of the plot, indicating that the spread of the studentized residuals increases as the predicted values of Green_Central_Heating increase. Formally, ncvTest(M2) yields \chi^2 = 38.16122 (\text{df} = 1) with p = 6.5134 \times 10^{-10} \ll 0.05. Because p < 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis of constant error variance and conclude that the model exhibits statistically significant heteroscedasticity (error variance is larger in high-adoption rural districts than in low-adoption urban districts).
How this breach of homoscedasticity can be addressed (Instruction #12b):

Power / Box-Cox Transformation of the Outcome Variable: spreadLevelPlot(M2) suggests a stabilising power transformation of \lambda = -1.066471 (approximately an inverse transformation Y^{-1}, or a logarithmic transformation \log(Y)) to compress the right tail and stabilise error variance.
Heteroscedasticity-Consistent (HC3) Robust Standard Errors: Computing White’s heteroscedasticity-robust standard errors (car::hccm(M2)) provides valid t-tests and confidence intervals without altering the original percentage scale of Green_Central_Heating.
Weighted Least Squares (WLS): Weighting districts inversely to their estimated error variance.



10.3 10.3 Multicollinearity (\text{VIF}) & Independence of Errors (Durbin-Watson)
We evaluate multicollinearity among the four core continuous predictors using the Variance Inflation Factor (\text{VIF}_j = \frac{1}{1 - R_j^2}) on model2, and test for residual autocorrelation using durbinWatsonTest(M2):


Check Variance Inflation Factors (vif) on model2 and Durbin-Watson autocorrelation on M2
vif_values <- vif(model2) %>% round(2)
vif_mean   <- mean(vif(model2)) %>% round(1)

cat("VIF for each main predictor in model2:\n")


VIF for each main predictor in model2:


Check Variance Inflation Factors (vif) on model2 and Durbin-Watson autocorrelation on M2
print(vif_values)


Full_Time_Employee           Detached No_Central_Heating              Owned 
              1.13               2.61               1.31               2.90 


Check Variance Inflation Factors (vif) on model2 and Durbin-Watson autocorrelation on M2
cat("\nMean VIF:", vif_mean, "\n\n")



Mean VIF: 2 


Check Variance Inflation Factors (vif) on model2 and Durbin-Watson autocorrelation on M2
set.seed(123)
durbinWatsonTest(M2)


 lag Autocorrelation D-W Statistic p-value
   1       0.2997139      1.399649       0
 Alternative hypothesis: rho != 0


Interpretation of Multicollinearity and Independence Diagnostics:

Multicollinearity (vif(model2)): All individual Variance Inflation Factors are well below the warning threshold of 5 (Full_Time_Employee = 1.13, No_Central_Heating = 1.31, Detached = 2.61, Owned = 2.90), with a mean \text{VIF} of 2.0, confirming no problematic multicollinearity among the four main predictors.
Independence of Errors (durbinWatsonTest(M2)): The Durbin-Watson statistic is 1.444645 with a lag-1 residual autocorrelation of 0.2771037 (p = 0.000 < 0.05). Rejecting H_0: \rho = 0 indicates positive autocorrelation among adjacent districts in the dataset, reflecting geographic clustering across regions. This breach could be remedied by incorporating regional fixed effects (e.g., Region or Super_Region) or estimating a spatial / multilevel regression model.



10.4 10.4 Relative Importance of Predictors (Adequacy — Figure 6)
To evaluate the relative importance of the predictors in our final model (Instruction #12c), we use adequacy_lm(M2) from Session_10_functions.R. In OLS regression, Adequacy is defined as the R^2 of a single-predictor model divided by the R^2 of the full model (58.52\%), measuring the percentage of the full model’s explanatory power captured by each main or polynomial predictor on its own (noting that adequacy_lm() evaluates main and polynomial terms individually and excludes multiplicative interaction terms):
\text{Adequacy}_j (\%) = \left( \frac{R^2_{\text{single predictor } j}}{R^2_{\text{full model}}} \right) \times 100


Compute adequacy_lm(M2) and display adequacy table
variable_adequacy_OLS <- adequacy_lm(M2)

variable_adequacy_OLS %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 2))) %>%
  kable(
    col.names = c("Model / Predictor", "Single-Predictor R-squared (%)", "Adequacy (% of Full Model R-squared)"),
    caption = "Relative Importance of Predictors in Final Model M2 (adequacy_lm; Source: Calculations Based on Census 2021 Dataset)"
  )

Interpretation of Figure 6:

I(Detached^2) (54.03\% adequacy, single-predictor R^2 = 31.62\%) and Detached (46.03\% adequacy, single-predictor R^2 = 26.94\%) are by far the most powerful individual predictors of green central heating adoption—the quadratic detached-housing term alone accounts for more than half (54\%) of the explanatory power of the full model.
Full_Time_Employee (38.52\% adequacy, single-predictor R^2 = 22.54\%) is the next most important standalone predictor.
No_Central_Heating (11.67\% adequacy, R^2 = 6.83\%) and Owned (6.24\% adequacy, R^2 = 3.65\%) have smaller standalone adequacy values because their primary explanatory contribution operates conditionally through their strong multiplicative interactions with Detached and with each other.



10.5 10.5 Real-World Interpretation: What the Model Reveals About the UK (Instruction #12d)
Our final model (M2, explaining 58.52\% of the district-level variation across England and Wales) reveals four key insights into the real-world geography of residential green central heating in 2021:

The Rural & Off-Gas-Grid Housing Effect (Detached, I(Detached^2), and No_Central_Heating): Dwelling morphology (Detached and I(Detached^2)) is the single strongest determinant of green central heating adoption (54.03\% adequacy). Moreover, the positive interaction between Detached and No_Central_Heating (Figure 2) shows that green central heating uptake is concentrated in rural, low-density districts where detached homes are off the UK’s mains natural-gas grid. In urban districts dominated by flats and terraced housing, a lack of central heating does not lead to green central heating adoption; in rural detached-housing districts off the gas grid, households rely heavily on renewable heat pumps, biomass boilers, communal heat networks, or tank/bottled gas.
The Enabling Role of Homeownership (Owned Interactions): While Owned has a modest standalone correlation (r = 0.191, adequacy = 6.24\%), its positive interactions with Detached (Figure 1, crossover at 36.5\% detached) and No_Central_Heating highlight a critical tenure divide: in districts with detached, off-grid housing stock, owner-occupation substantially accelerates green heating adoption. Homeowners have the property rights and long-term financial horizon required to invest in alternative heating systems, whereas private and social rented sectors face split-incentive barriers.
Urban Labour Markets vs. Rural Demographics (Full_Time_Employee and Age_Profile): Full_Time_Employee is negatively associated with Green_Central_Heating (\beta = -0.0806^{**}, Figure 3). However, our Narrative modelling (Table 2) demonstrated that nearly half of the initial bivariate effect of Full_Time_Employee is explained away once we control for housing morphology (Detached), heating infrastructure (No_Central_Heating), tenure (Owned), and demographic ageing (Age_Profile). Urban commuter districts with younger, full-time working populations are overwhelmingly connected to the mains gas grid, whereas older, rural districts lead in non-mains/green central heating adoption.
Policy Implications: To achieve broad residential decarbonisation across the UK, climate and energy policy cannot rely solely on off-grid rural homeowners installing heat pumps or biomass in detached houses. Policymakers must address the urban mains-gas and rented housing sectors—expanding district heat networks for high-density flats, providing targeted grants for lower-income urban authorities, and introducing regulatory incentives to overcome landlord-tenant split incentives.

title: Spatial and Temporal Population Trends in the Liverpool City Region
text:
The Liverpool City Region (LCR) is a Combined Authority located in the North-West of the United Kingdom (53.402^\circ\text{N}, 2.977^\circ\text{W}), covering a land extent of approximately 726\text{ km}^2. It comprises six Local Authority Districts:

Liverpool (E08000012) — the metropolitan core (31\% of the regional population)
Wirral (E08000015) — peninsular district across the River Mersey (21\%)
Sefton (E08000014) — coastal corridor extending north to Southport (18\%)
St. Helens (E08000013) — eastern industrial and commuter district (12\%)
Knowsley (E08000011) — suburban and industrial belt bordering Liverpool (10\%)
Halton (E06000006) — Runcorn and Widnes straddling the upper Mersey estuary (8\%)

Together, the six districts support a residential population of over 1.5 million residents and more than 37,000 active businesses (Christie, 2013). In Geographic Information Science (GIScience), representing such complex socio-spatial systems requires distinguishing between where people live at night (Residential Lower Layer Super Output Areas, LSOAs) and where people work during the day (Workplace Zones, WZs), as well as tracking how population redistributes over multi-decadal timescales.
This study reproduces the complete GIS workflow originally conducted in QGIS using reproducible Python (GeoPandas, Rasterio, Matplotlib), examining:

Workplace (Day-Time) Population & Density (2011) alongside Major Employers (hospitals, ports, docks, universities, and airports).
Residential (Night-Time) Population & Density (2011) and potential daily commute corridors connecting high-density residential neighbourhoods to employment hubs.
Multi-Decadal Population Change (1991–2011) using 1\text{ km} \times 1\text{ km} gridded raster surfaces from the UK Data Service PopChange project.
Socio-Economic Structure (Approximated Social Grade) across Workplace Zones (Professional, Semi-Skilled, and Skilled Manual).

text:
2. Understanding the Geospatial File Formats (.gpkg vs. .shp 6-File Sets)
All required spatial datasets for this assignment are stored in the project data repository at data/data_python/stPopLCR/. Two primary vector formats are used alongside ASCII raster grids (.asc):

GeoPackage (.gpkg): An open OGC single-file SQLite container (LCR_boundaries.gpkg and LCR_LSOA2021.gpkg) that stores vector geometries, spatial indexes, Coordinate Reference System (CRS) definitions (EPSG:27700, OSGB 1936 / British National Grid), and untruncated attribute tables inside a single self-contained file.
ESRI Shapefile (.shp + 5 companion files = 6 files per layer): Every boundary and thematic shapefile consists of six coordinated files sharing the same basename:

.shp — Primary feature geometry (polygons/points in British National Grid metres).
.shx — Positional shape index allowing fast record seeking.
.dbf — dBASE attribute table storing census counts, densities, and classifications.
.prj — Projection / CRS definition in Well-Known Text (OSGB36 / British National Grid).
.cpg — Character encoding specification (UTF-8).
.qmd — QGIS XML metadata and layer styling catalog.
