Thematic Analysis
Dataset & Source
Spatial Unit
Classification Method
Cartographic Rationale




Day-Time Population
CDRC 2011 Census Workplace Data Pack (WP201EW) & OS VectorMap District (FunctionalSite)
Workplace Zones (WZs)
Natural Breaks (Jenks, 6 classes)
Workplace counts have an extreme right-skewed range (113\text{–}5,754); Jenks minimises within-class variance and maximises between-class contrast.


Day-Time Density
CDRC 2011 Workplace Zones (WorkPop / Area_ha)
Workplace Zones (WZs)
Equal Count (Quantiles, 5 classes)
Treating density as an ordinal categorical variable (Very Low to Very High) allows direct rank-order comparison against residential density.


Night-Time Population
CDRC 2011 Census Residential Data Pack (KS102EW)
LSOAs (2011)
Natural Breaks (Jenks, 6 classes)
Captures skewed residential population counts (988\text{–}3,552) and isolates extreme institutional/student clusters (\text{Pop} > 3,000).


Night-Time Density
CDRC 2011 Residential LSOAs (Pop2011 / Area_ha)
LSOAs (2011)
Equal Count (Quantiles, 5 classes)
Ordinal quantile classification highlights top-tier residential concentrations (\text{Density} > 73\text{ persons/ha}) to trace commute flows.


1991–2011 Pop Change
UK Data Service PopChange 1\text{ km} Grids (TP91Bs & URPopAll)
1\text{ km} \times 1\text{ km} Raster Cells
Equal Interval (5 classes)
Divides the net change range into ordinal growth/decline tiers (Very Negative to Very Positive) to pinpoint urban regeneration clusters.


Social Grade
CDRC 2011 Workplace Table WP613EW (Approximated Social Grade)
Workplace Zones (WZs)
Equal Interval (3 classes)
Partitions workplace zones into Skilled Manual, Semi-Skilled, and Professional occupational profiles.

5. Residential (Night-Time) Population & Density Analysis

5.1 Figure 3: Residential (Night-Time) Population Distribution (2011)
Residential Lower Layer Super Output Areas (LSOAs) are constructed so that each neighbourhood contains an average of 1,500 residents (typically 400 to 1,200 households). Across the Liverpool City Region, total residential population in 2011 is 1,506,940, compared with 987,210 in Workplace Zones — indicating a maximum difference of 519,730 residents (accounting for non-working dependents, retirees, students, and out-commuters).
Using Natural Breaks (Jenks) across 6 classes (988–1306, 1306–1479, 1479–1668, 1668–1955, 1955–2451, 2451–3552), Figure 3 highlights in red the highest-population LSOAs (\text{Population} > 3,000) around the Royal Liverpool University Hospital and University of Liverpool (UoL) campus (LSOA E01033768 / student accommodation corridor).

6.1 Figure 5: Gridded Population Change (1\text{ km} \times 1\text{ km}) Between 1991 and 2011

Key Findings & Methodological Conclusions

Major Employment Hubs: Daytime employment in the LCR is heavily anchored by major institutional and transport sites, including the Port of Liverpool, Liverpool Docks, Liverpool John Lennon Airport, Liverpool John Moores University, and major NHS hospitals (Arrowe Park, Whiston, Aintree, Broadgreen, St Helens, and Halton General).
Daytime vs. Nighttime Contrasts & Commute Patterns: Total daytime workplace population across the LCR is 987,210 compared to a nighttime residential population of 1,506,940 (a difference of 519,730, reflecting both non-working residents and net out-commuting). Comparing high-density residential clusters (\text{Density} > 73\text{ persons/ha} in Sefton Park/Wavertree, Bebington, New Brighton/Egremont, and Stockbridge Village) with high-density workplace clusters (\text{Density} > 51\text{ workers/ha} in Liverpool City Centre and Birkenhead) highlights primary daily commuting bottlenecks along the Queensway Tunnel, Edge Lane, and Liverpool Road.
Divergent Regional vs. National Demographic Trends (1991–2011): While the National Mean population density increased from 223.10 to 246.20\text{ persons/km}^2 between 1991 and 2011, the LCR Mean declined slightly from 2087.17 to 2065.31\text{ persons/km}^2 due to suburban and post-industrial population shrinkage across outer districts—strongly counterbalanced by intense urban core re-densification in Liverpool City Centre, Wavertree, Litherland, Sutton, New Boston, and Widnes.
GIScience Limitations (MAUP & Classification Sensitivity): Direct overlay comparison between Daytime and Nighttime populations is constrained by the Modifiable Areal Unit Problem (MAUP) because Workplace Zones (431 in Liverpool) and Residential LSOAs (298 in Liverpool) have non-nested geometries. Furthermore, choropleth interpretation is sensitive to the choice of classification scheme (Jenks vs. Quantiles vs. Equal Interval).

title: Retail Site Selection & Catchment Analysis for a New C-Store with Click & Collect in Liverpool
text:
The rapid growth of e-commerce and hybrid Click & Collect (C&C) grocery fulfilment has transformed urban retail location strategy. Rather than relying solely on large out-of-town superstores, major UK grocery retailers increasingly deploy neighbourhood convenience stores (c-stores) equipped with Click & Collect facilities to capture time-poor commuters, small urban households, and digitally engaged neighbourhoods.
In this assignment, we conduct a multi-stage GIS site-selection analysis across Liverpool (E08000012, 298 LSOAs) to identify the optimal location for a new Marks & Spencer (M&S) convenience store with a Click & Collect (C&C) facility. Originally developed across QGIS, ArcGIS Pro (Network Analyst), and R, the entire spatial workflow and cartographic output series (map1 through map6) are reproduced here directly from the underlying shapefiles in Python.

text:
4 Stage 1: Demand Screening — Online Grocery Shopping & Deprivation

4.1 Map 1: Online Grocery Shopping Prevalence Across Liverpool LSOAs (IUC 2018)
The Consumer Data Research Centre (CDRC) 2018 Internet User Classification (IUC 2018) segments Great Britain neighbourhoods into 10 distinct digital engagement profiles using Small Area Estimation (SAE) and gradient-boosted decision trees trained on British Population Survey (BPS) online shopping transactions, Ofcom broadband infrastructure, and ONS Census demographics.
Based on each IUC group’s Buy Groceries Online propensity z-score in the CDRC User Guide, Liverpool’s 298 LSOAs are classified into four ordinal Online Grocery Shopping Prevalence tiers (OrdinalTes):

High Prevalence (4, Blue Hatching ///): e-Cultural Creators (GRP 1, z = +1.6), e-Professionals (GRP 2, z = +1.4), e-Veterans (GRP 3, z = +0.9), and e-Rational Utilitarians (GRP 5, z = +0.65) — 61 LSOAs (20.5\%).
Moderate Prevalence (3, Green Hatching ///): e-Mainstream (GRP 6, z = +0.05) — 38 LSOAs (12.8\%).
Low Prevalence (2, Orange Hatching ///): Digital Seniors (GRP 8, z = -0.10) and Settled Offline Communities (GRP 9, z = -0.35) — 8 LSOAs (2.7\%).
Very Low Prevalence (1, Red Hatching ///): Youthful Urban Fringe (GRP 4, z = -0.45), Passive and Uncommitted Users (GRP 7, z = -0.45), and e-Withdrawn (GRP 10, z = -1.60) — 191 LSOAs (64.1\%).

4.2 Map 2: Overlaying Deprivation (IMD 2019) with Online Grocery Shopping Prevalence
A new Marks & Spencer C-Store with Click & Collect requires a catchment that is not only digitally engaged (High Prevalence) but also economically affluent enough to sustain premium convenience expenditure. In Map 2, we classify the English Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD 2019) Rank across Liverpool (1 = most deprived in England, 32,844 = least deprived) into three tiers:

More Deprived (Rank 10 – 1,416, Solid Red): Severely deprived neighbourhoods concentrated in north Liverpool (Kirkdale, Everton, Anfield, Walton) and outer social housing estates (Speke, Norris Green).
Moderate (Rank 1,416 – 15,000, Salmon Pink): Transitional middle-income urban neighbourhoods.
More Affluent (Rank 15,000 – 31,562, White): Affluent suburban and waterfront neighbourhoods (Allerton Road, Mossley Hill, Childwall, Woolton, Wavertree, and Liverpool City Centre Waterfront).

Overlaying the hatched Online Grocery Shopping Prevalence layer reveals a striking spatial inverse correlation: High Online Grocery Shopping Prevalence (blue hatching over white/pink background) clusters tightly in south-central and central Liverpool around the Allerton Road, Smithdown Road, Woolton, and City Centre corridors, as well as an affluent pocket north of Old Swan.

6.1 Map 6: Optimal Site Selection & Euclidean Fixed Buffers vs. Network Drive-Distance Buffers
Synthesising the demand and supply surfaces from Maps 1–5 identifies an unserved, high-potential gap in Childwall / Wavertree / North Allerton at British National Grid coordinates E: 340,650.3, N: 388,487.1 (near the Queens Drive A5058 / Childwall Valley Road arterial intersection):

Strong Online Grocery Demand & Affluence: Located directly inside a contiguous cluster of High Online Grocery Shopping Prevalence (IUC 2018 e-Veterans and e-Professionals) and Low Deprivation / High Affluence (IMD 2019 Rank > 15,000).
High Daytime & Small-Household Demand: Positioned along a high-daytime-population and moderate-to-high 1–2 person household density corridor.
Zero Internal Cannibalisation: Situated 3.6\text{ km} south of M&S Fincham (L12 2AP), 5.8\text{ km} east of M&S Central Liverpool (L1 1JD), and 6.9\text{ km} north-west of M&S Speke (L24 1YD).
Realistic Road-Network Catchment Gap: While simple Euclidean circular buffers (500\text{ m} for C-Stores and 1,500\text{ m} for Supermarkets) overestimate accessibility across railway lines, parks, and cul-de-sacs, computing Road-Network Drive-Distance Buffers along RoadLiv.shp (18,171 road links) reveals that the competing Tesco Allerton Road and Sainsbury’s Woolton 1,500\text{ m} network service areas contract substantially, leaving our new M&S site (Location 69, network service area = 566,250\text{ m}^2) with an uncontested local catchment.

text:
8 Key Conclusions & Strategic Recommendations

Optimal M&S Click & Collect Location: The selected site at E: 340,650.3, N: 388,487.1 (Wavertree / Childwall / North Allerton border) sits at the nexus of Liverpool’s most affluent, digitally engaged residential suburbs (e-Veterans and e-Professionals, IMD Rank > 18,000) while maintaining high arterial road visibility and workplace accessibility.
Avoidance of Cannibalisation & Direct Superstore Overlap: The site is completely separated from Marks & Spencer’s three existing Liverpool stores (L1 1JD City Centre, L12 2AP Fincham, and L24 1YD Speke) and lies outside the 1,500\text{ m} road-network drive-distance service areas of both competing Click & Collect supermarkets (Tesco Allerton Road and Sainsbury’s Woolton).
Superiority of Network Drive-Distance over Euclidean Buffers: Whereas a 500\text{ m} Euclidean circle covers 78.5\text{ ha} (785,398\text{ m}^2) by assuming isotropic straight-line travel across barriers, the 500\text{ m} Road-Network Service Area covers 56.63\text{ ha} (566,250\text{ m}^2 — a 27.9\% reduction), accurately reflecting real street connectivity and physical barriers.
